q: An orders API handles 2,000 concurrent requests, each mostly waiting for PostgreSQL. What does Node use while those requests wait?
options: One thread per request, taken from a large internal pool
The libuv thread pool, one of its 4 threads per database query
The operating system's asynchronous socket APIs; the main thread only runs a callback when data arrives
A separate event loop per open connection
explain: Database connections are network sockets, and libuv watches them through epoll, kqueue or IOCP without a thread per connection. The main thread runs a callback only when a socket has data. The thread pool is the tempting answer, but it serves fs, dns.lookup, async crypto and zlib, not sockets: with only 4 threads it could not hold 2,000 waiting queries.

q: In which phase of the event loop do setImmediate callbacks run?
options: The timers phase, right after the timeouts that are due
The check phase, right after the poll phase
The poll phase, together with I/O callbacks
Before the loop starts, like process.nextTick
explain: setImmediate callbacks have their own phase, check, which comes right after poll. That is why "immediate" really means "after this round of I/O". process.nextTick is not a phase at all: its queue is drained after every callback.

q: Which of these operations waits for a libuv thread pool thread?
options: Reading the body of an incoming HTTP request
A query sent over an open PostgreSQL connection
A setTimeout(fn, 100) callback
fs.promises.readFile('./invoice.pdf')
explain: File system calls, in callback or promise style, run on the thread pool because there is no portable asynchronous file API. Request bodies and database queries travel over sockets, which use the OS asynchronous APIs, and timers live in the loop itself.

q: What is true about the libuv thread pool size?
options: It equals the number of CPU cores, detected at startup
It is 4 by default and is set with the UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE environment variable when the process starts
It grows on demand up to 1024 threads
It is 4 per worker thread, so each worker brings its own pool
explain: The default is 4 regardless of cores, and UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE (maximum 1024) changes it at startup. The libuv documentation says the pool is global and shared across all event loops, so worker threads share it rather than bringing their own.

q: A handler spends 600 ms of CPU building a report. A colleague makes the builder function async. What changes for the other requests in the same process?
options: Nothing: the 600 ms still run on the main thread and still block them
They are no longer blocked, because async functions run on the thread pool
They are blocked only half as long, because await splits the work
They are no longer blocked, because V8 runs async functions on another core
explain: An async function runs synchronously until its first await, and a CPU loop has nothing to await, so the work stays on the main thread. Measured on Node 24: a 10 ms timer fired after about 400 ms while an async function with no await was computing. The thread pool never runs your JavaScript.

q: On Node 24 with default flags, a promise rejects and no code handles it. What happens?
options: A warning is printed and the process keeps running
The rejection is silently ignored
The rejection is retried on the next turn of the loop
The error is printed and the process exits with code 1
explain: Since Node 15 the default mode is --unhandled-rejections=throw: the rejection is raised as an uncaught exception, and with no handler the process exits with code 1 (verified on Node 24). Printing a warning and continuing was the behaviour before Node 15.

q: In what order are the lines printed?
options: timer, sync done, sum done
sync done, timer, sum done
sync done, sum done, timer
sum done, sync done, timer
explain: sumUpTo has no await, so the whole loop runs synchronously before sync done is logged. Its result is delivered in a microtask, which runs before the loop reaches the timers phase, so sum done beats the timer, which fired late (about 400 ms instead of 10, measured). "async" never means "on another thread".

q: On a 16-core server with default settings, you start 8 crypto.pbkdf2 calls at once, each needing about 250 ms of CPU. When does the last one finish?
options: After about 250 ms: there are enough cores for all eight
After about 500 ms: they run in two waves of four
After about 2 seconds: they run one by one on the main thread
After about 250 ms, but the main thread is blocked meanwhile
explain: Asynchronous pbkdf2 runs on the libuv pool, which has 4 threads regardless of cores, so eight jobs run in two waves (measured on Node 24: four finished together, the other four about one hash-duration later). With UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=8 all eight finished together. The main thread stays free throughout.

q: During login peaks (asynchronous password hashing), calls to a partner API by hostname become slow, while CPU sits at 40%. The partner says its latency is normal. What is the most likely cause?
options: The hashes block the main thread, so responses are read late
The partner API rate-limits you during your peaks
fetch opens a new thread per call and the OS runs out of threads
fetch resolves the hostname with dns.lookup, which queues on the thread pool behind the hashes
explain: Asynchronous pbkdf2 or scrypt occupy the 4 pool threads, and dns.lookup, used by fetch and http.request by default, waits for one. Measured on Node 24: with the pool busy, fetch to localhost waited for the hashes while fetch to 127.0.0.1 returned at once. The main thread is not blocked, since async hashing runs on the pool.

q: A nightly import runs Promise.all over 1,000 fs.promises.readFile calls with default settings. What really happens?
options: The OS reads all 1,000 files in parallel through its asynchronous file API
At most 4 reads run at once on the thread pool; the rest wait in its queue
They run one after another on the main thread
Node starts 1,000 threads, one per read
explain: File system calls use the libuv pool, 4 threads by default, so 996 requests queue behind the first four. That queue also delays dns.lookup and async crypto for the rest of the process, which is why you bound the concurrency yourself (for example 10 to 20 files at a time) instead of firing everything.

q: What happens when this code runs?
options: The worker dies silently and the main thread prints "main still alive"
The main thread receives the error as a normal message
Node restarts the worker automatically
The error is emitted as an 'error' event on the Worker; with no listener, the whole process exits with code 1
explain: An uncaught error ends the worker and is emitted as 'error' on the Worker object, and an 'error' event with no listener throws. Measured on Node 24: the process exited with code 1 before the timer fired. A worker pool must listen for 'error', reject the job and replace the worker; Piscina does this for you.

q: In code review you find this handler. What is the problem?
options: It keeps serving from an unknown state; it should log at fatal level and exit so the orchestrator restarts the process
It should also catch unhandled rejections, then keep serving
logger.error is too slow; console.error would be fine
It must be registered inside every request handler to work
explain: Node's documentation says it is not safe to resume normal operation after uncaughtException: connections, locks or half-written state may be broken. Log (pino's fatal flushes synchronously), exit with code 1, and let Kubernetes restart the pod. Adding a rejection handler that also continues makes the same mistake twice.

q: What does the last line print?
options: [1, 2, 3]
[1]
[]
It depends on how fast save is
explain: forEach calls the async callback and ignores the promise it returns, so the log runs before any save finishes. Measured: [], then [1, 2, 3] a moment later. Even a very fast save resolves after the current synchronous code, so the answer does not depend on timing.

q: The API gateway, the Orders API and its HTTP client each make up to 4 attempts (1 + 3 retries) on failure. The payment provider is down. How many calls can one customer request send to it?
explain: Retries multiply: each of the 4 gateway attempts triggers 4 Orders API attempts, each triggering 4 client attempts, so 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. That is why the SRE book recommends retrying at one layer only, and returning a "do not retry" signal upward.

q: Your team adopts a retry budget of 10% per client, as in Google's SRE book. What does it change during a widespread outage?
options: Each request gets at most 10% of its timeout for retries
Retries stop once they exceed 10% of the client's requests, so extra load stays near 1.1× instead of nearly 3×
Only 10% of requests are allowed to fail before an alert fires
Retries are delayed by 10% more after each attempt
explain: The budget is a ratio of retries to requests per client: past 10%, failures go back to the caller without retrying. The SRE book combines it with at most 3 attempts per request and says it reduces the growth to about 1.1×. A per-request limit alone still allows nearly 3× the load when everything fails.

q: With cockatiel, the payments policy is wrap(retry(…, { maxAttempts: 3 }), circuitBreaker(…), timeout(2_000, TimeoutStrategy.Aggressive)). What does the 2-second timeout apply to?
options: To each attempt, because the first policy in wrap is the outermost
To the three attempts together
Only to the first attempt
To the time the circuit stays open
explain: The cockatiel docs define wrap(a, b, c) as a.execute(() => b.execute(() => c.execute(fn))), so the timeout is innermost and restarts for every attempt. To bound the whole operation, put a timeout outside the retry as well, or pass a deadline signal to execute.

q: In an ES module on Node 24, loadOrders resolves after 100 ms and loadInvoices rejects after 10 ms. What happens?
options: It prints "caught …" after 100 ms
The rejection is silently ignored
It prints "caught …" after 10 ms
The process exits with code 1 before the try runs
explain: While the code waits on orders, invoices rejects with no handler attached yet. Node treats it as an unhandled rejection and exits with code 1; measured, nothing was printed. await Promise.all([loadOrders(), loadInvoices()]) attaches handlers to both and the same code is caught normally.

q: Checkout calls auditLog.write(event) without awaiting it, to keep the response fast. A colleague proposes void auditLog.write(event) to satisfy no-floating-promises. What do you answer?
options: Fine: void handles the rejection
Better to await it, since fire-and-forget is never acceptable
Disable the rule for this file, since audit writes rarely fail
void silences the rule but a rejection still crashes the process; attach a .catch that logs it
explain: The rule's docs warn that voiding a promise does not handle it or change runtime behaviour, and an unhandled rejection exits the process. A .catch that logs keeps the response fast and makes failures visible. Fire-and-forget is acceptable when its failure is handled and the work is not critical.

q: writable.write(chunk) returns false. What does it mean?
options: The chunk was dropped and must be written again
The stream is closed and will reject further writes
The buffer has reached its highWaterMark: the chunk is queued, and you should stop writing until 'drain'
An error happened and an 'error' event will follow
explain: The chunk is accepted and buffered; false is a request to pause. Measured with a mark of 10 bytes: writes of 5, 5 and 1 bytes returned true, false, false, and 'drain' fired once the buffer was empty. Nothing is dropped, which is exactly why ignoring the signal fills memory.

q: On Node 24.11, what is the default highWaterMark of fs.createReadStream(path)?
options: 16 KiB
64 KiB
1 MiB
16 objects
explain: Measured: readableHighWaterMark is 65,536 for file read streams. The general default for byte streams (including fs.createWriteStream) is 16 KiB, and 16 objects is the object-mode default, which is why 16 KiB is the tempting wrong answer.

q: With its defaults, what does new Upload({ client, params: { Bucket, Key, Body: stream } }).done() do with a 22 MiB catalogue stream?
options: It reads the whole stream into memory, then sends one PutObject
It starts a multipart upload, sends 5 MiB parts with up to 4 in flight, then completes the upload
It sends 22 parts of 1 MiB, one after the other
It writes the stream to a temporary file, then uploads the file
explain: Measured against a fake S3: CreateMultipartUpload, parts of 5, 5, 5, 5 and 2 MiB, then CompleteMultipartUpload. partSize defaults to 5 MiB (the S3 minimum) and queueSize to 4, so memory stays around 20 MiB per upload. Only a body smaller than one part became a single PutObject.

q: The Orders API lets the accounting firm download monthly invoice archives of up to 2 GB, often over slow connections. What happens with this route?
options: The file is read at the speed of the client
res.write throws once the client falls behind
Chunks are dropped when the client cannot keep up
The return value of write is ignored, so unsent data piles up in the response buffer, up to the whole file
explain: Measured with a 31 MiB source and a slow destination: the destination buffered 31.3 MiB, the entire input, against 16 KiB with pipeline. Nothing is dropped and nothing throws, which is what makes the bug invisible until memory runs out. Fix: await pipeline(file, res).

q: Which call to write is the first to return false?
options: The 1st, because 1 MB is already above 16 KiB
The 16th, because in object mode the mark counts objects (16 by default), so about 16 MB is buffered by then
None: object-mode streams have no backpressure
The 17th, because the mark is only exceeded after 16 objects
explain: Measured: the call at index 15, the 16th, returned false. In object mode highWaterMark counts objects whatever their size, so large rows can hold far more memory than the number suggests; lower the mark or batch smaller.

q: A fraud job scans for await (const row of Readable.from(readOrders())) and breaks at the first suspicious order. readOrders is an async generator that closes a cursor in its finally. What happens on break?
options: The stream is destroyed and the generator's finally runs, so the cursor is closed
The generator keeps running in the background until the query ends
The stream is paused and the cursor stays open until garbage collection
An ERR_STREAM_PREMATURE_CLOSE error is thrown out of the loop
explain: Measured: after break, stream.destroyed was true and the generator's finally had run. Leaving a for await loop early calls return() on the iterator, which destroys the stream; no error is thrown to the caller.

q: This Fastify route limits catalogue files to 20 MiB. A supplier uploads a 25 MiB file. What happens?
options: Fastify answers 413 before the upload starts
The route answers 201 and stores a 20 MiB truncated object; only part.file.truncated says so
request.file() throws RequestFileTooLargeError and nothing is uploaded
upload.done() rejects and the multipart upload is aborted
explain: Measured with @fastify/multipart 10.1.6: 201, a 20 MiB object completed in the bucket, and truncated set to true, with no error. When you stream the file yourself, the library's README tells you to listen to 'limit' or check truncated; destroying the stream on 'limit' made upload.done() reject and abort the multipart upload (measured).

q: The supplier portal, a browser app, will let suppliers upload product videos of up to 2 GB. The backend only needs to know where each video is stored. Which design do you propose?
options: The API returns a presigned PUT URL; the browser uploads straight to S3, and the API records the key afterwards
The API streams the multipart body into Upload from @aws-sdk/lib-storage
The API reads each video with toBuffer() and sends one PutObject
The browser sends base64 chunks in JSON requests that the API reassembles
explain: When the server does nothing with the bytes, they should not pass through it: no memory, bandwidth or request timeout spent on 2 GB bodies. Streaming into Upload is the right choice only when the server must scan, transform or encrypt the content, or the client cannot talk to S3. Buffering and base64 multiply memory use.

q: According to RFC 9110, which methods are idempotent?
options: GET and POST, because both are the most common methods
Only the safe methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE
PUT, DELETE and the safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE)
Every method except PATCH, which RFC 5789 excludes
explain: RFC 9110 §9.2.2: "PUT, DELETE, and safe request methods are idempotent." The tempting answer "every method except PATCH" forgets POST, which is neither safe nor idempotent; that is why POST /orders needs an idempotency key to be retried.

q: An order resource has status, shippingAddress and note. The app sends PUT /orders/ord_42 with only { "note": "leave at door" }. What does that request mean?
options: Replace the whole order with this body, so the omitted fields are reset or removed
Change the note and keep the other fields, exactly like a PATCH
Nothing: PUT can only create resources, so the server must answer 405
Append the note to the order history, because PUT is not idempotent
explain: PUT sends the complete new state of the resource at that URL; what you omit is not kept. Treating it like PATCH is the tempting misreading: to change one field, send PATCH with a JSON Merge Patch body (RFC 7396). PUT is idempotent, and it can create or replace.

q: A customer with a valid access token calls DELETE /products/prd_3, a route reserved for back-office staff. Which status fits?
options: 401 Unauthorized, with a WWW-Authenticate header
403 Forbidden: the caller is known but not allowed
400 Bad Request, because the request should not have been sent
409 Conflict, because the role conflicts with the operation
explain: The credentials are valid, so authentication succeeded; the refusal is about permission, which is 403. 401 is for missing or invalid credentials, and RFC 9110 requires it to carry a WWW-Authenticate challenge so the client can authenticate; sending 401 here would make the app log in again for nothing.

q: Customer A requests GET /orders/ord_99, which belongs to customer B. Which response does RFC 9110 explicitly allow in order not to reveal that the order exists?
options: 401 Unauthorized, so the client tries other credentials
200 with an empty object, so the client sees nothing
403 Forbidden, with a detail explaining the order belongs to someone else
404 Not Found, as if the order did not exist
explain: RFC 9110 §15.5.4 says a server that wishes to hide the existence of a forbidden resource MAY respond with 404. A 403 would confirm that ord_99 exists, which leaks information about other customers. A 200 with an empty body hides the error from every generic tool.

q: In an RFC 9457 problem, which member should the app's code use to decide how to react?
options: type, the URI that identifies the kind of problem
title, the short summary of the problem type
detail, the explanation of this occurrence
instance, the URI of this occurrence
explain: RFC 9457 says consumers MUST use the type URI as the primary identifier of the problem. detail is for humans and clients SHOULD NOT parse it; title is advisory text that may be localised. Machine-readable data goes in extension members.

q: An API answers HTTP 200 with the body {"type":"about:blank","title":"Not Found","status":404}. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: the status member in the body is what clients read
The type must be a real URL, never about:blank
The response line must carry the same status as the body; generic software only sees the 200
Problem bodies are only allowed with 5xx status codes
explain: RFC 9457: "Generators MUST use the same status code in the actual HTTP response." Caches, retry logic and monitoring never read the body, so they treat this failure as a success. about:blank is a valid type, and problems are used with any 4xx or 5xx code.

q: The app retries POST /orders with an Idempotency-Key it already used, but with a different amount. What does the IETF Idempotency-Key draft recommend?
options: Replay the response of the first request
422 Unprocessable Content, with a problem body
409 Conflict, as for a request still running
Run the new request and overwrite the stored response
explain: Draft -08 §2.7: reusing a key with a different payload SHOULD get 422. 409 is the answer for a retry while the original is still being processed. Replaying would hide a client bug: the app would believe the second order was created.

q: Orders d, c, b, a, newest first. Page 1 is LIMIT 2 OFFSET 0 and returns [d, c]. A new order e is created, then page 2 is fetched with LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2. What came back (measured on PostgreSQL 18)?
options: [b, a], because the offset ignores new rows
[a], because one row moved to page 1
[e, d], because new rows go to the end
[c, b], so c is shown twice
explain: Measured with PGlite: [c, b]. OFFSET counts rows, so a new row at the top shifts every row down by one and c appears on both pages. The keyset query WHERE (created_at, id) < (c's values) still returned [b, a].

q: Which change can ship without a new API version, according to GitHub's published list?
options: Renaming the response field total to totalCents
Making the optional currency parameter required
Adding an optional giftMessage field to the order response
Removing an endpoint that the logs show is rarely called
explain: Adding a response field is additive: tolerant readers ignore fields they do not know. Renaming a field, making a parameter required and removing an operation are all in GitHub's breaking list. A rarely called endpoint still has callers: deprecate it with Deprecation and Sunset headers first.

q: The shop will open Orders API v2 to delivery partners, who must build their integrations before the server exists. Which approach fits best?
options: Code-first, generating the document once the server is finished
Design-first: write and review the OpenAPI document with the partners, then implement it
tRPC, so the partners share the server's TypeScript types
No contract document; partners read the generated SDK code
explain: When consumers must agree on the contract before code exists, the document comes first and both sides build from it. Code-first is a good fit when one team owns server and clients, but here it would make partners wait. tRPC only works for TypeScript clients in the same codebase.

q: The POST /webhooks/payments handler sometimes receives the same payment.succeeded event twice. What should it do?
options: Answer 409 the second time so the sender stops retrying
Process each delivery: senders guarantee each event arrives once
Compare the event timestamps and keep the most recent one
Store each processed event id with a unique constraint and skip duplicates
explain: Retries make duplicates normal; Stripe documents that endpoints may receive the same event more than once and that order is not guaranteed. So the receiver deduplicates on the event id (webhook-id in Standard Webhooks). Answering 409 is a non-2xx response, so the sender would keep retrying it.

q: Customer support emails contain links like https://api.example.com/orders/ord_42/cancel?token=… handled by a GET route. After a chat tool started showing link previews, orders get cancelled on their own. Which fix would you ship?
options: Make the link open a page whose button sends POST /orders/ord_42/cancellation
Keep GET but block the preview bot's user agent
Keep GET but require a second token in the query string
Return 202 Accepted instead of 200 from the GET route
explain: GET is safe by definition, so crawlers and link previewers call it freely; RFC 9110 says a resource MUST disallow an unsafe action when it is accessed with a safe method. Blocking one user agent fixes this bot and not the next one; the state change must move behind POST.

q: An order search takes nested filters too large for a URL. Which statement is accurate as of 2026?
options: Send GET with a JSON body: Node's fetch supports it and caches handle it
Use QUERY (RFC 10008), safe and idempotent with a body, if the whole path supports it; otherwise a documented POST /orders/search
Use PUT /orders/search, because PUT is idempotent and accepts a body
Split the filters across several GET requests and merge the results on the client
explain: RFC 10008 (June 2026) defines QUERY as safe and idempotent with a request body; Fastify 5.12.7 routed it natively in our test. GET with a body is not an option: measured, Node's fetch throws "Request with GET/HEAD method cannot have body." PUT means "replace the resource at this URL", which a search is not.

q: What is the production problem with this v1 handler?
options: The 201 should be a 200, because the order is not paid yet
reply.send without await leaks the promise and the response is never sent
Failures go out as 200, so alerting, retry logic and error-rate dashboards see successes
The body of an error must be a string, so the object breaks serialization
explain: Without reply.code, Fastify sends 200, so an out-of-stock order is invisible to every tool that reads only the status. The fix is a problem body with the right status, such as 409 or 422 with a documented type. Returning reply.send from an async handler is the correct Fastify pattern.

q: A Fastify 5.12.7 app has only GET /orders. A client sends DELETE /orders. What did it receive (measured)?
options: 405 Method Not Allowed with Allow: GET, HEAD
200 with an empty body, because DELETE is idempotent
501 Not Implemented, because the method is unknown
404 with {"message":"Route DELETE:/orders not found",…}
explain: Measured: Fastify answered 404 with its default JSON body, not the 405 that RFC 9110 describes (a 405 MUST include an Allow header). It is a common interview follow-up: know your framework's defaults, and add 405 handling yourself if your contract promises it.

q: During a database failover, every request to the Orders API fails for about 30 seconds. Which response helps clients most?
options: 429 Too Many Requests with RateLimit headers
503 Service Unavailable with Retry-After: 30
500 Internal Server Error with the database error in detail
200 with a "degraded" flag in the body
explain: RFC 9110 defines 503 for temporary overload or maintenance, and Retry-After tells clients when to come back. 429 means this client exceeded its quota, which is false here and misleads per-client backoff. A 500 tells clients nothing about retrying, and the database error must never reach them.

q: What is the bug in this error handler?
options: For a 500, detail exposes the internal error message (SQL, hostnames) to clients
about:blank cannot be used with a status other than 404
title must be different for each occurrence of the error
statusCode is never set on Fastify errors, so everything becomes a 500
explain: An unexpected error message can contain a SQL statement, a hostname or a secret; a 500 should say only that an unexpected error occurred, with a request id, and log the rest. With about:blank the title should be the status phrase, which this code does correctly. Fastify sets statusCode on its own errors, such as 400 for invalid JSON.

q: An idempotency layer looks up the key, creates the order if the key is unknown, then saves the key with the response. Two retries of POST /orders with the same key arrive 5 ms apart. What happens?
options: The second retry waits on a lock until the first finishes
The database rejects the second order because the key is unique
Both see an unknown key and both create an order; the key must be reserved before the work
The second retry gets 409, because the first one is still running
explain: Check-then-act across an await is a race: nothing marks the key as taken until the end. Reserving first (INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING) gives exactly one owner, and the other request sees an in-progress key and gets 409. The unique key only protects the idempotency table, not the order that was already created twice.

q: This statement returns 0 rows. What should the request do next?
code:
INSERT INTO idempotency_keys (account_id, key, fingerprint)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT (account_id, key) DO NOTHING
RETURNING key;
options: Run the operation: 0 rows means the insert succeeded silently
Retry the INSERT until it returns 1 row
Answer 500, because the insert failed with a unique violation
Read the existing row: replay if completed, 409 if in progress, 422 if the fingerprint differs
explain: Measured with PGlite: the first insert returned 1 row (this request owns the key) and the second returned 0 rows because the key existed. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING raises no error; a plain INSERT would have failed with 23505. Zero rows means someone else owns the key, so the request reads it and decides.

q: With Stripe's API v1, a POST with an idempotency key fails parameter validation. The client fixes the body and retries with the same key. What does Stripe document?
options: The retry gets the stored validation error, because the first response is saved
The retry runs: results are saved only once execution begins, and a validation failure saves nothing
The retry gets 422, because the body differs from the first request
The retry gets 409 until the 24-hour expiry has passed
explain: Stripe: "If incoming parameters fail validation … we don't save the idempotent result", so the client can retry. Saving the first response, "including 500 errors", applies only once the endpoint has started executing. The 422-for-a-different-body rule applies to a stored key, and there is none here.

q: Orders o1, o2, o3 share the same created_at; o4 is older. Page 1, sorted by created_at DESC, id DESC with limit 2, returned [o3, o2]. Page 2 uses WHERE created_at < $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 2 with o2's timestamp. What did it return (measured)?
options: [o4]: o1 is skipped because it shares the boundary timestamp
[o1, o4]: the database keeps insertion order
[o2, o1]: rows equal to the boundary are included
An error, because the sort has duplicates
explain: Measured with PGlite: [o4]. Strictly less than the timestamp excludes every row with that timestamp, including o1, which was never shown. Comparing the tuple (created_at, id) < (o2's values) returned [o1, o4]: the id tie-breaker makes the order total.

q: A teammate decodes cursors with JSON.parse(Buffer.from(cursor, 'base64url').toString()) and no validation, arguing that Node rejects invalid base64. What is true?
options: They are right: Buffer.from throws on characters outside the base64url alphabet
Validation is useless because cursors are encrypted by base64url
Buffer.from does not throw: '%%%not-base64' decoded to junk bytes, so parse in a try and validate the shape
Cursors should be plain JSON in the query string so that no decoding is needed
explain: Measured on Node 24: Buffer.from('%%%not-base64', 'base64url') returned junk bytes without throwing, and a well-formed cursor can still carry a wrong shape or a fake timestamp. Base64url is an encoding, not encryption. Decode in a try, validate with a schema, answer 400 otherwise, and sign it if tampering matters.

q: The API adds "partially_refunded" to the order status enum, an additive change in GitHub's list. The Android app then crashes on some orders. Why, and what prevents it?
options: Adding enum values is breaking in every API, so a v2 was required
The server should have sent a Sunset header for the old enum
The client switch was exhaustive with no default; document that enums can grow and make clients handle unknown values
JSON cannot carry new string values without a schema change on the client
explain: Additive for the server is not harmless for a strict client: an exhaustive switch or a closed generated enum type fails on a value it does not know. The contract must say enums can grow, and generated clients should keep unknown values. Sunset announces a removal; nothing was removed here.

q: In October 2026, a script calls GitHub's REST API without an X-GitHub-Api-Version header. Which version does it get, according to GitHub's docs?
options: 2022-11-28, the default for requests without the header
2026-03-10, the latest version
An error, because the header is required
Whichever version the token was created with
explain: GitHub documents that requests without the header use 2022-11-28, although 2026-03-10 is the latest version, and that versions stay supported for 24 months after the next one is released. A version pinned by default is how dated header versioning protects old scripts.

q: A pull request renames the response field amount to amountCents. All server tests pass. Which CI step stops it before it breaks the mobile app?
options: A unit test that compares the handler output with a snapshot
Running the OpenAPI linter on the new document only
Regenerating the TypeScript client in the server repository
A breaking-change diff of the OpenAPI document against main, such as oasdiff breaking --fail-on ERR
explain: Server tests were updated with the rename, so they pass; only a comparison with the previous contract sees that a field consumers rely on disappeared. A linter checks style rules within one document, and a snapshot updated in the same pull request records the new shape rather than protecting the old one.

q: Which pairing of use case and API style is the most defensible?
options: A public API for third-party developers in many languages: tRPC
High-volume calls between internal Go and Node services, some streaming: gRPC
A single React app and its Node backend in one TypeScript monorepo: gRPC
A partner API that must work with plain curl and HTTP caches: GraphQL
explain: gRPC fits internal, polyglot, high-volume and streaming calls with Protocol Buffers contracts. tRPC only serves TypeScript clients sharing the codebase, so it fails for a public API; a TypeScript monorepo is tRPC's home rather than gRPC's. curl and HTTP caching point to REST.

q: A webhook receiver verifies the HMAC like this, and every valid webhook is rejected. Why?
options: HMAC-SHA256 cannot be verified in Node without a native module
The secret must be passed as a string, not a Buffer
Re-serialising the parsed JSON changes the bytes, so the HMAC is computed over a different body
The receiver must answer 200 before verifying, or the sender times out
explain: The signature covers the exact bytes sent. Measured: {"a": 1,  "b":2} parsed and stringified came back as {"a":1,"b":2}, so the HMAC differs. Verify over the raw body (measured: a JSON content-type parser with parseAs: 'string', registered in an encapsulated Fastify plugin, gave the webhook route the raw string), then parse it. node:crypto computes HMAC-SHA256 natively.

q: What is a composition root?
options: The root module that every NestJS app must declare
A base class that all services extend to receive dependencies
A global registry that any file can query for a dependency
The one place, run once at startup, that creates the concrete adapters and passes them to the code that needs them
explain: The composition root builds the object graph explicitly, for example buildApp(config) creating the pool, the repository and the use case. A global registry queried from anywhere is the service locator pattern, which hides dependencies instead of passing them in.

q: A Nest service needs an OrderRepository, which is a TypeScript interface. Why does it need @Inject(ORDER_REPOSITORY)?
options: Interfaces do not exist at runtime, so Nest cannot resolve them from the parameter type and needs a token
Because @Inject makes the provider request-scoped
Because Nest can only inject classes from the same module without it
Because the decorator turns the interface into an abstract class
explain: Nest reads constructor parameter types recorded by emitDecoratorMetadata; an interface is erased by the compiler, so there is nothing to look up. A Symbol or string token registered with { provide: TOKEN, useClass: … } fills the gap. @Inject has no effect on scope.

q: What is the default scope of a Nest provider?
options: One instance per request
One instance per module that imports it
One instance for the whole application (singleton)
A new instance for each consumer (transient)
explain: Providers are singletons unless declared otherwise. Scope.REQUEST and Scope.TRANSIENT are opt-in, and request scope spreads to every consumer, which is why singletons with a context store are preferred.

q: In which order do these run for a successful request in NestJS?
options: Middleware, pipe, guard, interceptor, handler
Middleware, guard, interceptor, pipe, handler
Guard, middleware, pipe, interceptor, handler
Middleware, interceptor, guard, pipe, handler
explain: The Nest docs and a measurement on Nest 12.3.2 agree: middleware, guards, interceptors (before), pipes, then the handler, then interceptors on the way out. Guards come before pipes, so an unauthenticated request is rejected before its body is validated.

q: On Nest 12, how do you validate a request body with a Zod schema without an extra library?
options: Call schema.parse(body) inside every handler
Wrap the schema with createZodDto and use ValidationPipe
Add class-validator decorators generated from the schema
Write @Body({ schema: CreateOrderSchema }) and register StandardSchemaValidationPipe
explain: Nest 12 accepts any Standard Schema library on @Body, @Query and @Param, and StandardSchemaValidationPipe validates those parameters. createZodDto comes from the separate nestjs-zod library and pairs with its own ZodValidationPipe, not with class-validator's ValidationPipe.

q: In the old Express 5 server.ts, an async route throws after an await, and a four-parameter error handler is registered last. What happens?
options: The process crashes with an unhandled rejection
The request hangs until the client times out
Express sends its default HTML 500 page
The error reaches the error handler, which answers with the mapped response
explain: Express 5 passes a rejected promise from a handler to next(err). Measured on Express 5.3.0: this route's error reached the handler, which answered a 404 Problem Details. The hang or crash happened in Express 4 without a wrapper such as express-async-errors.

q: A NestJS app registers a global guard, interceptor, pipe and exception filter that each log their name. OrdersService.get throws OrderNotFoundError, which the filter handles. What is logged?
options: middleware > guard > interceptor:before > pipe > handler > service > interceptor:error > filter
middleware > guard > pipe > interceptor:before > handler > service > filter > interceptor:error
middleware > interceptor:before > guard > pipe > handler > service > filter
middleware > guard > interceptor:before > pipe > handler > service > filter
explain: Measured on Nest 12.3.2 with the Fastify adapter: the interceptor wraps the handler as an RxJS stream, so it sees the error before the filter turns it into a response. The tempting last option forgets that interceptors are on the error path too, which matters when an interceptor maps or logs errors.

q: A singleton TenantContext provider was changed to Scope.REQUEST to hold the current tenant. OrdersController injects it. What happens to the controller?
options: Nothing: controllers are always singletons
It is constructed again for every request, as is every provider in the chain that depends on TenantContext
Nest refuses to start because controllers cannot depend on request-scoped providers
It keeps the instance created for the first request
explain: Request scope bubbles up the injection chain (Nest docs). Measured on Nest 12.3.2: a controller injecting a request-scoped provider was constructed twice for two requests. Storing the tenant with nestjs-cls keeps everything singleton.

q: A Fastify 5 service has no setErrorHandler. A handler fails with new Error('connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.3.7:5432'). What does the client receive?
options: A 500 whose JSON body contains "message":"connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.3.7:5432"
A 500 with a generic "Internal Server Error" message only
A 502 Bad Gateway, since the database is unreachable
The connection is reset without a response
explain: Measured on Fastify 5.12.7: {"statusCode":500,"error":"Internal Server Error","message":"connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.3.7:5432"}. The generic body is what NestJS does by default, not Fastify; a custom error handler that maps through toProblem and logs the details is required.

q: A developer tries to run a Nest service without a build, using Node 24's type stripping: node src/main.ts. What happens?
options: It runs, but dependency injection fails at the first request
It fails to parse: type stripping does not run decorators, so the @ is a syntax error
It runs normally: Node 24 supports decorators natively
It runs only if reflect-metadata is imported first
explain: Measured on Node 24.11: SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token at @Injectable(). Nest also needs emitDecoratorMetadata, which only a compiler (tsc or SWC) can produce, so Nest projects keep a build step; reflect-metadata cannot help a file that does not parse.

q: A NestJS 12 app has no custom exception filter. A service throws new Error('connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.3.7:5432'). What does the client receive?
options: A 500 with the original error message in the body
A 500 with {"statusCode":500,"message":"Internal server error"}
A 500 with an application/problem+json body
A 503, because the error looks like a connection failure
explain: Measured on Nest 12.3.2 (Fastify adapter): Nest's built-in filter answers any unrecognised exception with that generic body. It does not leak the message, but it is not Problem Details either, so a global @Catch() filter calling toProblem is still the way to get one format.

q: A Nest app has a global ProblemFilter and a controller-level filter @Catch(OrderNotFoundError). The controller throws OrderNotFoundError. Which filters run?
options: Only the controller-level filter: the closest matching filter handles it and exceptions do not pass from filter to filter
Both, controller first, then global
Both, global first, then controller
Only the global filter, because global filters always win
explain: The Nest docs: filters are checked from route to controller to global, and a handled exception is not passed on to another filter. So a controller filter that answers differently silently bypasses the global Problem Details mapping, which is a good reason to keep one global filter.

q: A Nest app on the Fastify adapter runs fine locally, but in its Docker container every request from outside fails to connect. main.ts calls await app.listen(3000). Likely cause?
options: Fastify listens on localhost by default; listen on 0.0.0.0 inside the container
The Fastify adapter needs enableShutdownHooks() to accept connections
Port 3000 is reserved inside Docker containers
Nest needs the Express adapter in containers
explain: The Nest docs for the Fastify adapter: Fastify listens only on localhost by default, so pass '0.0.0.0' to accept connections from other hosts, which includes Docker's port mapping. Shutdown hooks only concern signals, and nothing reserves port 3000.

q: With StandardSchemaValidationPipe registered globally, a client POSTs {"sku":"A","quantity":2,"extra":1}. What does the handler receive?
options: The raw body, including extra, since the pipe only validates
A 400 error, because extra is not in the schema
{ sku: 'A', quantity: 2 }: the schema's output, with the unknown key removed
An instance of a generated DTO class
explain: Measured on Nest 12.3.2: the handler received {"sku":"A","quantity":2} as a plain object. The pipe passes the schema's output by default (transform: true), and Zod objects strip unknown keys; a 400 would need z.strictObject.

q: A plan node shows Buffers: shared hit=3 read=4762. What does it tell you?
options: 4,765 rows were read in total: 3 of them through an index lookup and 4,762 straight from the table heap
4,765 pages of 8 kB: 3 found in PostgreSQL's memory, 4,762 requested from the OS or disk
The node ran 3 times against the shared cache and 4,762 times against the disk, once per row
3 rows matched the filter, and 4,762 rows were read and then thrown away by the filter
explain: Buffers count 8 kB pages, not rows: hit pages were found in PostgreSQL's shared memory, read pages had to be requested. Rows thrown away appear on a different line, Rows Removed by Filter. Since PostgreSQL 18, EXPLAIN ANALYZE prints these figures by default.

q: To check the slow cleanup job of the login sessions, you run EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expires_at < now() on production. What happens?
options: Only the plan with estimates, because ANALYZE switches to a read-only mode for writes like DELETE
An error: ANALYZE is only allowed with SELECT, so you must rewrite the DELETE as a SELECT first
The plan is printed and the rows are really deleted: ANALYZE executes the statement
The rows are deleted only after an explicit COMMIT
explain: ANALYZE runs the statement to measure it. Measured on PostgreSQL 18.6: EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE removed all 100 rows; inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK they came back. Without an explicit transaction the statement autocommits, so no COMMIT is needed for the damage.

q: After creating an index on orders (customer_id, created_at), the plan of the "my orders" query (WHERE customer_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20) has no Sort node any more. Why?
options: The index keeps each customer's entries in date order, read backwards for DESC
PostgreSQL caches the sorted result of the previous call and reuses it while the table is unchanged
With LIMIT 20 the sort is so small that EXPLAIN hides it from the plan output
The table itself is stored sorted by created_at, because the rows were inserted in date order
explain: A B-tree keeps its entries sorted and its leaf pages linked, so it can return rows in index order, forwards or backwards (measured: Index Scan Backward, 23 pages). The table is not sorted by customer: one customer's orders sit on 40 different pages. A sort that runs is always shown, however small.

q: Which update can be a HOT update, one that writes no index entry at all?
options: Any update of an indexed column, as long as the page still has enough free space for the new version
Any update on a table with the default fillfactor = 100, since its pages are packed efficiently
An update of a non-indexed column, when the new row version fits in the same page
Any update made inside an explicit transaction
explain: HOT needs both conditions: no indexed column changed, and room on the page for the new version. Measured with fillfactor = 90: 2,000 HOT updates out of 2,000 for the non-indexed total_cents, 0 for the indexed status; with the default fillfactor = 100 the full pages gave 0 HOT updates.

q: The only secondary index on orders is (customer_id, created_at). Which query cannot use it to jump straight to its rows?
options: WHERE customer_id = $1
WHERE customer_id = $1 AND created_at >= $2
WHERE customer_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20
WHERE created_at >= $1 AND created_at < $2
explain: Leftmost-prefix rule: the index is sorted by customer first, so one day of orders is spread across all 10,000 customer sections. Measured: an Index Only Scan over the whole index (1,539 pages, Index Searches: 1), no jumping. The three other queries constrain the leading column.

q: PostgreSQL 18 adds the B-tree skip scan. When does it actually help?
options: When the query skips a leading column that has few distinct values
When the leading column is unique, so that each jump into the index finds exactly one row
Always: column order in composite indexes no longer matters at all since PostgreSQL 18
Only for Index Only Scans on covering indexes built with an INCLUDE clause
explain: Skip scan descends the index again for each distinct value of the leading column. Measured: with (status, created_at) (4 statuses) a date-only query showed Index Searches: 9 and read 60 pages; with (customer_id, created_at) (10,000 customers) there was no skipping. It rescues a low-cardinality leading column; it does not make column order irrelevant.

q: A plan shows Index Only Scan with Heap Fetches: 5000 for 5,000 rows. What is going on?
options: The index lacks a column that the query reads
The pages are not yet all-visible in the visibility map; a VACUUM fixes it
The index is corrupted, and PostgreSQL falls back to the table to read each row safely
The statistics are stale, so the planner guessed the wrong number of rows for this scan
explain: Measured on a 100,000-row table: right after inserting 5,000 rows, Heap Fetches: 5000; after VACUUM, Heap Fetches: 0. A missing column would give a plain Index Scan, not an Index Only Scan. The visibility map is maintained by (auto)vacuum.

q: customers has an index on email. Why does WHERE lower(email) = lower($1) still do a Seq Scan?
options: The table is too small: with 10,000 rows the planner never bothers with an index at all
Query parameters such as $1 stop PostgreSQL from using indexes on text columns
B-tree indexes cannot store text values longer than a few characters, such as email addresses
The index stores email, not lower(email); index the expression itself
explain: Measured: the plain index served email = $1, but the lower() comparison removed 9,999 of 10,000 rows in a Seq Scan. An index on (lower(email)) gave an Index Scan, and making it UNIQUE rejected USER42@example.com with error 23505.

q: The database CPU is high after a release. Where do you look first to find the statements that cost the most?
options: auto_explain, to read the plan of every statement
pg_stat_user_indexes
Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on each query of the codebase
pg_stat_statements, ordered by total_exec_time
explain: pg_stat_statements aggregates every normalized statement with its calls and total time, so a cheap query called 50,000 times shows up next to a slow report. auto_explain then gives you the plan of the guilty statement; it is the second step, not the first.

q: Why must the team not run a plain CREATE INDEX on the production orders table?
options: It locks the table against reads and writes until the build ends, so even the page fails
It rewrites the whole table, which doubles its size on disk for the duration of the build
Every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on the table waits until the build ends, while reads continue
It cannot run while autovacuum works on the table, so it fails at random times in production
explain: The CREATE INDEX documentation says a plain build locks the table against writes for the whole build, while other transactions can still read it; measured, pg_locks showed a ShareLock, which conflicts with the lock every write takes. Reads are not blocked, which is the tempting wrong answer: the outage comes from checkout's inserts queuing up. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY avoids it.

q: In this join plan, how many rows did the items scan return in total?
code:
Nested Loop  (actual rows=49.00 loops=1)
  ->  Limit  (actual rows=20.00 loops=1)
        ->  Index Scan Backward using orders_customer_created_idx on orders  (actual rows=20.00 loops=1)
  ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on order_items i  (actual rows=2.45 loops=20)
        Recheck Cond: (order_id = orders.id)
explain: actual rows is an average per loop: 2.45 rows × 20 loops = 49, which matches the Nested Loop's own actual rows=49.00 (measured on the items of the page's 20 orders). Reading 2.45 as the total is the classic mistake; PostgreSQL 18 prints the decimals precisely because the figure is an average.

q: A colleague created an index on (created_at, customer_id). The plan of the "my orders" query shows Index Scan Backward, Index Cond: (customer_id = 4242) and no Sort. Is the index fine?
options: Yes: Index Scan, right Index Cond, no Sort, so it is optimal
Yes, if declared with created_at DESC
No: it will switch to a Seq Scan as the table grows
No: it walks the dates and checks the customer entry by entry, 767 pages against 23
explain: A non-leading column can appear in the Index Cond, but it is checked entry by entry instead of being used to jump. The node name hides it; the buffers (767 measured against 23 with (customer_id, created_at)) and the cost reveal it, and the work grows with the table. A B-tree reads backwards just as well, so DESC changes nothing.

q: The fulfilment dashboard runs WHERE status = $1 AND created_at >= $2 ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 50 for every status. Which single index do you create?
options: (created_at, status)
(status, created_at)
Two indexes, (status) and (created_at)
(created_at) INCLUDE (status)
explain: Equality column first, then the range and sort column: the index jumps to one status, then reads its rows already in date order, and LIMIT 50 stops early. With created_at first, the status is checked entry by entry. A partial index would fit a single status, but this dashboard queries every status.

q: orders has both (customer_id) and (customer_id, created_at), neither unique. In review, what do you propose?
options: Keep both: the single-column index is always faster for equality, the composite for sorting
Drop the composite: it is slower for equality
Drop (customer_id): the composite serves its queries, and writes pay for both
Replace both with (created_at, customer_id), which also serves the date filters
explain: By the leftmost-prefix rule, WHERE customer_id = $1 can use the composite. Measured: after 10 calls of the "my orders" query, idx_scan was 10 for the composite and 0 for orders_customer_idx. Swapping the columns would break the customer lookup instead.

q: A worker polls WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 50; pending orders are 1 % of a large, busy table. Which index do you ship?
options: (status), then a sort of the pending rows in memory
(status, created_at) on the whole table
(created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'
(created_at), read from the oldest order onwards
explain: The partial index stores only the pending rows, already in date order: measured 104 kB against 15 MB for (status, created_at), with an Index Scan, no Sort and 52 pages. Inserts of finished orders never touch it. (status, created_at) also works, at 150 times the size and with a write cost on every order.

q: This daily report does a Seq Scan although orders has an index on created_at. Which fix do you ship?
code:
SELECT count(*) FROM orders
WHERE (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date = $1;
options: Compare the bare column with a half-open range: created_at >= $1 AND created_at < $2
Create an index on (created_at::date)
Run SET enable_seqscan = off first
Run ANALYZE orders
explain: The index stores created_at, not the computed date. Measured: the cast version scanned 400,000 rows, the half-open range read 6 pages. An index on (created_at::date) is refused (error 42P17: casting a timestamptz depends on the time zone setting, so it is not immutable), and disabling Seq Scans is a session hack, not a fix.

q: Customers are soft-deleted (deleted_at is set). Rule: one live account per email, whatever the case, and a deleted customer may sign up again. Which index enforces it?
options: UNIQUE (email), plus a check in the signup service
UNIQUE (lower(email)) on every row, live or deleted
UNIQUE (lower(email), deleted_at), so that deleted rows differ
UNIQUE (lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
explain: The partial unique index only covers live rows. Measured: with a deleted Ada@Example.com, inserting ada@example.com was accepted and a second live ADA@example.com failed with 23505. Adding deleted_at to the key fails silently: live rows all hold NULL there, and NULLs count as distinct by default, so live duplicates pass.

q: You enable auto_explain with log_min_duration = 500ms and log_analyze = on on a busy server. What must you watch?
options: The overhead: log_analyze times every statement, logged or not
Disk space in pg_stat_statements, where auto_explain stores every plan it captures
Each statement now runs twice, once to return its rows and once to produce its plan
Nothing: statements faster than 500 ms are not touched by auto_explain in any way
explain: The documentation warns that log_analyze instruments every statement, whether or not it ends up logged, and that this can hurt performance badly; auto_explain.log_timing = off and auto_explain.sample_rate limit it. The plans go to the server log, not to pg_stat_statements, and the statement runs once.

q: On the primary, pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan has been 0 for three weeks for orders_status_idx. What do you do?
options: Drop it now with a plain DROP INDEX
Check the replicas, a full business cycle and constraints, then DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY
Ignore the counter: idx_scan only counts Index Only Scans, never plain index scans
Run REINDEX first, because a zero counter usually means the index is corrupted
explain: Each server keeps its own counters, so a reporting replica can use an index the primary never touches, and a month-end job may not have run yet. idx_scan counts every scan of the index, of any kind. Dropping on a live table should not take a write-blocking lock, hence CONCURRENTLY.

q: A nightly job deletes expired pending orders that never received items, and it gets slower every week. pg_stat_user_tables.seq_scan for order_items grows by one per deleted order. What do you ship?
options: An index on orders (status, created_at), so the job finds the orders to delete faster
An index on order_items (order_id): each delete checks that no item references the order
Run ANALYZE order_items, so the foreign key check switches to the primary key index
Raise work_mem, so the foreign key checks of the job are hashed in memory instead
explain: REFERENCES creates no index, and before deleting an order PostgreSQL checks that no item still references it. Measured: deleting 10 orders without an index on order_items (order_id) ran 10 sequential scans of the million-row table; with the index, none. An index on orders helps find the rows to delete, not the check on the other table, and the primary key of order_items is on id.

q: A product manager asks for an index on every column the back office can filter on, "to be safe". What do you answer?
options: Each index slows every insert and many updates and adds WAL: add one only for a query you measured
Fine: PostgreSQL maintains an index only once a query has used it, so unused ones cost nothing
Fine, as long as they are single-column indexes, which cost almost nothing on writes
Fine, provided the table uses fillfactor = 90, which makes every update a HOT update
explain: Every index is maintained on every write, used or not. Measured on 100,000 inserts: 18.6 MB of WAL with no secondary index, 59.9 MB with four, and the single-column (status) index alone added about 7 MB. A free tenth of each page does not help an update of an indexed column: measured at fillfactor = 90, 0 of 2,000 status updates were HOT.

q: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on orders has shown no progress for 20 minutes, and a finance report query has been running for an hour. What is the build most likely doing?
options: Holding a lock that blocks writes, as a plain CREATE INDEX does, until the report ends
Sorting the whole index in memory before it writes its first page to disk
Waiting for transactions older than itself, such as the running report, to finish
Retrying in a loop after a deadlock with autovacuum on the same table
explain: The CREATE INDEX documentation says a concurrent build must wait for existing transactions that could modify or use the index to terminate, before each of its two scans and, after the second, for transactions whose snapshot predates it. Writes keep flowing during that wait: a concurrent build does not take the write-blocking lock of a plain build. So check for long-running transactions before you start a build.

q: Your migration tool runs each file inside BEGIN … COMMIT. One file contains CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_status_idx ON orders (status). What happens?
options: The index is built concurrently as asked, only more slowly because of the surrounding transaction
It fails with error 25001: it cannot run inside a transaction block
PostgreSQL silently builds it without CONCURRENTLY, blocking writes for the whole build
The index is created but left invalid
explain: Measured on PostgreSQL 18.6: error 25001 inside a transaction block. A concurrent build runs several transactions of its own, so it must run outside one; configure the tool to run that migration without a transaction. An invalid index is what a failed concurrent build leaves behind, not this error.

q: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS coupons_code_lower_key … failed on a duplicate. You delete the duplicate and re-run the same migration. Result?
options: The index is built and enforces uniqueness
An error: the name already exists
A notice "already exists, skipping"; the index stays invalid and unenforced
The index becomes valid on its own
explain: Measured: indisvalid = false after the failure, the notice on the re-run, still invalid, and a duplicate insert went through. IF NOT EXISTS only checks the name. Check pg_index.indisvalid after every concurrent build, and recover with DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY and a new build.

q: The checkout decrements product 7's stock, then the INSERT INTO orders fails because the database restarts. What is stored afterwards?
options: The stock decrement without the order
Neither the decrement nor the order
The order without the decrement
The decrement, and the order once the database is back
explain: Atomicity: nothing of an uncommitted transaction survives, so the decrement is undone with it (measured on PostgreSQL 18.6: when the second statement failed after the first write, the first write was undone). Durability only applies to work whose COMMIT returned, so there is nothing to "finish" after the restart.

q: Product 7 has 5 units. Two checkouts run this code at the same time, interleaved as shown. What is the final stock?
options: The second write fails with a serialization error
explain: Alice writes 3, then Bob writes 5 − 3 = 2 from his stale read, so her decrement is overwritten: a lost update, with no error at the default Read Committed level (measured on PostgreSQL 18.6). 0 is the correct business result, which only an atomic statement, a lock or a version check would give.

q: What is PostgreSQL's default isolation level, and when does it take its snapshot?
options: Read Committed: a new snapshot at the start of each statement
Repeatable Read: one snapshot at the first statement of the transaction
Serializable: one snapshot at BEGIN
Read Committed: one snapshot at BEGIN
explain: Measured: SHOW transaction_isolation returns read committed, and the documentation says each statement sees data committed before that statement began. The "one snapshot per transaction" behaviour belongs to Repeatable Read and Serializable, and it starts at the first statement, not at BEGIN.

q: Customer 42 owns 1 console; the limit is 2. In two tabs, two transactions each count the customer's units (1), see room, and each insert an order for 1 unit. At Repeatable Read, what happens?
options: The second insert fails with 40001
The second transaction waits for the first one
The second count sees the first insert and refuses
Both commit and the customer ends with 3 consoles
explain: Both commit: this is write skew. Each transaction inserted a different row, so there was no same-row conflict for Repeatable Read to detect (measured on PostgreSQL 18.6 with this pattern). At Serializable the second insert failed with 40001 instead.

q: Transaction 753 has updated product 7 from 1 unit to 0 and not committed. Another session runs SELECT stock FROM products WHERE id = 7. What happens?
options: It waits until 753 commits or rolls back
It returns 1 immediately
It returns 0 immediately
It fails with 55P03
explain: Measured: the old version came back at once, with xmax = 753 marking who is replacing it. Under MVCC readers never wait for writers and never see uncommitted data; only locking reads such as FOR UPDATE wait.

q: A CSV export script runs BEGIN, then hangs on a slow upload, and its connection stays idle inside the open transaction. With PostgreSQL's default settings, which is true?
options: PostgreSQL rolls it back once deadlock_timeout (1 s by default) has passed
It holds locks on the rows it touched, but other tables are not affected
It keeps its locks and blocks VACUUM cleanup in every table
Autovacuum terminates the session during its next run on that table
explain: Measured: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and transaction_timeout are both 0 (off), and with one transaction open, VACUUM reported 100 dead versions "not yet removable" in an unrelated table. deadlock_timeout only governs deadlock checks for sessions that are waiting on a lock.

q: UPDATE products SET stock = stock - $2 WHERE id = $1 AND stock >= $2 RETURNING stock returns no row. What does it mean?
options: The stock cannot cover the quantity, or the product does not exist
Another transaction holds the row, so the statement gave up
A CHECK constraint rejected the new stock
The update succeeded but RETURNING needs a transaction
explain: Measured with this statement shape: decrements succeeded while the value lasted, then the same decrement matched 0 rows. A locked row makes the statement wait, not return empty, and a CHECK violation is an error (23514), not an empty result.

q: Another checkout holds customer 42's row locked. You run SELECT id FROM customers WHERE id = 42 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT. Result?
options: It waits until the other transaction commits or rolls back, then locks
It returns an empty result, because locked rows are left out
It returns the row as last committed, without taking the lock
Error 55P03: could not obtain lock on row in relation "customers"
explain: Measured. NOWAIT turns a wait into an immediate error you can map to "busy, try again". Returning no row is what SKIP LOCKED would do.

q: The versioned UPDATE orders … WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2 matches 0 rows for a PATCH /orders/1042 with If-Match: "1". What should the API do?
options: Retry the update automatically with the current version from the database
Answer 412 Precondition Failed so the client reloads and decides again
Answer 404 Not Found, since no row matched the id and version
Wait one second, then retry once with version 1 before giving up
explain: The order changed since version 1 was read (measured: the stale save matched 0 rows). Retrying with the current version would overwrite the customer's change without anyone seeing it, recreating the lost update.

q: Which errors should a generic "retry the transaction" helper retry automatically?
options: 40001 (serialization failure) and 40P01 (deadlock)
Every SQLSTATE that starts with 40
Every error, up to five attempts
23505 (unique violation) and 55P03 (lock not available)
explain: The PostgreSQL documentation recommends retrying 40001 unconditionally and 40P01 as advisable. Class 40 also contains 40003 (statement completion unknown), where rerunning may apply the change twice, and 23505 may be a permanent error that only fails again.

q: A code review shows this checkout. What is the bug?
options: The two statements must be merged into one statement to be atomic
It needs SERIALIZABLE, otherwise the two statements are not atomic
Each pool.query may run on a different connection
COMMIT must be sent before the second statement, not after it
explain: node-postgres documents it: "Do not use transactions with the pool.query method", because each call can take a different client. Take one client with pool.connect(), run every statement on it, and release it in finally. Isolation levels do not change atomicity.

q: Inside the webhook transaction, the first insert fails with 23505 and the code catches it and continues. What does the second query do?
options: It fails with 25P02: the transaction is aborted
It updates the order as usual, since the error was caught
It updates the order as it was when the transaction began
It fails with 23505 again, because the error is replayed
explain: Measured: after any error, PostgreSQL rejects every statement until ROLLBACK. Use ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING to make the duplicate a normal outcome, or a savepoint (ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT made the transaction usable again in the same test).

q: A statement fails inside a transaction, the code swallows the error and then sends COMMIT. What happens?
options: COMMIT fails with 25P02, so the caller sees the error
COMMIT returns without error, and nothing is saved
COMMIT saves the statements that succeeded before the error
COMMIT hangs until the client sends an explicit ROLLBACK
explain: Measured on PostgreSQL 18.6: no error, command tag ROLLBACK, and the earlier update was not stored. That is why a transaction helper must rethrow, and why swallowing errors inside a transaction leads to silent data loss.

q: The per-customer limit lets two concurrent checkouts of customer 42 both pass. You must stay at Read Committed. Which fix closes the race?
options: Wrap the count and the insert together in one BEGIN/COMMIT block
Add FOR UPDATE to the SELECT sum(quantity) so the orders are locked
Run only the count at Repeatable Read so it reads a stable snapshot
Lock the customer row with SELECT … FOR UPDATE before counting
explain: Locking the customer row makes every checkout of that customer take turns, so the count cannot go stale (measured: a second locker got 55P03 under NOWAIT). FOR UPDATE on an aggregate is rejected with 0A000, and a transaction alone or Repeatable Read still let write skew through (measured).

q: What does PostgreSQL 18 do with this query?
code: SELECT sum(quantity) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 FOR UPDATE;
options: Fails with 0A000: FOR UPDATE is not allowed with aggregate functions
Locks every order row of customer 42
Locks the whole orders table
Locks the matching order rows and also blocks future inserts for customer 42
explain: Measured. The documentation says locking clauses cannot be used where returned rows cannot be identified with table rows, such as aggregation. Even if it worked, it could not lock orders that do not exist yet; that is why you lock the parent customer row.

q: At Repeatable Read, Bob's transaction read product 7, then Alice's checkout updated product 7 and committed. Bob now runs UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 7. What happens according to the documentation?
options: Bob re-applies his update to the new committed version, as Read Committed does
Bob waits for Alice forever, because his snapshot predates her commit
Bob fails with 40001: could not serialize access due to concurrent update
Bob silently updates the old version he saw, overwriting Alice’s committed change
explain: The documentation: a Repeatable Read transaction cannot modify or lock rows changed by other transactions after it began, and fails with that 40001 message; it must be retried from the start. Re-applying to the new version is the Read Committed behaviour.

q: Product 7 has 1 unit. Two checkouts at Read Committed run the statement below at the same time with $2 = 1. What is the outcome?
code:
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - $2
 WHERE id = $1 AND stock >= $2;
options: Both succeed, and the CHECK constraint then fails the second with 23514
One succeeds; the other rechecks its WHERE on 0 units and updates 0 rows
The second fails with 40001 because the row changed under it
Both succeed and the stock ends at 0: one sale is lost
explain: The documentation: at Read Committed, the second updater waits for the first to commit, then re-evaluates its WHERE clause on the updated row. 0 >= 1 is false, so it matches nothing and the route refuses the sale. 40001 is what Repeatable Read would raise instead.

q: Your logs show occasional 40P01 errors on bundle checkouts: some baskets reserve product 7 then 9, others 9 then 7. Which fix would you ship first?
options: Raise deadlock_timeout to 10 s so the cycle has time to resolve
Move checkouts to Serializable so PostgreSQL orders the transactions
Lock each product with FOR UPDATE NOWAIT and answer 409 when busy
Lock all the basket's products first, in ascending id order, then reserve
explain: A consistent lock order removes the cycle, which the documentation calls the best defence; keep the 40P01 retry as a safety net. A larger deadlock_timeout only delays detection, and Serializable does not prevent waits on row locks.

q: Your API uses version-based optimistic concurrency on orders. A client sends a PATCH without If-Match. With a strict policy, what is the right response?
options: 428 Precondition Required
412 Precondition Failed
409 Conflict
200, applying the change to the current version
explain: 428 says "this request must be conditional", while 412 means a condition was sent and failed. Applying the change without a version check silently allows the lost update the version column exists to prevent.

q: The first payment webhook handler opened a transaction, recorded the payment, sent the confirmation email over HTTP (sometimes 30 s), then committed. Which design would you ship?
options: Keep the single transaction and raise the pool size so slow calls do not exhaust it
Record the payment and an outbox row, commit, and let a relay send the email
Keep it, and set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout to 60 s to end stuck sessions
Run the whole handler at Serializable with retries so concurrent deliveries cannot conflict
explain: The HTTP call must leave the transaction: during the wait it holds locks and a connection, and blocks VACUUM cleanup. A bigger pool only moves the bottleneck, and retrying a transaction that already sent an email sends it twice.

q: Product 7's row is at xmin = 752, ctid = (0,1). Transaction 753 updates its stock and commits. What does SELECT xmin, ctid FROM products WHERE id = 7 show next?
options: 752, (0,1): the row was overwritten in place by 753
753, (0,1): same position, but the creator is now 753
752, (0,2): moved to a new position, creator unchanged
753 and a new ctid such as (0,2): a new row version
explain: Measured: 753 | (0,2). An update writes a new version created by the updating transaction, and the old one stays as a dead version until VACUUM removes it. That is why update-heavy tables depend on autovacuum.

q: What is wrong with this use of the retry helper at Serializable?
options: Nothing is wrong: the helper reruns the update, so a conflict is always resolved
It should catch 40001 inside the callback and rerun the UPDATE there
The read and decision sit outside the callback, so retries use stale data
Serializable rejects an UPDATE that sets a constant value
explain: The documentation says the retry must rerun "all logic that decides which SQL to issue". Here every attempt reuses the old stock, so a retry can still oversell. Catching 40001 inside the callback would be worse, since the transaction is already aborted (25P02).

q: The provider redelivers the same event, with the same event id. What does this statement return on the replay?
code:
INSERT INTO payments (order_id, amount_cents, provider_event_id)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT (provider_event_id) DO NOTHING
RETURNING id;
options: The id of the existing payment, since the conflicting row is returned
Zero rows, so the handler stops and the route answers 200
Error 23505: duplicate key value violates unique constraint
A second payment row with a new id
explain: Measured: 1 row the first time, 0 rows on the replay. RETURNING only returns rows actually inserted, so the existing id is not returned; read it with a second query if you need it. Without ON CONFLICT the replay would raise 23505.

q: The team moves the Orders API to Serializable. What must change in the application code for this to be safe?
options: Nothing: Serializable only adds waiting, so existing code keeps working unchanged
Add FOR UPDATE to every read so Serializable has fewer conflicts to detect
Raise deadlock_timeout so the extra waits do not turn into errors
Run every transaction through a retry-on-40001 helper, side-effect free
explain: Serializable adds aborts, not waits: the documentation says applications must be prepared to retry serialization failures and to treat data read as valid only after commit. The documentation even suggests removing explicit FOR UPDATE locks made unnecessary by Serializable.

q: Flash sale: 10,000 requests per second try to reserve the last 500 consoles. Which approach do you pick first?
options: UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = $1 AND stock > 0, checking the row count
SELECT stock, check it in Node, then UPDATE products at Serializable with retries on 40001
Optimistic locking with a version column on products and automatic retries on 0 rows
SELECT stock … FOR UPDATE, check it in Node, then UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1
explain: The rule fits in the WHERE, so one atomic statement is correct at Read Committed and holds the row lock only for that statement. On a single hot row, Serializable and optimistic retries would mostly produce conflicts, and FOR UPDATE holds the lock across two round trips.

q: A bug leaves connections "idle in transaction" after an exception. Which setting makes PostgreSQL end such sessions on its own?
options: lock_timeout
statement_timeout
idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
deadlock_timeout
explain: The documentation: it terminates a session idle inside an open transaction for longer than the limit (measured default 0, disabled). statement_timeout only limits a running statement, and an idle session is not running one.

q: A product's German price changes from 4,900 to 5,900 cents. Last month's German orders must still show 4,900. How should order_lines be modelled?
options: Only a foreign key to product_prices, and join to read the price
Store the unit price and product name on the line when the order is placed
Keep a price_history view computed from today's prices
Store the price on the line and keep it in sync with product_prices through a trigger
explain: The price at order time is a different fact from today's price, so it is stored on the line as a snapshot. A foreign key alone, or a trigger that follows the catalogue, would rewrite the history of orders already placed.

q: On 1 million rows, why was the primary key index on uuidv7() smaller than the one on uuidv4() (30 MB against 38 MB)?
options: UUIDv7 values are stored in 12 bytes instead of 16, because the timestamp part is packed
PostgreSQL compresses UUIDv7 values in B-tree indexes
New values sort after older ones, so they are appended instead of splitting pages
UUIDv7 indexes are built as hash indexes, which store a 4-byte hash of each key
explain: Both are 16 bytes (pg_column_size returned 16). The first 48 bits of a v7 are a millisecond timestamp, so inserts arrive in order like a sequence; random v4 keys land anywhere and leave split pages partly empty.

q: Order numbers such as DE-2026-000042 are printed on invoices, and each country numbers its orders on its own sequence. Where does the number belong?
options: In a number column with UNIQUE (country_code, number), next to a technical primary key
It should be the primary key of orders
In a number column with UNIQUE (number)
Generated by the application only, with no constraint, because it is a display value
explain: A natural key is kept unique by a constraint while a stable technical key is what foreign keys point to. A global UNIQUE (number) would forbid France and Germany from both having order 42, and no constraint at all lets duplicates in under concurrency.
