q: On PostgreSQL 18, which statement rewrites the 50-million-row orders table?
options: ADD COLUMN note text
ADD COLUMN currency text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'EUR'
ADD COLUMN created_at timestamptz DEFAULT now()
ADD COLUMN public_id uuid DEFAULT uuidv7()
explain: Measured with the table's file node: a volatile default must be computed per row, so the table is rewritten under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. A constant, or now() evaluated once per statement, is stored in the catalog, which has avoided the rewrite since PostgreSQL 11.

q: The API exposes customer ids generated with uuidv7() in referral links. A privacy review raises a concern. Which one is real?
code: SELECT uuid_extract_timestamp('01a18894-dd17-7000-a15a-095851f37549');
options: Anyone can guess the next customer's id from the current one
UUIDv7 ids can collide across servers, so one customer may see another's account
The id reveals when the account was created, to the millisecond
The id contains the server's MAC address
explain: The first 48 bits of a v7 are its creation time in milliseconds, and uuid_extract_timestamp returned it exactly (it returns NULL for a v4). The remaining bits are random, so ids are not guessable; the MAC address belonged to UUIDv1.

q: You need a public_id uuid filled for every row of the live orders table, without a long lock. Which sequence would you ship?
options: ADD COLUMN public_id uuid, then SET DEFAULT uuidv7(), then backfill in batches
ADD COLUMN public_id uuid NOT NULL DEFAULT uuidv7() in a single statement, run at night when traffic is low
ADD COLUMN public_id uuid DEFAULT uuidv7() with lock_timeout set
ADD COLUMN public_id uuid GENERATED ALWAYS AS (uuidv7()) STORED
explain: Measured: adding the column and then setting the default caused no rewrite, new rows got an id, existing rows stayed NULL for the backfill. A volatile default in ADD COLUMN rewrites the table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, and lock_timeout only limits the wait for the lock, not the rewrite.

q: After a complete backfill, how do you make orders.total_cents NOT NULL on the busy 50-million-row table?
options: ALTER COLUMN total_cents SET NOT NULL with lock_timeout = '3s'
ADD CONSTRAINT … CHECK (total_cents IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID, VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, then SET NOT NULL
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on total_cents, then SET NOT NULL
ALTER COLUMN total_cents SET DEFAULT 0, which turns existing NULLs into zeros and forbids new ones
explain: Validation scans under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, so reads and writes continue, and the final SET NOT NULL reported that existing constraints prove the column has no NULLs instead of scanning. A plain SET NOT NULL scans under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE; lock_timeout bounds the wait, not the scan.

q: A migration runs ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text, a catalog-only change. Yet the API stops answering for two minutes. What most likely happened?
options: Adding a column rewrote the table
The new column invalidated every index on the table
The migration tool held its advisory lock for two minutes, blocking the application's own queries
The ALTER queued behind a long transaction, and every query on the table queued behind the ALTER
explain: A waiting lock request blocks later conflicting requests too (the PostgreSQL docs call it a soft block, ahead in the wait queue). The fix is SET lock_timeout in migrations, whose default is 0 (wait forever), plus a retry. Adding a nullable column measured no rewrite.

q: A backfill picks each batch with the first query. Halfway through, it is much slower than at the start. What explains it?
options: The IS NULL filter cannot use any index, so every batch reads the whole table from disk
The updated rows are still locked by earlier batches, so the query waits for them
It rescans every row already filled: 1,182 buffers against 10 for the keyset query
LIMIT forces a sort of the whole table
explain: Measured with 90,000 of 100,000 rows done: the plan used the primary key index but showed Rows Removed by Filter: 90000 and 1,182 buffers; the keyset version read 10. Each batch gets slower, so the total cost grows with the square of the table.

q: For the UK launch you must rename orders.zip_code to orders.postal_code, with rolling deploys. Which plan is safe?
options: RENAME COLUMN in the migration, and deploy the code that uses postal_code in the same release
Add postal_code, sync and backfill it, switch reads then writes, drop zip_code later
Create a view named orders exposing both names, then rename the table
RENAME COLUMN at night, when no old instance is running
explain: During a rolling deploy, old instances still query zip_code, so an instant rename breaks them even though the rename itself is fast. Expand / migrate / contract keeps every intermediate schema compatible with both versions; relying on a night window is downtime with better timing.

q: Which statement about Prisma 7 is correct?
options: It generates a Rust query engine binary that the client starts at run time
Its client is written in TypeScript and every database needs a driver adapter, such as @prisma/adapter-pg
Its schema is declared in TypeScript files, like a Drizzle schema
It no longer ships migrations, so teams use drizzle-kit with it
explain: The Prisma 7 upgrade guide describes a Rust-free client and makes driver adapters mandatory (for PostgreSQL, @prisma/adapter-pg, which uses pg). The Rust engine is what Prisma 7 removed, and the schema is still a schema.prisma file with Prisma Migrate.

q: The finance team wants Orders API reports written with CTEs and window functions, every column typed, and migrations kept in plain SQL files. Which tool fits best?
options: Kysely: a type-safe query builder that does not own the schema
Sequelize: models give the types and it handles migrations
TypeORM: decorators describe each column precisely
postgres.js: tagged templates infer the result types from the SQL
explain: Kysely types SQL you write, including complex queries, and leaves the schema and migrations to you. postgres.js keeps SQL readable but does not infer result types from the SQL text, and Sequelize and TypeORM are legacy ORMs with a model-first approach.

q: With Drizzle 0.45, db.query.orders.findMany({ where: …, with: { items: true } }) loads 20 orders with 2 items each. How many SQL statements were sent?
options: 21: one for the orders and one per order
2: one for the orders and one for all the items
1: a LATERAL join that aggregates the items with json_agg
40: one per item
explain: Measured with a query logger: one statement, LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT coalesce(json_agg(…), '[]') …). Two statements is what Prisma's query strategy does (one per table), and 21 is the N+1 loop.

q: The N+1 loop of the order history page takes 3 ms on a laptop and 250 ms in production for the same customer. What explains the gap?
options: Production runs PostgreSQL with more data, so each query plan is worse
The ORM caches queries on the laptop but not in production
The pool is smaller in production, so the queries run one at a time
Each query is a network round trip in production, and the loop pays it once per row
explain: A local database answers in microseconds, so 200 extra queries cost almost nothing; over the network each one costs a round trip (about 1 ms), paid sequentially by the loop. The queries run one at a time because the loop awaits each one, not because of the pool size.

q: The customers table has 3 rows. How many rows does this return?
code:
const email = "nobody@example.com' OR '1'='1";
await pool.query("SELECT id FROM customers WHERE email = '" + email + "'");
options: 0, because no customer has that email
A syntax error, because of the unbalanced quote
All 3, because OR '1'='1' is true for every row
Only the customers whose email contains a quote
explain: Measured on PostgreSQL 18.6: 3 rows. The quote in the input closes the string literal and the rest becomes SQL; the quotes balance, so there is no syntax error. With WHERE email = $1 and the same input as a parameter, the query returned 0 rows.

q: To let clients choose the sort of an order list, you run SELECT id, created_at FROM orders ORDER BY $1 with the value 'created_at'. What happens?
options: It sorts by the created_at column
It runs, but sorts by the constant text 'created_at', so the order does not change
It fails with a syntax error, because parameters are not allowed after ORDER BY
It is an SQL injection vulnerability
explain: Measured: the query runs and the rows keep their order, because a parameter is always a value, here the same constant for every row. Only a table name in FROM $1 is a syntax error (42601). Map the client's choice through an allowlist of SQL fragments you wrote.

q: A pg.Pool has max: 10 and the default connectionTimeoutMillis. A code path leaks a client on each error. What happens after 10 such errors?
options: The pool closes the leaked clients after idleTimeoutMillis and recovers
The pool opens new connections beyond max to keep serving
Every new checkout fails at once with 53300
Every new checkout waits with no time limit, because the default timeout is 0
explain: Leaked clients are checked out, not idle, so the idle timeout never applies to them, and the pool never exceeds max. With the default connectionTimeoutMillis: 0 the node-postgres docs say requests wait forever; measured with 500 ms, the checkout failed after 503 ms with "timeout exceeded when trying to connect".

q: Behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, which statement keeps working as intended?
options: SET statement_timeout = '5s' once after connecting
LISTEN order_created to receive notifications
SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '5s' inside each transaction
SELECT pg_advisory_lock(42) held across several transactions
explain: SET LOCAL lasts until the end of the transaction, which is exactly how long the client keeps the server connection in transaction mode. PgBouncer's feature map marks SET, LISTEN and session-level advisory locks as never supported in that mode, because the next transaction may run on another connection.

q: One Orders API pod runs 600 queries per second, and a query takes 10 ms on average. By Little's law, how many connections are busy on average?
options: 600, one per query in flight each second
About 6
10, the default max of the pool
explain: Little's law: busy connections = queries per second × average query time = 600 × 0.010 s = 6. The pool's max is a ceiling, not the need; if a pool of 10 stays full at this load, queries are slower than measured or connections are held while doing other work.

q: In a code review you see this Drizzle query. What is the problem?
options: None: the sql tag parameterises everything inside it
Only a performance issue: the plan cannot be reused
None, as long as the email was validated as an email format
sql.raw pastes the text into the SQL, so email can inject; use ${email} directly
explain: Measured: sql.raw produced WHERE email = 'nobody@example.com' OR '1'='1', with no placeholder. The tag parameterises plain ${value} substitutions only. Format validation is not a defence: many valid-looking inputs still contain quotes.

q: In late October 2026, a developer runs npm install prisma on a Prisma 7 project and CI fails because prisma generate no longer exists. Which fix would you ship?
options: Pin prisma@7 (with @prisma/client@7), and plan the move to Prisma 8 separately
Delete the lockfile so npm resolves a coherent set of versions
Replace prisma generate with prisma migrate dev, which generates the client
Downgrade to Prisma 6, the last version with a stable CLI
explain: The prisma package's latest tag points to 8.0.0-rc.28, whose CLI has no generate, while @prisma/client stays on 7.10.1; Prisma's release status page tells Prisma 7 projects to lock both packages to version 7. In Prisma 7, migrate dev no longer runs generate, and Prisma 6 only gets security patches until 19 November 2026.

q: This handler works in every test. In production, after a few days, all requests hang. What is the bug?
options: The two statements should run with Promise.all to release the client sooner
When a query throws (a duplicate reservation, say), release() is skipped and the connection leaks
pool.connect() opens a new TCP connection on every call
The UPDATE takes a row lock that is never released
explain: An exception skips the release() line, so each failure removes one connection from the pool until none is left; measured with max: 1, the next checkout timed out. Put it in a finally, or better, use a transaction helper, since these two writes belong together. Without BEGIN each statement autocommits, so no lock stays held.

q: The Orders API scales from 4 to 16 pods at peak, each with max: 10, against a PostgreSQL with max_connections = 100. At peak, some pods log 53300. What do you ship?
options: Set max_connections = 1000 so every pod fits
Lower idleTimeoutMillis so idle connections close faster
Put a transaction-mode pooler in front (PgBouncer, RDS Proxy) and size each pod's pool from the budget
Raise each pod's max to 20 so requests stop waiting
explain: 16 × 10 = 160 connections exceed the 97 available, so new connections fail with 53300 (too_many_connections). A pooler lets many client connections share few server connections. Raising max_connections costs a server process per connection and only moves the queue, and idle timeouts do not help when the connections are busy at peak.

q: A service configures new pg.Pool({ statement_timeout: 5000, … }). After moving behind a default PgBouncer, every connection attempt is refused. Why, and what is the clean fix?
options: PgBouncer does not support pg's SCRAM authentication; switch to md5
pg sends statement_timeout as a startup parameter, which PgBouncer refuses by default; set it per role with ALTER ROLE … SET
Transaction mode forbids timeouts entirely; move the timeout to the HTTP layer
The value must be a string such as '5s'; PgBouncer rejects numbers
explain: pg's source adds statement_timeout to the startup message, and PgBouncer's docs say any parameter it does not track "will raise an error". A role default applies to every new server session, through any pooler (or you can list the parameter in ignore_startup_parameters). Timeouts themselves work fine in transaction mode.

q: Which statement about prepared statements behind PgBouncer 1.26 in transaction mode is correct?
options: Protocol-level named prepared statements work, since max_prepared_statements defaults to 200; SQL PREPARE does not
No prepared statement works; every driver must disable them
SQL PREPARE works, but protocol-level statements do not
They work only in session mode, whatever the version
explain: PgBouncer 1.21 added support for protocol-level named prepared statements, and 1.24 enabled it by default with max_prepared_statements = 200. SQL-level PREPARE/DEALLOCATE are still listed as never supported. Disabling statements (prepare: false) is only needed with older or other poolers, such as Supabase's shared pooler.

q: An edge function of the shop, on Neon, must read a gift card balance, decide in code, then debit it, in one transaction. Which way of connecting fits?
options: neon() over HTTP, sending the three statements one after another
neon() with sql.transaction([...]), the HTTP batch form
A direct TCP connection with pg, opened and closed in each invocation without a pooler
Pool or Client from @neondatabase/serverless over WebSockets
explain: The decision happens between statements, so this is an interactive transaction, and Neon's docs reserve those for Pool/Client over WebSockets. The HTTP sql.transaction() form is non-interactive: all queries are fixed before it runs. Separate HTTP calls are separate transactions.

q: A logged-in customer changes GET /orders/ord_a1 to GET /orders/ord_b1 and receives another customer's order. Which OWASP API risk is it?
options: API2 Broken Authentication
API1 Broken Object Level Authorization
API5 Broken Function Level Authorization
API8 Security Misconfiguration
explain: The caller is correctly authenticated, so it is not API2; what is missing is the check that this particular object belongs to them, which is BOLA. API5 is about whole functions, such as a customer reaching an admin route, not about one object among many of the same kind.

q: In the authorization code flow with PKCE, an attacker steals the authorisation code from the redirect. Why can they not exchange it for tokens?
options: The token endpoint also requires the code_verifier, which only the client that started the flow holds
The code is encrypted with the IdP's private key
The code is bound to the attacker's IP address and rejected
The code expires before an attacker can use it
explain: The client sent only the hash of the verifier (the challenge) in the authorize URL; at the token endpoint it must present the verifier itself, and the IdP checks that its SHA-256 matches. Codes are short-lived, but a short lifetime alone does not stop an attacker who uses the code at once.

q: With passkeys implemented through SimpleWebAuthn, what does the Orders API store for each credential?
options: A salted Argon2id hash of the passkey
The private key, encrypted with a server secret
A shared secret that the device and the server both use to sign
The credential id, the public key and a signature counter
explain: The device keeps the private key; the server keeps the credential id, the public key to verify signatures and the counter it updates after each login (SimpleWebAuthn's documentation). There is no shared secret, which is why a database leak reveals nothing an attacker can log in with.

q: Which setting is one of the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet minimums for Argon2id?
options: m=19456 (19 MiB), t=2, p=1
m=1024 (1 MiB), t=1, p=1
m=19456 (19 MiB), t=1, p=4
N=2^17, r=8, p=1
explain: OWASP lists five equivalent Argon2id settings, including 19 MiB with two passes and parallelism 1, and 46 MiB with one pass. N=2^17, r=8, p=1 is real too, but it is the scrypt setting, not an Argon2id one.

q: The login handler returns 401 immediately when the e-mail is unknown, and runs a 65 ms Argon2id verification when it exists. What is the problem?
options: Nothing, as long as both cases return the same status code
The unknown-e-mail path wastes no CPU, which is the desired behaviour
The response time reveals which e-mails have accounts; verify against a dummy hash so both paths cost the same
The 401 should be a 404 for unknown e-mails
explain: Identical status codes are not enough when the timing differs by a full hash: an attacker can enumerate accounts by measuring. Checking the password against a dummy hash made with the same settings makes both paths cost the same, and the body stays identical.

q: What does the HttpOnly attribute on the BFF's session cookie protect against?
options: The browser attaching the cookie to requests sent from another site
A script injected into your page (XSS) reading the cookie and sending it to an attacker
The cookie being sent over plain HTTP
A sibling subdomain overwriting the cookie
explain: MDN: HttpOnly forbids JavaScript access through document.cookie, but the browser still sends the cookie with requests. Stopping cross-site sending is SameSite, HTTPS-only is Secure, and subdomain overwrites are stopped by the __Host- prefix.

q: A request with Origin: https://evil.example reaches the Orders API (Fastify), which has no CORS plugin. What happened when this was measured?
options: Fastify rejected it with 403
Fastify answered 204 to a preflight and blocked the request
The browser refused to send the request
Fastify answered a normal 200 without any Access-Control-* header; only a browser would hide the response from the script
explain: CORS is enforced by browsers on what a script may read, not by the server on what it accepts: the handler ran and returned 200. That is why CORS is not access control, and why state-changing requests need CSRF protection and authorisation of their own.

q: A service expects HS256 and calls jwtVerify(token, secret, { issuer, audience }) without algorithms. A token signed with HS512 and the same secret arrives. What did jose 6.2.12 do?
options: Rejected it with JOSEAlgNotAllowed
Accepted it
Rejected it with JWSSignatureVerificationFailed
Threw a TypeError about the key length
explain: Measured: accepted, with protectedHeader.alg equal to HS512. With algorithms: ['HS256'] it was rejected with JOSEAlgNotAllowed. The signature is valid for the algorithm the token names, which is exactly why the verifier, not the token, must choose the algorithm.

q: The mobile app's refresh tokens are rotated on every use. The server receives a refresh token that was already exchanged an hour ago. What should it do?
options: Treat it as stolen: revoke the whole token family and require a new login
Issue new tokens, since the token is still within its lifetime
Ignore the request and return the tokens issued an hour ago
Return 429 so the client slows down
explain: With rotation, a legitimate client never presents an old refresh token again, so reuse means someone copied it; revoking the family cuts off both the attacker and the copied chain. Issuing new tokens would hand the attacker a fresh session.

q: Why put AND customer_id = $2 in the query rather than load the order by id and check the owner in the handler?
options: The database checks ownership faster than JavaScript
It removes the need to verify the access token
A forgotten check returns nothing instead of another customer's data, and "not yours" looks exactly like "not found"
PostgreSQL refuses queries on the orders table without it
explain: Run against PostgreSQL 18, customer A asking for customer B's order got an empty result, so the route answered the same 404 as a missing id. The point is structural safety, not speed; the caller's id still comes from a verified session or token.

q: The login endpoint, running on six replicas, is under a credential-stuffing attack: thousands of e-mails tried from thousands of IPs. Which rate-limiting design do you ship?
options: An in-memory limit of 5 attempts per IP on each replica
A global limit of 100 logins per minute for the whole service
Limits per account and per IP, with counters in a shared store such as Redis, answering 429 with Retry-After
Locking each account permanently after 5 failures
explain: Stuffing spreads across many accounts and many IPs, so you need both keys, and in-memory counters on six replicas multiply the limit by six. A global limit locks out real customers during the attack, and permanent lockouts let an attacker deny service to any account they name.

q: A reviewer approves this SSRF guard for order-update webhooks. A business customer then registers the URL https://hooks.slack.com@169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/. What happens?
options: The guard rejects it because the string contains an @
The guard accepts it and fetch calls 169.254.169.254, because everything before @ is user information, not the host
The guard accepts it but fetch refuses URLs with credentials
The guard accepts it and fetch calls hooks.slack.com
explain: Measured: new URL('https://hooks.slack.com@169.254.169.254/latest').hostname is 169.254.169.254. A string prefix test checks text, not the destination; parse with new URL, compare hostname against an allow-list, and add redirect: 'error'.

q: An internal tool mints tokens without an exp claim. The Orders API verifies them as below. What happens to such a token with jose 6.2.12?
options: It is accepted, and stays valid forever
It is rejected with JWTExpired
It is rejected with JWTClaimValidationFailed: missing required "exp" claim
It is accepted for the default lifetime of 15 minutes
explain: Measured: without requiredClaims: ['exp'], a token with no expiry was accepted. The "missing required exp" error appears only once you list exp in requiredClaims; jose has no default lifetime unless you set maxTokenAge.

q: A test issues a token with exp = T and calls jwtVerify with currentDate exactly equal to T and no clock tolerance. Which assertion passes?
options: The token is accepted, because it expires after T
The token is accepted only if iat is before T
The token is rejected with JWSSignatureVerificationFailed
The token is rejected with JWTExpired
explain: Measured: one second before exp was accepted and exactly exp was rejected with JWTExpired ("exp" claim timestamp check failed), so exp is exclusive. Pin such boundaries with an injected clock rather than the real one.

q: During a signing-key rotation, the IdP removed the old key from its JWKS at the same moment it started signing with the new one. Access tokens live 15 minutes. What does the Orders API see?
options: Tokens signed with the old key fail with JWKSNoMatchingKey until they expire, so users get 401s; the old key should have stayed published for at least the token lifetime
Nothing: jose falls back to the newest key in the set
Tokens signed with the new key fail until the JWKS cache expires
jose throws JWKSMultipleMatchingKeys for every token
explain: Measured with a local JWKS: once the old key was gone, its tokens failed with JWKSNoMatchingKey. New-key tokens are fine, because an unknown kid triggers a refetch. The safe order is publish the new key, sign with it, and remove the old one after the longest token lifetime.

q: A colleague wants to drop the native dependency and hash passwords with Node's built-in crypto.argon2() (callback form). Measured on Node 24.11.1, what did that call do?
options: It ran entirely on the libuv thread pool, like crypto.scrypt
It threw ERR_FEATURE_UNAVAILABLE, because Argon2 is not in Node 24
It returned only after about one hash duration, blocking the event loop; eight parallel calls froze it for about 480 ms
It printed an experimental warning and fell back to scrypt
explain: Argon2 has been in node:crypto since v24.7.0, but on 24.11.1 the callback call itself took about 65 ms at m=19456, t=2 before returning. @node-rs/argon2 ran eight hashes in 132 ms with the loop never blocked more than 39 ms, so it is the safer choice until a re-measurement shows otherwise.

q: What happens when this runs on Node 24 (OWASP's scrypt setting, no other option)?
options: It prints 32 after about a quarter of a second
It throws ERR_CRYPTO_INVALID_SCRYPT_PARAMS: memory limit exceeded
It prints 32 at once, because N is silently capped
It throws because the salt must be a string
explain: Measured: this setting needs about 128 × N × r = 128 MiB, above Node's default maxmem, so it throws. With a larger maxmem it worked (about 380 ms here), and in a server you would use the async scrypt anyway.

q: The shop's React single-page app currently keeps the access and refresh tokens in localStorage. What does RFC 10017 (OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications) recommend for a business application like this?
options: Move the tokens to sessionStorage
Encrypt the tokens in localStorage with a key from the server
Keep the tokens in memory and refresh on every page load
A backend-for-frontend that runs the OAuth flow, keeps tokens server-side, and gives the browser an HttpOnly session cookie
explain: RFC 10017 ranks the BFF as the most secure browser architecture and strongly recommends it for business applications. Any storage JavaScript can read, including sessionStorage or an in-page decryption key, is readable by an injected script too.

q: A team proposes the OAuth “resource owner password credentials” grant so the shop's mobile app can post the customer's password directly to the token endpoint. What does RFC 9700 say?
options: It is allowed for first-party mobile apps
It must not be used
It is allowed if combined with PKCE
It is deprecated but acceptable until OAuth 2.1 is published
explain: RFC 9700, the current OAuth security best practice, states that the password grant MUST NOT be used, and the OAuth 2.1 draft drops it. The app should use the authorization code flow with PKCE in the system browser, which also lets the IdP offer passkeys and SSO.

q: The BFF uses a SameSite=Lax session cookie. The auditor asks for a proper CSRF defence on POST /orders/:id/cancel. Which answer matches the OWASP CSRF cheat sheet?
options: Add a CSRF token (synchroniser or signed double-submit) or reject cross-site requests using Sec-Fetch-Site, with an Origin check as fallback; SameSite stays as defence in depth
Nothing: SameSite=Lax fully prevents CSRF
Add a strict CORS policy listing only your front-end origin
Mark the cookie HttpOnly
explain: OWASP calls SameSite useful defence in depth that does not replace a proper CSRF defence. CORS does not stop a form POST from being sent, and HttpOnly stops scripts reading the cookie, not the browser attaching it.

q: An attacker finds an XSS bug in a single-page app that stores its JWT access token in localStorage. What can they do?
options: Nothing, because the token is signed
Read the claims but not use the token, which is bound to the browser
Read the token and use it from their own machine until it expires
Modify the claims, since the payload is only base64url
explain: A bearer token works for whoever presents it, so the attacker can replay it anywhere until exp. Editing the claims fails (measured: JWSSignatureVerificationFailed). Only sender-constrained tokens (DPoP) or keeping tokens out of the page (BFF) limit this.

q: Customer A requests GET /orders/ord_77/invoice, and order ord_77 belongs to customer B. What should the Orders API answer?
options: 403 Forbidden, to be explicit about the reason
401 Unauthorized, so the client logs in again
200 with the amounts removed
404 Not Found, exactly as for an id that does not exist
explain: A 403 confirms that the order exists, which helps an attacker enumerate ids. 401 means "who are you?", which is wrong for an authenticated caller. When a caller may legitimately know an object exists (a shared resource they lost access to), 403 can be the right product choice.

q: The shop adds business accounts: buyers belong to teams, teams belong to a company account, orders belong to the company, and a company can share its order history with its accounting firm, whose staff then see those orders. Which authorisation model and tool fit best?
options: RBAC with a role claim from the IdP
ReBAC with a Zanzibar-style system such as OpenFGA
ABAC with a single rule on the order's owner
No model: check customer_id in every query
explain: Access here follows chains of relationships (buyer in team, team in company, company shares with firm), which is what relationship-based access control models directly. A role cannot say "orders of this company", and an owner check ignores sharing; OpenFGA is the CNCF incubating project built for this.

q: Which automated test is most likely to catch a BOLA regression in the Orders API before production?
options: A test that requests every route without a token and expects 401
A load test that checks the p99 latency of each route
For every route that takes an id, log in as customer A, request customer B's object, and expect the same 404 as a missing id
A unit test of the JWT verification function
explain: BOLA happens to authenticated callers, so tests without a token pass while the bug is present. Only a test that crosses ownership, customer A asking for customer B's object, exercises the missing check; token verification tests cover API2, not API1.

q: The BFF (Express 5) uses app.use(express.json()) with no options. A client posts a 101 KiB JSON body. What happens?
options: It is parsed normally; Express has no default limit
413 with the error type entity.too.large, because the default limit is 100 KB
The connection is reset without a response
400 with a JSON syntax error
explain: Measured: a body just under 100 KiB returned 200 and a 101 KiB body returned 413 entity.too.large. Fastify's default bodyLimit is 1 MiB (also measured, with FST_ERR_CTP_BODY_TOO_LARGE); set the limit your API actually needs.

q: A popular package's maintainer account is phished and a malicious version is published at 14:00; it is detected and removed at 16:30. The Orders API's CI runs pnpm install at 15:00 with pnpm 12 defaults. What protects it?
options: The lockfile alone, whatever the version range
pnpm audit, which flags the version as soon as it is published
Nothing, because the version satisfies the semver range
minimumReleaseAge (1,440 minutes by default) skips versions published less than a day ago, and dependency install scripts are blocked unless allowed
explain: pnpm's documentation lists minimumReleaseAge: 1440 and blocked dependency builds as defaults; together they avoid most hours-long compromises like the September 2025 ones. A lockfile helps only if CI installs it frozen and nobody updates it in that window, and an audit database knows about a malicious version only after someone reports it.

q: The Orders API's Dockerfile contains ARG NPM_TOKEN and RUN npm ci with the token, and the image is pushed to a shared registry. What is wrong, and what is the fix?
options: Nothing, as long as the registry is private to the company
The token must be passed with ENV instead of ARG
Build arguments persist in the image, so anyone who pulls it can read the token; use a build secret (RUN --mount=type=secret) and rotate the token
The token is safe because registries encrypt images at rest
explain: Docker's documentation says build arguments and environment variables are inappropriate for secrets because they persist in the final image, where anyone who pulls it can read them. Build secrets are mounted only for the RUN step, and a token that may have leaked must be rotated.

q: The product JSON is identical for every shopper. You want the CDN to keep it for 5 minutes, browsers for 1 minute, and the CDN to keep serving it for 10 more minutes while it refreshes. Which header?
options: private, max-age=300, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=600
public, max-age=60, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=600
no-cache, max-age=60, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=600
public, no-store, max-age=60, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=600
explain: s-maxage sets the freshness for shared caches such as a CDN and overrides max-age there, while browsers use max-age. stale-while-revalidate allows serving the stale copy while refreshing. private forbids the CDN from storing it at all, and no-store forbids every cache.

q: What does Cache-Control: no-cache mean on a response?
options: No cache of any kind may store the response; it must be fetched from the server every time.
Only the browser may store it; a CDN or proxy must forward every request to the server.
Caches may store it, but must revalidate it with the server before each reuse.
Caches store it but serve it only while the origin server is down or answering with errors.
explain: Per MDN, no-cache allows storage but requires revalidation before every reuse, typically answered with 304 Not Modified. The directive that forbids storage is no-store; confusing the two is the common mistake. Serving stale on errors is stale-if-error.

q: Why must an in-process cache in front of Redis have a short TTL, of seconds rather than minutes?
options: Because lru-cache cannot keep an entry for longer than one minute, whatever ttl you pass.
Because with a long TTL, lru-cache evicts the most frequently read keys first to make room.
Because Redis closes the connection of clients that keep a local copy of its keys for too long.
A Redis DEL does not reach the other replicas' copies; only their TTL bounds staleness.
explain: Each Node instance keeps its own copy, and the write path only deletes the Redis key. Nothing tells the other replicas, so their TTL (or a broadcast such as Redis pub/sub) is the only bound on staleness. lru-cache has no such duration limit, and an LRU evicts the least recently used entries, not hot ones.

q: You start a new Node service that talks to Redis 8. Which client do you pick, as of October 2026?
options: node-redis (the redis package), the client the Redis docs recommend.
ioredis, because Redis Inc. now develops it more actively than any other Node client.
kafkajs, because the same client speaks both the Kafka and the Redis protocols.
iovalkey, because Redis 8 only accepts connections from clients that also support Valkey.
explain: The Redis docs recommend node-redis for Node.js, and the ioredis README says its maintenance is best-effort and that node-redis is recommended for new projects. iovalkey is a fork of ioredis that tracks Valkey; it is not required for Redis. kafkajs is a Kafka client.

q: An admin changes the price of product 42, which is cached with cache-aside. What should the write path do?
options: Delete the key first, then update the database, so that no reader can see the old price.
Update the database, then write the new price into the cache so that the next read is a hit.
Update the database, then delete the key once the transaction has committed.
Update the database only, and let the TTL replace the old price when it expires.
explain: Deleting after the commit means the next read loads the new row. Deleting before lets a reader reload the old row in between and cache it for a whole TTL. Writing the value instead of deleting can leave the older of two concurrent updates in the cache, and relying on the TTL alone serves the old price until it expires.

q: The product response now includes the member discount of the logged-in shopper, and it is still cached under catalogue:v3:product:42:fr-FR. What do you change?
options: Lower the TTL to 10 seconds so that a wrong discount never stays visible for long.
Cache only the shared product data, and apply the discount per request after reading it.
Add random jitter to the TTL so that two shoppers rarely read the same cached entry.
Move this cache into an in-process LRU so that each replica keeps its own copy of the entry.
explain: Per-user data under a shared key is a data leak: the next shopper reads the first shopper's discount. Keep the key for what is the same for everyone and compute the personal part per request. A shorter TTL or a local cache only makes the leak shorter or spreads it differently; jitter changes when keys expire, not who reads them.

q: A cache without request coalescing receives 100 concurrent reads of the same cold key, while the 50 ms database load is running. How many times does the loader run?
options: Once
Twice
About 50 times
100 times
explain: Every read that misses before the first load has stored a value starts its own load. Measured on Node 24: 100 loader calls without coalescing, 1 with single flight. That pile-up on one expiring key is a cache stampede.

q: A new fraud-detection service must read every order.paid event of the last 7 days, without disturbing the services that already consume them. Which model allows that?
options: A log such as Kafka, where each consumer group reads from its own offset.
A queue such as SQS: the new service receives every message the other services have not deleted yet.
A job queue such as BullMQ: completed jobs are replayed when a new worker process starts.
Any broker, as long as consumers acknowledge each message before they process it.
explain: Kafka's docs state that events are not deleted after consumption and are kept for a per-topic retention period, so a new consumer group can start from the past. A queue deletes messages once processed, and competing consumers split them instead of each seeing all of them. Acknowledging before processing gives at-most-once delivery, not replay.

q: A team starts a Node service that produces to Kafka and plans to use kafkajs. What should you tell them?
options: kafkajs is the client Confluent maintains and supports, so it is the safe default for new services.
kafkajs is fine as long as the topic has fewer than 12 partitions and the messages stay small.
Its last release, 2.2.4, dates from February 2023; prefer Confluent's KafkaJS-compatible client.
Node cannot produce to Kafka directly; the events have to go through SQS or SNS first.
explain: npm shows kafkajs 2.2.4, published in February 2023, as the latest version, and its repository has an open "Looking for maintainers" issue. Confluent publishes @confluentinc/kafka-javascript (1.11.0), built on librdkafka, with a KafkaJS-compatible API and a migration guide. kafkajs was never Confluent's client.

q: Which consumer design gives an exactly-once effect on top of at-least-once delivery?
options: Acknowledge the message before processing it, so that the broker never has a reason to redeliver it.
Insert the message id and apply the effect in one transaction, so the primary key rejects duplicates.
Check with a SELECT whether the id was processed, then apply the effect and insert the id.
Configure the broker for exactly-once delivery, which makes deduplication in the consumer unnecessary.
explain: The primary key decides which delivery wins, and the shared transaction makes the id and the effect commit or roll back together (measured on PGlite: a failed effect left no id behind). Acknowledging first gives at-most-once and can lose messages. Select-then-insert lets two concurrent deliveries both pass the check, and broker guarantees stop at the broker.

q: The payment webhook commits the paid status of order 981, then publishes order.paid. The replica is killed between the two calls. What is the result?
options: The broker publishes the event when the process restarts.
PostgreSQL rolls the paid status back because the publish did not happen.
The event is published twice when the process restarts.
The order is paid, but no other service will ever hear about it.
explain: This is the dual-write problem: two systems and no transaction across them, so nothing remembers that a publish was due. The transactional outbox fixes it by committing the event as a row in the same transaction as the paid status and letting a relay publish it later.

q: After a deploy, shoppers report seeing someone else's cart. The cart route sits behind a CDN and now returns the header below. What do you ship?
code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: max-age=0, s-maxage=60
Content-Type: application/json
options: Send private, no-store: s-maxage lets the CDN share one cart with everyone.
Lower s-maxage to 5 seconds, so that a wrong cart stays visible for a much shorter time.
Add stale-while-revalidate=0 so that the CDN never serves a stale copy of a cart.
Keep the header and add the user id inside the JSON body, so that the client can detect a wrong cart.
explain: MDN notes that s-maxage, like public, allows a shared cache to store a response to a request carrying Authorization. Per-user responses need private (no shared storage) or no-store. A shorter s-maxage still leaks carts, only for less time.

q: A shopper opens product 981 ten seconds before the catalogue team creates it. What do shoppers see next, with this read path?
options: The product at once, because creating a row in the database bypasses the cache entirely.
The product after the next deploy, because every deploy flushes the Redis instance.
A "not found" for up to a day: negative results need a short TTL.
An error page, because Redis refuses to store a JSON value whose found field is false.
explain: The negative result is cached for 86,400 seconds, so every read hits the cached "not found" until it expires. Negative caching protects the database from repeated lookups of missing ids, but its TTL must be short (seconds), and a create should delete the key like any other write. Redis stores any string, and a deploy does not flush it.

q: To get coalescing for free, a developer caches the loader's promise. The first load fails. What does this print?
options: db timeout, ok, ok, then calls 2
db timeout three times, then calls 1
db timeout, db timeout, ok, then calls 3
An unhandled rejection stops the process after the first line
explain: A cached promise caches its rejection: the map keeps the rejected promise and every later call gets the same error without calling the loader. Measured on Node 24: three "db timeout" and calls 1. Each await has a .catch, so there is no unhandled rejection. Remove the in-flight entry when the load settles and store only successful values.

q: A reader starts loading product 42 with a 50 ms query. 5 ms later an admin commits a new price and deletes the key. The reader's query had already read the old row. What is in the cache afterwards?
options: Nothing at all, because the delete was the last operation that touched the key.
The new price, because a delete forces every reader that is still running to reload.
An error, because Redis rejects a SET on a key that was deleted during the load.
The old price, until the TTL expires: the slow load writes after the delete.
explain: The load finishes after the invalidation and writes what it read before the update. Measured on Node 24 with the same timings: the cache ended with the old value. The TTL bounds the damage; a version number in the key or a short TTL on that data narrows the window.

q: Your API runs 20 replicas, each with in-process single flight in front of Redis. A hot key expires in Redis at peak traffic. How many database loads can that cause at most, and what reduces it further?
options: Up to 20, one per replica; a shared lock or stale-while-revalidate goes further.
One, because single flight is coordinated across replicas through Redis itself.
As many as there are requests, because single flight only protects a single caller at a time.
None, because Redis reloads expired keys from the database by itself before they are read.
explain: Single flight shares a promise inside one process only, so each replica can start one load. To go lower you need something shared or something that avoids the miss: serve the stale value while one caller refreshes, refresh early with a probability, or let one caller win a Redis lock. Redis never loads data from your database.

q: With XFetch, a value took 200 ms to compute and beta = 1. Over 100,000 reads, how often does a read refresh early with 60 s left, and with 50 ms left?
options: Never with 60 s left, and every single time once only 50 ms are left.
About 1% of reads with 60 s left, and about 10% of reads with 50 ms left.
Practically never with 60 s left, and about 78% of reads with 50 ms left.
About 50% in both cases, because Math.random() is uniform.
explain: The head start -computeMs * ln(random) is exponentially distributed, so the chance to refresh is about e^(-remaining / computeMs). Measured: 0.000 with 60 s left, 0.007 with 1 s, 0.368 with 200 ms and 0.779 with 50 ms. It is never certain, which is why one reader, not all of them, usually refreshes first.

q: Each of 12 API replicas keeps a 10-minute lru-cache in front of Redis. After a price change, the write path deletes the Redis key. What do shoppers see, and what is the usual fix?
options: The new price at once, because lru-cache subscribes to Redis keyspace deletions by default.
The old price for up to 10 minutes; shorten the L1 TTL or broadcast invalidations.
The old price until the next deploy, because in-process caches never expire entries on their own.
The old price until the Redis TTL ends, because Redis delays deletes until the key expires.
explain: The local copies know nothing about the Redis DEL, so each replica serves its copy until its own TTL ends. Either keep the L1 TTL short enough to be acceptable staleness, or send an invalidation message to every replica. lru-cache does expire entries by TTL, and Redis applies a DEL immediately.

q: Five teams want the order events; each consumes at its own pace, and analytics must be able to re-read the last 7 days after a bug fix. Which design fits best?
options: A BullMQ queue with one worker per team, each worker reading every job in the queue.
An SNS topic fanned out to one SQS queue per team, each team draining its own queue.
A single RabbitMQ quorum queue shared by the five teams, with one consumer per team.
A Kafka topic keyed by order id, with one consumer group per team.
explain: Kafka keeps the events after consumption, each consumer group has its own offset, and moving an offset back replays the past. SNS to SQS gives each team its own queue and pace, which is a good fit without the replay requirement, but SQS deletes processed messages. A single shared queue makes the teams compete for messages, and a BullMQ queue is built for jobs, not for many independent consumers.

q: The API calls enqueueConfirmation('o-981'), times out, and the client retries, so the add runs twice with jobId: 'confirmation-o-981' while the first job is still waiting. How many emails are queued?
options: Two, because BullMQ queues every call to add.
Two, and the second add rejects with a duplicate-id error.
One: an add with a job id that already exists is ignored.
None: the two adds cancel each other out.
explain: The BullMQ docs state that adding a job with an existing id means it "will just be ignored". An id built from the business key (the order id) turns a retried enqueue into a no-op. Once the job has been removed, the id can be reused; custom ids must not contain a colon.

q: An SQS consumer takes 45 seconds to process a message, and the queue keeps the default visibility timeout. What happens?
options: After 30 s the message reappears and a second consumer may process it in parallel.
SQS waits for the consumer to finish, because the message has already been received once.
The message is deleted after 30 seconds, so the work done by the consumer is lost.
The message moves straight to the dead-letter queue because it exceeded the timeout.
explain: Per the SQS docs, the visibility timeout defaults to 30 seconds and starts when the message is delivered; if it is not deleted in time, it becomes visible again. Set the timeout above the processing time or extend it with ChangeMessageVisibility, and keep the consumer idempotent. The DLQ only receives a message after maxReceiveCount receives.

q: Two deliveries of the same message are handled at the same moment by this consumer. How many points does the customer end up with?
options: 10: the second delivery sees the first one's row and returns duplicate.
20: both checks run before either insert, so both deliveries add the points.
10: the second insert into processed_messages fails and undoes its points.
10: PostgreSQL runs the two handlers one after the other automatically.
explain: Measured on PGlite: both SELECTs ran before either insert, both returned processed, and the balance was 20. Nothing rolls the points back, since each statement commits on its own and ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING does not fail. Insert the id first, in the same transaction as the effect, and let the primary key decide.

q: A consumer inserts the message id into processed_messages in its own auto-committed statement, then applies the effect in a separate transaction. The effect fails on a deadlock. What happens on redelivery?
options: The message is processed normally, because the failed effect was rolled back by its transaction.
The broker detects that processing failed and skips the message to protect the queue.
The id insert is rolled back automatically, together with the effect that failed afterwards.
The id is already recorded, so the redelivery is skipped and the effect is lost.
explain: The id committed on its own before the effect, so the consumer believes the work was done and the message is lost for good. Recording the id and applying the effect must commit together; measured on PGlite, doing both in one transaction left no id behind when the effect threw, and the next delivery succeeded.

q: The payment provider has a 2-minute outage. 2,000 jobs fail and all retry after exactly 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s… The provider recovers but falls over again at each retry wave. What do you change?
options: Raise the number of attempts so that the jobs keep trying for longer after the outage.
Shorten the base delay so that the jobs complete sooner once the provider has recovered.
Add random jitter to the backoff so that the retries spread out.
Retry immediately in a loop until the provider answers, so that no time is wasted.
explain: Exponential backoff without jitter keeps every job on the same schedule, so the retries hit the provider together. Jitter randomises each wait; BullMQ exposes it as jitter on the backoff options, and the AWS Builders' Library article explains the effect. More attempts or shorter delays add load during the outage, and a tight loop is the worst case.

q: The orders topic has 12 partitions and the producer sends events without a key. A consumer sometimes sees order.refunded before order.paid for the same order. Why, and what is the fix?
options: Kafka gives no ordering guarantee at all, so the consumer must sort the events by timestamp.
Without a key, one order's events can land in different partitions; key by order id.
The consumer group has too few members; adding one consumer per partition restores the order.
The topic must have a single partition, which is the only way to get any ordering in Kafka.
explain: Kafka's docs say events with the same key are written to the same partition and each partition is read in write order. Keying by the order id keeps one order's events in sequence while the topic still has 12 partitions of parallelism. One partition would also work but caps the consumer group at one active consumer; adding consumers does not fix ordering.

q: The outbox relay publishes a message, the broker acknowledges it, and the relay crashes before setting published_at. What happens next?
options: It publishes the message again after restarting; consumers deduplicate on the id.
The message is lost, because the broker already had it and the relay never retries it.
The broker recognises the outbox id and silently drops the second copy of the message.
PostgreSQL rolls back the order, since its outbox row was never marked as published.
explain: The row is still unpublished, so the next pass publishes it again: an outbox relay is at-least-once by design. The consumer's processed-messages table absorbs the duplicate. A broker does not know your outbox ids (SQS FIFO deduplication only covers a 5-minute window on sends), and the order committed long before.

q: A relay claims a batch with this query and publishes the rows in the order they come back. In which order are the events published?
code:
UPDATE outbox SET claimed_until = now() + interval '30 seconds'
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT id FROM outbox
  WHERE published_at IS NULL
  ORDER BY created_at
  LIMIT 100
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
RETURNING id, aggregate_id, payload;
options: In created_at order, because the subquery sorts the rows before they are updated.
In primary-key order, because RETURNING always follows the primary-key index.
In no guaranteed order (measured: newest first); sort again in an outer query.
In a random order that changes on every call, because SKIP LOCKED shuffles the rows.
explain: The ORDER BY in the subquery decides which rows are claimed, not the order UPDATE ... RETURNING returns them in. Measured on PGlite (PostgreSQL 18.6): the rows came back newest first. Wrap the update in a CTE and add ORDER BY created_at to the outer SELECT. SKIP LOCKED only skips rows that another transaction has locked; it does not shuffle anything.

q: The Debezium connector that reads the outbox was stopped on Friday. On Sunday the primary database runs out of disk. What happened?
options: The outbox table grew without limit, because Debezium deletes outbox rows only while it runs.
Its replication slot kept all the WAL the connector had not read yet.
PostgreSQL wrote every outbox row twice while the connector was away, to replay them later.
Kafka pushed its retained order events back into the database when the connector stopped.
explain: The PostgreSQL docs warn that replication slots prevent removal of required WAL even when nothing is connected. A stopped CDC connector therefore makes WAL accumulate on the primary: monitor slot lag and drop slots that are no longer used. Debezium does not delete outbox rows, and Kafka never writes back into PostgreSQL.

q: The stock reservation SQL compared quantities the wrong way, and every checkout test used a mocked repository. Which test would have caught the bug most cheaply?
options: A unit test of checkout with a stricter mock of reserve
An integration test of the repository against a real PostgreSQL
An E2E test that buys the last unit through the public API on staging
A snapshot test of the SQL string
explain: Only a test that runs the SQL on a real PostgreSQL can see that it refuses the last unit, and with PGlite or Testcontainers it runs in milliseconds per test. A stricter mock still never runs the SQL, and a snapshot only proves the string did not change, not that it is right.

q: In POST /orders, which piece of code is the best candidate for plain unit tests?
options: The route handler that validates the body and calls the repositories
The SQL statement that reserves stock
The function that computes the cart total with discounts and free shipping
The composition root that wires the real dependencies
explain: A pure rule with many boundary cases (exactly 50.00, a discount that crosses it, a rounding) is exactly what unit tests do well: a table of inputs and outputs, no doubles, microseconds. The handler and the SQL are glue whose bugs only show with the real framework and database, so they belong to integration tests.

q: An in-memory order repository backed by a Map that really stores, filters and sorts orders is which kind of test double?
options: A stub
A spy
A mock
A fake
explain: A fake is a working implementation that takes a shortcut, here memory instead of PostgreSQL. A stub only returns canned answers, a spy records calls, and a mock is checked against expected calls.

q: Why test the PaymentsClient adapter with MSW rather than with vi.fn() replacing fetch?
options: Because vi.fn() cannot return a promise
Because MSW sends the requests to the real payments service in a sandbox
Because with MSW the real fetch, URL building, headers and JSON parsing all run; only the network answer is simulated
Because MSW makes the test independent of the HTTP status codes
explain: MSW intercepts at the network level, so the adapter's whole request and response handling is exercised. A vi.fn() in place of fetch only checks the calls you expected to make. MSW never contacts the real service: unhandled requests warn or fail depending on onUnhandledFrame.

q: What does Vitest 5.0.5 do with this test, where charge(true) rejects with the message card declined?
options: It passes
It passes with a warning about the missing await
It times out after 5 seconds
It fails, because the assertion promise was not awaited
explain: Measured: it fails with “Promise returned by expect(actual).rejects.toThrow(expected) was not awaited”, even though the rejection matches. Write await expect(charge(true)).rejects.toThrow('card declined') in an async test.

q: A bug makes charge() succeed when it should reject. What does this test report?
options: It passes, because the expect inside catch never runs
It fails with “expected PaymentDeclinedError”
It fails with an unhandled rejection
It times out waiting for the rejection
explain: Measured: green with zero assertions run. Adding expect.assertions(1) made it fail with “expected number of assertions to be 1, but got 0”; simpler still is await expect(charge(declinedCard)).rejects.toBeInstanceOf(PaymentDeclinedError).

q: Every test in a file passes, but one test started an async function without awaiting it, and that function threw 10 ms later. What does vitest run do?
options: Reports all green and exits with code 0, since no test failed
Fails the test that started the function
Hangs until the timeout, then exits with code 0
Reports the tests as passed, prints one unhandled error, and exits with code 1
explain: Measured: “Tests 2 passed”, then “Vitest caught 1 unhandled error during the test run”, “Errors 1 error”, and exit code 1. Vitest cannot always tell which test caused it, so it does not mark one as failed, but the run is red. Fix the floating promise; in production it would crash the process.

q: A checkout test asserts expect(orders.update).toHaveBeenCalledWith('ord_1', { status: 'paid' }). A refactor merges two updates into one call and the behaviour stays right. What does this tell you about the test?
options: It pins the implementation: it fails on a harmless refactor and would pass with wrong SQL; checking the stored state would be better
It is a good test: interaction tests should fail on every change of the calls
It is fine, because toHaveBeenCalledWith only compares the first argument
It would pass after the refactor, because Vitest compares calls loosely
explain: A mock checks the conversation, not the outcome, so it breaks when the conversation changes and stays green when the real UPDATE is wrong. Reading the order back from a fake or from PostgreSQL tests the behaviour itself. toHaveBeenCalledWith compares all arguments.

q: After upgrading MSW from 2.x to 3.0.3, the setup still calls server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }). A test now calls a URL with no handler. What happens?
options: MSW throws at listen() because of an unknown option
The request fails with an MSW error, as in v2
MSW returns an empty 200 response
MSW only prints a warning, because the option was renamed to onUnhandledFrame and the old name is ignored
explain: Measured on MSW 3.0.3: with the old option the run printed “[MSW] Warning” (the default) and the request went on to the network; with onUnhandledFrame: 'error' it printed “[MSW] Error”. The v3 release notes list the rename.

q: The payments team renames id to chargeId in the charge response. Your MSW handlers still return id. What would stop this before either side deploys?
options: More unit tests of PaymentsClient with MSW
A nightly E2E run in a shared staging environment
A Pact consumer test whose pact file the payments service verifies in its pipeline, gated by can-i-deploy
Generating TypeScript types from your own MSW handlers
explain: Your MSW handlers only encode your belief, so they stay green. The pact file records that you read id; the provider's verification replays it against its real code and fails on the rename, and can-i-deploy blocks the release. A staging E2E run would catch it only after a deploy.

q: The Orders API also exposes a public partner API, used by dozens of marketplaces you do not know. Which approach to contract checking fits best?
options: Consumer-driven Pact tests, asking each marketplace to send a pact file
Publishing an OpenAPI document, validating responses against it in your tests, and reviewing changes for breaking ones
Mocking each marketplace's client in your own test suite
Relying on E2E tests against your production API
explain: Consumer-driven contracts need consumers who write and share pact files, which unknown external partners will not do. A published OpenAPI document, checked by the provider on every change, is the practical contract. Pact fits a few internal services whose teams cooperate, like orders and payments.

q: The Orders API team has dashboards but cannot explain why checkout is sometimes slow. What is the difference between monitoring and observability?
options: Monitoring uses metrics, observability uses logs.
Monitoring watches conditions decided in advance; observability is having data rich enough to answer new questions without shipping new code.
Observability is the commercial name of monitoring tools sold since 2020.
Monitoring is for infrastructure, observability is for front-end code.
explain: Monitoring answers questions you planned (is the error rate above 1 %?). Observability is a property of the system: its metrics, traces and logs let you ask a new question, such as "only card payments?", during an incident. It is not a split by signal: both use all three.

q: In traceparent: 00-138c098a7695ac4edcfb9373ac0caa0c-8b36f03cdd5e6492-01, sent by the Orders API to the payment provider, what is 8b36f03cdd5e6492?
options: The trace id shared by the whole request.
A signature proving the caller is trusted.
The id of the service that started the trace.
The id of the calling span, which becomes the parent of the receiving service's span.
explain: The W3C format is version, trace id (32 hex), parent span id (16 hex) and flags. The 32-hex field before it is the trace id; the 16-hex field is the caller's span. Nothing in the header is a signature, so it must never be trusted for security.

q: A pino logger is created with redact: ['*.password']. Which values are redacted in this call?
options: All three.
Only user.password.
password and user.password.
None: wildcards need **.
explain: Measured on pino 10.4: only user.password became [Redacted]. The wildcard stands for exactly one level, so it matches neither the top-level key nor the deeper one. List every path you log, and prefer logging only the fields you need.

q: What does pino 10.4 write for logger.error({ error: err }, 'payment failed'), where err is an Error('boom') with err.code = 'E_X'?
options: The message, the stack and the code under error.
Only the stack.
Only {"code":"E_X"} under error: the message and the stack are lost.
The string "[object Error]".
explain: Measured: "error":{"code":"E_X"}. An Error's message and stack are not enumerable, and only the err key has pino's error serializer, which wrote type, message, stack and code. Always log errors as { err }.

q: Why must customerId never be a label of http_requests_total?
options: Every distinct value creates a new time series, so the number of series grows with the number of customers until the metrics backend runs out of memory.
Prometheus labels cannot contain digits.
It would make the counter decrease when a customer is deleted.
Labels are public, so the id would leak to anyone scraping /metrics.
explain: Each label combination is a separate series kept in memory: unbounded values mean unbounded cardinality. Customer ids belong in logs and span attributes, which are designed for high-cardinality data. The /metrics endpoint is internal, so leaking is not the main problem.

q: Out of 1,000 checkouts, 980 take 80 ms and 20 take 2.5 s. Which statement is true?
options: The mean (128.4 ms) and the p99 (128.4 ms) agree, so latency is fine.
The p50 is 2.5 s because slow requests dominate.
The p95 is 2.5 s and the p99 is 80 ms.
The mean is 128.4 ms and looks fine, while the p99 is 2.5 s: one customer in fifty waits that long.
explain: Mean = (980 × 80 + 20 × 2,500) / 1,000 = 128.4 ms. The 990th value is one of the slow ones, so p99 = 2.5 s, while p50 and p95 are 80 ms. That is why latency is recorded as a histogram and read as percentiles.

q: The checkout SLO of the Orders API is: 99.9 % of POST /orders requests answered within 500 ms, over 30 days. What is its error budget?
options: 0.1 % of the checkouts may be slower, the equivalent of 43.2 minutes with every checkout slow over the 30 days.
99.9 % of the checkouts.
0.1 % of the checkouts in every 5-minute window.
8.76 hours per month.
explain: The budget is what the SLO allows to fail: 0.1 %, which over 30 days (43,200 minutes) is the equivalent of 43.2 minutes during which every checkout misses the target. 8.76 hours is 0.1 % of a year, not of a month; and the budget is spent over the whole window, not per 5 minutes.

q: The liveness probe of every Orders API pod runs SELECT 1. PostgreSQL is unreachable for 40 seconds. What happens?
options: Nothing: probes ignore dependency errors.
Kubernetes removes the pods from the Service and adds them back when the database returns.
Every pod fails liveness and is restarted, they all reconnect at once when they boot, and a 40-second blip becomes a longer outage.
Kubernetes restarts the database pod instead.
explain: A failed liveness probe means "restart the container", and the Kubernetes docs warn that wrong liveness probes cause cascading failures. Option B describes readiness, which is exactly why the database check belongs there.

q: What does an event loop utilization (ELU) of 0.97 on an Orders API pod tell you?
options: The pod uses 97 % of its memory limit.
The loop is busy almost all the time, so callbacks queue up and latency rises: look for synchronous CPU work.
97 % of requests are served from the event loop rather than the thread pool.
The garbage collector runs 97 % of the time.
explain: ELU is the fraction of time the loop is busy rather than idle, from 0 to 1. Measured: below 0.01 idle, about 0.8 when blocking 100 ms out of 110. Near 1 the pod is saturated; a CPU profile shows which functions use the time. It says nothing directly about memory.

q: The new payment flow ships behind an OpenFeature flag: flags.getBooleanValue('new-payment-flow', false, context). The flag provider is misconfigured and the flag does not exist. What happens?
options: The call throws and the request fails with a 500.
The call waits until the provider has the flag.
It returns true, so the new flow is used everywhere.
It returns the default false, with an error code FLAG_NOT_FOUND in the evaluation details.
explain: Measured with @openfeature/server-sdk 1.23.0: an unknown flag returned the default value and reported FLAG_NOT_FOUND through getBooleanDetails, without throwing. That is why the default should always be the old, safe behaviour.

q: What is wrong with this manual span?
options: When charge throws, the span is never ended, so it is never exported, and the error is not recorded on it.
startActiveSpan cannot take an async callback.
order.id is too high-cardinality for a span attribute.
The span must be ended before the await, or it measures nothing.
explain: Exactly the failing payments, the ones you need to see, produce no span. Use try/catch/finally: record the exception, set the status to ERROR, and end the span in finally. High-cardinality ids are fine on span attributes; that rule is for metric labels.

q: The Orders API uses parentbased_traceidratio at 10 %. A support engineer finds a checkout log line with "trace_flags":"00" and cannot find its trace in Tempo. What do you tell them?
options: The Collector is losing spans: open an incident.
This is expected: the request was not sampled, but the trace id is still created and propagated, so logs carry it.
The pino instrumentation wrote a fake id because the SDK had not started.
Tempo deletes traces after five minutes.
explain: Measured with a 50 % head sampler: unsampled requests still had trace_id in their logs, with flags 00. If every slow or failed checkout trace must be kept, add tail sampling in the Collector, which decides after seeing the whole trace.

q: What does pino 10.4 write for the last call?
code:
const log = logger.child({ requestId: 'req-1' });
log.info({ requestId: 'dup' }, 'duplicate key');
options: "requestId":"dup" only: the call overrides the binding.
"requestId":"req-1" only: bindings are immutable.
An error, because the key is already bound.
Both keys, "requestId":"req-1" then "requestId":"dup", in the same JSON line.
explain: Measured: {"level":30,"requestId":"req-1",…,"requestId":"dup","msg":"duplicate key"}. pino concatenates for speed, so the line holds a duplicate key, and which value a log backend keeps depends on its parser. Do not reuse bound keys in calls.

q: The payment client logs the headers it sends: log.info({ req: { headers: { Authorization: 'Bearer sk_live_…' } } }, 'calling provider'). The logger has redact: ['req.headers.authorization']. What happens?
options: The token is redacted: pino paths are case-insensitive.
The token is written in clear, because redaction paths are case-sensitive and this object uses Authorization.
pino refuses to log a key that resembles a secret.
The whole headers object is removed.
explain: Measured on pino 10.4: authorization was redacted, Authorization was not. Incoming Node headers are lowercase, which hides the trap until you log an object you built yourself. The safe fix is to not log headers of outgoing calls at all.

q: A histogram has buckets [0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5] and observes 0.03, 0.2, 0.25 and 0.7 seconds. What is the value of _bucket{le="0.25"}?
explain: Buckets are cumulative and le means less than or equal, so 0.03, 0.2 and 0.25 all count. Measured with @prometheus-io/client 0.16.1: 1, 1, 3, 3, 4, 4, and +Inf 4, equal to _count.

q: The Orders API's Dockerfile ends with CMD ["npm", "start"]. Every deploy, pods take exactly 30 seconds to stop and in-flight checkouts are cut. Why?
options: npm does not forward SIGTERM, so Node never runs its shutdown code and Kubernetes sends SIGKILL at the end of the grace period.
npm starts Node in development mode, which ignores signals.
The readiness probe takes 30 seconds to fail.
30 seconds is how long Node needs to garbage-collect before exiting.
explain: The docker-node best practices say to start node directly so signals reach it "instead of npm swallowing them". Kubernetes waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 s by default) after SIGTERM and then kills the process, which matches the symptom exactly.

q: Another team already runs the OTel SDK and a Collector for traces, and stores metrics in Mimir. They need RED metrics for their service. What do you advise?
options: Add prom-client, expose /metrics, and add a Prometheus scrape job.
Write request counts to the logs and compute rates from them in Loki.
Compute p99 in the process and export it as a gauge.
Use OTel metrics from the same SDK: the HTTP instrumentation already records duration histograms, exported over OTLP to the Collector, which writes to Mimir.
explain: Measured: the HTTP instrumentation alone produced http.server.request.duration histograms in seconds. One SDK and one pipeline avoid duplicate instrumentation. prom-client is also deprecated in favour of @prometheus-io/client, and a per-process p99 gauge cannot be aggregated across pods.

q: The checkout fast-burn page fires when the burn rate exceeds 14.4 over the last hour and over the last 5 minutes. Why the 5-minute condition?
options: To page faster: 5 minutes is enough to detect any incident.
Because Prometheus cannot evaluate a 1-hour window alone.
So the alert only fires while the problem is still happening, and stops soon after a fix instead of firing for up to an hour.
To ignore errors from the first 5 minutes after a deploy.
explain: The 1-hour window makes the alert significant (2 % of the monthly budget consumed); the short window confirms the problem is still occurring. That is the multi-window recommendation of the Google SRE workbook. A 5-minute window alone would page on every short spike.

q: On-call is paged several times a week for "CPU above 85 %" while the error rate and latency of the Orders API stay normal. What change would you push for?
options: Raise the threshold to 95 %.
Page on SLO burn rates of symptoms (errors and latency), move CPU to dashboards or tickets, and link a runbook to every page.
Add more pods so CPU stays below 85 %.
Keep the page but route it to a different team.
explain: High CPU with happy users is not an incident; paging on causes trains people to ignore pages. Raising the threshold keeps the same flawed signal. Pages should mean "users are affected or about to be", with a runbook that says what to do.

q: On SIGTERM, the Orders API calls app.close() immediately. During every rolling deploy a few checkouts fail with connection errors. What is missing?
options: Failing readiness and waiting a few seconds first, because Kubernetes updates the endpoints in parallel with SIGTERM, so new requests still arrive just after the signal.
A liveness probe that fails on SIGTERM.
Calling process.exit(0) right after app.close().
A longer keepAliveTimeout.
explain: Per the Kubernetes docs, the control plane evaluates endpoint removal "at the same time" as the kubelet starts the shutdown. If the server stops accepting at once, requests routed in those seconds fail. Failing liveness would make Kubernetes restart the container, which is not the goal.

q: Measured on Fastify 5.12: a request in flight when app.close() was called completed, but app.close() resolved 73 seconds later. What explains it, and what is the fix?
options: The onClose hooks run one per second; register fewer hooks.
The PostgreSQL pool waits for its idle timeout; lower it.
Fastify waits for the readiness probe to fail 3 times.

The connection became idle after close started and was kept for Fastify's 72 s keep-alive timeout; call server.closeIdleConnections() repeatedly during the close, with closeAllConnections() at a deadline.
explain: Fastify's default keepAliveTimeout is 72,000 ms. Idle connections are closed when close starts, but one that becomes idle later is not. With a 250 ms sweep of closeIdleConnections(), the close resolved in 310 ms, well inside the 30 s grace period.

q: The Orders API needs about 90 seconds at boot to warm a pricing cache. Its liveness probe allows 30 seconds, so new pods are killed in a loop. What is the right fix?
options: Remove the liveness probe.
Add a startup probe with a long enough allowance: liveness and readiness only start once it succeeds.
Make liveness check the cache, so it fails until the cache is warm.
Warm the cache after the pod becomes ready, in the request path.
explain: Per the Kubernetes docs, when a startup probe is configured, liveness and readiness are not run until it succeeds. Removing liveness loses protection against stuck processes, and a liveness that checks the cache would restart pods whenever the cache has trouble.

q: Memory of the Orders API grows until the pod is OOMKilled every two days. What is the bug in this code?
options: The await keeps each request's closure alive.
Map keys must be numbers to be collected.
A module-level Map is filled on every order and never evicted, so heap after GC grows with traffic: use a bounded cache with a TTL, or Redis.
The receipt should be stored in a WeakMap keyed by the string id.
explain: This is the measured leak pattern: heap after GC grew by about 7 MiB per 20,000 entries and only dropped after clear(). A WeakMap cannot have string keys, and the closures end when the function returns. Heap snapshot comparison would show the Map in the retainer chain.

q: You suspect a leak in the Orders API and want a heap snapshot from production. How do you take it?
options: Call v8.writeHeapSnapshot() on every pod at once, during peak, to capture the problem.
Remove one pod from the Service (or wait for it to be unready), then take snapshots on it, spaced in time, and compare them.
Take one snapshot right after the pod starts; it is enough to see the leak.
Use process.memoryUsage(), which contains the same data.
explain: Measured: writeHeapSnapshot() blocked for 4.5 s to write 67 MiB, and the Node docs say it needs about twice the heap in memory, which can itself trigger an OOM kill. A leak shows up as growth between snapshots, so one is never enough; memoryUsage only gives totals.

q: The Orders API runs with a 1 GiB memory limit and is OOMKilled under load, with no sign of a leak. Which change do you make first?
options: Set the heap size explicitly below the limit, for example --max-old-space-size-percentage=75 (which uses the cgroup limit) or --max-old-space-size=768, leaving room for Buffers and native memory.
Set --max-old-space-size=1024 so the heap uses the whole limit.
Remove the memory limit from the pod.
Call global.gc() after each request.
explain: The kernel kills the container when the whole process passes the limit, before V8 collects harder; the heap is only part of that memory. The percentage flag's source uses the constrained (cgroup) memory when there is one. A heap equal to the limit leaves no room for anything else.
