q: After a release, checkout p99 doubled, the database is idle, the traces show no slow child span, and ELU is near 1 on every pod. Which tool do you reach for first?
options: Clinic.js doctor, the standard Node tool.
A heap snapshot comparison.
More pods, then wait and see.
A CPU profile: --cpu-prof on a reproduction, or the inspector on one pod, and look at the hottest functions in DevTools.
explain: High ELU with an idle database points to synchronous CPU work in the process, which a CPU profile shows directly. Clinic.js is no longer actively maintained (its README says so), and heap snapshots answer memory questions, not CPU ones.

q: A release renames orders.total to orders.total_cents in the same migration that deploys the new code. The canary shows errors. Why is rollback hard, and what plan avoids it?
options: Canary deploys cannot be rolled back; use blue/green.

The old code still running reads a column that no longer exists, and rolling back the code does not restore it; expand and contract (add the column, write both, backfill, switch reads, drop later) keeps every step reversible.
Rollback is easy: kubectl rollout undo also reverts migrations.
Use a feature flag around the SQL query instead of a migration.
explain: During any progressive rollout, old and new versions run together, so the schema must work for both. kubectl rollout undo only changes the Deployment, never the database. Expand and contract is detailed in M10.

q: In a system design round, what is the interviewer mainly grading?
options: Whether your final diagram matches the architecture the company actually runs
How you reason: clarifying requirements, letting numbers drive choices, and naming what each choice costs
How many technologies you can name and place on the diagram
Whether you finish every step of the method before the time runs out
explain: There is no single right design, so the round grades the reasoning that leads to one. Matching the company's real architecture is not expected, and naming many technologies without a requirement behind them is a negative signal.

q: Which of these is a non-functional requirement for the flash-sale checkout?
options: Customers can reserve one console each
A reservation expires after 10 minutes
Checkout answers in under 300 ms at the 99th percentile during the spike
Customers receive a confirmation e-mail after paying
explain: A non-functional requirement says how well the system must work (latency, availability, scale, durability). The other three describe what the system does, so they are functional. The latency target under the spike is the kind of requirement that later justifies a cheap "sold out" answer from the cache.

q: You assume a million waiting customers, each refreshing the product page every 2 seconds. About how many page reads per second?
options: About 5,000
About 50,000
About 500,000
explain: 1,000,000 customers / 2 seconds = 500,000 reads per second (recomputed in Node). 5,000,000 comes from multiplying by the interval instead of dividing. At that rate the product page and its stock count must come from a CDN or a cache, never from the database.

q: A service handles 1 million requests a day, spread evenly. Roughly how many requests per second is that?
options: About 12
About 120
About 1.2
About 1,200
explain: 1,000,000 / 86,400 seconds ≈ 11.6, so about 12 per second. It is worth memorising: a million a day is a small load that one server handles easily, which is why the peak matters more than the daily total, as the flash sale shows with 1 million attempts in one minute.

q: Three services (e-mails, analytics, accounting) must each read every order.paid event, and a fraud service added next month must be able to replay last week's events. Which block fits?
options: A queue such as SQS, because it delivers each message to a worker
A log such as Kafka, because events stay for a retention period and each consumer reads the stream
A read replica of the orders database
A cache with a long expiry holding the latest events
explain: Kafka documents that events are not deleted after consumption and are kept for a configurable retention, so several consumers read the same stream and a new one can replay it. A queue hands each message to one consumer and deletes it once processed, so it cannot serve three readers plus a replay.

q: The "My orders" page reads from a read replica. Right after paying, a customer opens it and sees the order still waiting for payment. What is happening?
options: The cache-aside pattern returned an expired entry
The primary rejected the payment update and the webhook did not notice
The load balancer sent the request to an unhealthy instance
Replication lag: the read went to a replica that had not yet applied the write
explain: Replicas apply the primary's changes slightly later, so a read sent to a replica just after a write can miss it. The usual fix is read-your-writes: send that customer's reads to the primary for a short time after a write. No cache is involved in the scenario, so cache expiry does not explain it.

q: What does the CAP theorem actually constrain?
options: What a replicated store can do during a network partition: answer possibly stale data, or refuse to answer
Every distributed system at all times: it can only ever have two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance
The trade between latency and consistency when the network is healthy
Whether a database supports transactions across several tables
explain: CAP says that during a partition a system must choose between consistency (latest write or an error) and availability (a non-error answer from every working node). Without a partition both are possible, so "pick two at all times" is the popular misreading. The healthy-network trade between latency and consistency is what PACELC adds.

q: The payment webhook records each event id in a processed_events table. Why must that insert be in the same transaction as the effects?
options: Because PostgreSQL refuses an ON CONFLICT clause outside a transaction
To make the payment provider deliver each event only once
So that a crash leaves either both the id and the effects or neither, and a redelivery applies the effects exactly once
To make the insert faster by batching it with the updates
explain: If the id committed without the effects, a crash would make the redelivery skip work that never happened; if the effects committed without the id, the redelivery would apply them twice. Committing both together gives an exactly-once effect on top of at-least-once delivery. The provider still redelivers; the consumer makes that harmless.

q: A fixed window limiter allows 100 requests per minute. A client sends 100 requests at 59.9 s and 100 more at 60.0 s. How many are accepted?
options: 0, because the client exceeded the limit
explain: The counter resets at the minute boundary, so the second batch lands in a fresh window. Measured on Node 24: the fixed window accepted 200 while a sliding window counter accepted 100. That double burst at the boundary is the classic weakness of the fixed window.

q: A token bucket has capacity 5 and refills 2 tokens per second. A client sends 5 requests at t = 0. When is the next request allowed?
options: At t = 2,500 ms, when the bucket is full again
At t = 1,000 ms
Not before the next minute starts
At t = 500 ms
explain: 2 tokens per second is one token every 500 ms, and one token is enough for one request. Run with the module's token bucket: a sixth request at 0 ms is refused with a 500 ms wait, and the request at 500 ms is allowed. Waiting for a full bucket is not required.

q: The product team wants click counts on every short link. Which redirect status do you return?
options: 302, because caches may reuse a 301 and later clicks would not reach you
301, because it is the fastest for users
308, because it keeps the request method
200 with an HTML page that redirects with JavaScript
explain: RFC 9110 lists 301 and 308 as heuristically cacheable, and says that after a 302 the client ought to keep using the original URL. A cached 301 means clicks you never see and a target you cannot change. 308 has the same caching issue as 301.

q: Why use separate queues per channel and priority (for example push.urgent, push.bulk, sms)?
options: Because each provider requires its own queue technology
To guarantee that each message is delivered exactly once
So that a slow provider or a 10-million campaign cannot delay login codes or other channels
To reduce the storage cost of the queue
explain: One shared queue means a campaign burst or a slow SMS provider holds up everything behind it. Separate queues let urgent messages and healthy channels keep flowing with their own workers. Queue layout does nothing for exactly-once; deduplication handles duplicates.

q: The Orders API runs on 10 replicas behind a load balancer, each with an in-memory limiter of 100 requests per minute per customer. What can one client actually get?
options: Exactly 100 per minute
About 10 per minute
Up to about 1,000 per minute, spread across the replicas
Unlimited, because in-memory state resets on every request
explain: Each replica only counts what it sees, so a client spread evenly gets 10 × 100. The fix is shared state in Redis or Valkey with an atomic update, or dividing the limit by the replica count and accepting the imprecision. In-memory state does not reset per request; it lives as long as the process.

q: A teammate implements the distributed limiter like this. Under load, clients sometimes get more than the limit. Why?
options: The read and the write are two separate commands, so two replicas can both read the same count and both accept
The 60-second expiry resets the counter on every request
Number(null) returns NaN, so the comparison is always false
Redis converts the counter to a float and loses precision
explain: Between the GET and the SET, another replica can run the same GET and see the same value, so both accept the last slot: the check-then-act race of section 5, in Redis. The fix is one atomic operation, an INCR with an expiry or a Lua script, which Redis runs without interleaving other commands. The code uses ?? 0, so a missing key gives 0, not NaN.

q: A checkout attempt is refused, and the next token arrives in 1,001 ms. What do you send in Retry-After?
explain: RFC 9110 defines the delay form of Retry-After as a whole number of seconds. Rounding 1.001 s down to 1 invites a retry that is refused again, so round up to 2. Milliseconds (1001) and decimals (1.001) are not valid values.

q: The Valkey behind your limiters becomes unreachable. What do you do for the general per-customer limit and for the login-attempts limit?
options: Fail closed for both, since an unprotected API is worse than an unavailable one
Fail open for the per-customer limit and log an alert; fail closed for login attempts
Fail open for both, since availability always comes first
Stop the API replicas so the load balancer drains them until Valkey is back
explain: A limiter outage should not become an API outage: Stripe writes that requests should not be affected if Redis goes down. Login limits protect against brute force, and letting every attempt through is exactly what an attacker wants, so they fail closed. Treating both the same ignores what each limit protects.

q: Using the module's createTokenBucket, what does this print?
explain: After 30 s the bucket would hold 39 tokens, but the refill is capped at the capacity of 10, so 10 of the 15 requests pass (measured on Node 24). That cap is what bounds a burst after a quiet period. 15 or 30 would mean the bucket had no capacity limit.

q: The links table outgrows one primary and you must shard it. Which shard key?
options: The creation date, so recent links are stored together
The owner's country, so data stays close to users
A hash of the short code, since every redirect looks up exactly one code
The length of the target URL
explain: The hot path is "find the URL for this code", so hashing the code sends each lookup to exactly one shard and spreads load evenly. Sharding by date puts every new link, and most clicks, on the newest shard: a hot shard. Country gives very uneven shards and still needs the code to find the row.

q: At peak the shortener serves about 11,600 redirects per second. How do you count clicks?
options: Run UPDATE links SET clicks = clicks + 1 inside each redirect, in the same transaction
Publish a click event to a queue or log from the redirect and aggregate counts asynchronously
Use 301 redirects and read the counts from the browser cache
Count clicks in each instance's memory and never persist them
explain: An update per click turns the read path into a write path and makes viral links a hot row with lock contention. An event published to a queue or a log keeps the redirect a single cache read, and counts become eventually consistent, which the requirement allows. 301 hides clicks; memory-only counts are lost on restart.

q: A push worker calls the provider successfully, then crashes before acknowledging the queue message, which is redelivered. How do you avoid a duplicate push?
options: Configure the queue for exactly-once delivery, which solves it end to end
Store a dedup key such as (notification id, channel) and have the worker skip messages already sent
Acknowledge the message before calling the provider
Never retry push notifications
explain: Redelivery is normal at-least-once behaviour, and a dedup key checked before the call keeps duplicates rare. Acknowledging first turns duplicates into lost messages, and no queue setting makes a call to an outside provider exactly-once, since the provider is outside the queue's transaction.

q: The notification service inserts the notification row, commits, then publishes to the queue. Rarely, a notification is never sent. What do you change?
options: Publish to the queue first, then insert the row
Retry the publish three times inside the request
Write an outbox row in the same transaction as the notification and let a relay publish it
Use a faster queue so the gap between commit and publish is smaller
explain: Two separate writes can fail halfway: a crash after the commit and before the publish loses the message. The outbox makes the message part of the same transaction, and a relay publishes it later, at least once. Publishing first just moves the gap (a message for a row that never committed), and retries do not survive a crash.

q: With 10 million users and 5 notifications per user per day, plus the 9:50 push to every user delivered in 10 minutes, what drives the queue and worker sizing?
options: The campaign peak, about 16,700 per second, roughly 29 times the average
The daily total of 50 million, spread evenly over the day
The average of about 580 per second, with 20% headroom
The number of channels, since each needs one worker
explain: 10,000,000 / 600 s ≈ 16,700 per second, against an average of 50,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 580 (recomputed in Node: a ratio of 28.8). Sizing for the average would leave the campaign queued for hours. Queues absorb the burst, and autoscaled workers drain it at the rate providers accept.

q: Which of these features of the shop genuinely needs strong consistency?
options: The remaining-stock count shown on the product page
The unread badge count in the app's notification inbox
The "popular now" list on the home page
Taking one of the 10,000 consoles for a customer
explain: Two customers must never both get the last console, so the decision has to come from one authoritative place: a conditional update on the primary. The displayed stock count, badges and popularity lists tolerate a few seconds of delay, so they can be eventually consistent and served from caches or replicas.

q: A team of 8 engineers starts a new product with uncertain traffic. The interviewer asks how you would structure the backend. What is the strongest answer?
options: One microservice per entity from day one, so each can scale independently later
A modular monolith on managed PostgreSQL, with module boundaries that allow extracting a service when a concrete reason appears
A self-hosted Kubernetes cluster with Kafka between every component, to be ready for any scale
Serverless functions for each endpoint, with no shared database
explain: A modular monolith keeps transactions, refactoring and operations cheap for a small team, and strict module boundaries keep a later extraction possible. Splitting before there is a reason (independent scaling, release cadence, team ownership) adds network failures and operating cost with no benefit yet.

q: You finished the flash-sale design. The interviewer says: "Next year, 10 million customers and 100,000 units." What is your first move?
options: Shard the database, since it will be the bottleneck
Move every component to microservices so each scales alone
Redo the estimates and find which component crosses its limit first
Double every component's capacity, then multiply by five
explain: Scaling starts from numbers: attempts go from about 16,700 to about 167,000 per second and page reads to 5 million, while payments (about 170 per second) still fit one primary. So the stock row, the cache and the CDN are what change. Sharding first scales the part that was not the problem.

q: Your database waits until a replica in another region confirms each write before answering the client. No network partition is happening. In PACELC terms, what are you trading?
options: Availability for partition tolerance
Consistency for availability
Durability for throughput
Latency for consistency: each write is slower so that both regions agree
explain: PACELC says that Else, when there is no partition, a system trades latency against consistency. Waiting for the remote replica adds a cross-region round trip to every write in exchange for consistent data in both regions. Consistency versus availability is the choice CAP describes during a partition, which is not happening here.

q: A team of four starts a new service on AWS. Nobody in the company runs Kubernetes today. Which platform is the usual default in 2026?
options: EKS with managed node groups, so the team can grow into Kubernetes later
ECS on Fargate, with one service per container image
Lambda for every route, behind API Gateway
EC2 virtual machines running PM2 in cluster mode
explain: ECS on Fargate runs containers without servers or a cluster to upgrade, which suits a small team with no Kubernetes skills. EKS is the right call when the company already operates Kubernetes and its ecosystem; adopting it "for later" means owning nodes, add-ons and upgrades now. Lambda fits scheduled or spiky work better than a whole service.

q: Why does the Dockerfile copy package.json and package-lock.json, run npm ci, and only then copy src?
options: So the install layer stays cached when only the source changes
Because npm ci refuses to run when source files are present
To make the final image smaller, since fewer files are copied into it
Because COPY src fails unless node_modules already exists in the stage
explain: Per Docker's cache docs, when a layer changes, every layer after it is rebuilt. Copying the manifests first means a commit that changes only src reuses the cached npm ci layer. The order does not change the size of the final image; the multi-stage build does that.

q: The build stage stays on node:24-trixie-slim, but someone switches only the runtime stage to node:24-alpine to save space. The service uses a native addon compiled during npm ci. What is the risk?
options: Alpine images cannot run as a non-root user, so the pod security context rejects them
There is no Node 24 image for Alpine, so the stage silently falls back to an older Node
Alpine uses musl, not glibc, so the addon built in the Debian stage may not load
Alpine images end up larger than slim ones once the addon's libraries are added
explain: The docker-node README states that Alpine uses musl libc and that programs built for Debian's glibc in general do not run on it. The addon was compiled against glibc in the build stage, so it can fail at runtime. Alpine is in fact about 25 % smaller than slim, which is why people try it; build and run on the same libc.

q: The Dockerfile ends with CMD node dist/server.js (shell form). What happens on docker stop?
options: Node receives SIGTERM directly and runs its graceful shutdown handler
Docker sends SIGINT for shell-form commands instead, and Node exits on SIGINT by default
The container restarts at once, because the shell exits with code 143
/bin/sh -c does not pass the signal, so the container is killed after 10 seconds
explain: Docker's reference says the shell form runs the command under /bin/sh -c, which does not pass signals, so the program does not receive SIGTERM from docker stop. After the 10-second default the daemon sends SIGKILL, and requests in flight are cut. The exec form ["node", "dist/server.js"] fixes it.

q: Why does the workflow reference actions/checkout@3d3c42e… instead of actions/checkout@v7?
options: A tag can be moved to other code; a full commit SHA cannot
GitHub runs SHA-pinned actions faster, because their code is cached on the runner image
Version tags are not allowed for actions published by GitHub
A SHA makes the action update itself to the latest release
explain: GitHub's security guide says a tag "can be moved or deleted" if someone gains access to the action's repository. That happened in March 2026, when 76 of the 77 tags of trivy-action were force-pushed to malicious code. A SHA pins the exact code; updates come from a bot such as Dependabot proposing a new SHA.

q: The ECR repository has tag immutability on. A script tries to push a hotfix build under the tag 3f9c2a1, which the current release already uses. What happens?
options: ECR moves the tag to the new image and keeps the old image untagged in the repository
ECR stores both images under the same tag
The push is rejected with ImageTagAlreadyExistsException
ECR accepts the push but blocks pulls of the new image
explain: Per the ECR docs, once tag immutability is on, pushing an image with a tag already in the repository returns ImageTagAlreadyExistsException. That guarantee is what makes "this tag means this commit" true. Overwriting the tag is what a mutable repository, the default, would do.

q: In the deploy role's trust policy, what does the condition sub = repo:shop/orders-api:environment:production achieve?
options: It gives the role access to the production AWS account
Only that repository's jobs targeting production can assume the role
It keeps the temporary credentials valid until the environment is deleted in GitHub
It encrypts the OIDC token with the environment's secrets
explain: The sub claim of GitHub's OIDC token names the repository and the context of the job; with an environment, it is repo:ORG/REPO:environment:NAME. Matching it with StringEquals means a pull request run (subject …:pull_request) or another repository cannot assume the role. The condition restricts who; the permissions policy decides what.

q: The Orders API pods use EKS Pod Identity. What must the application code do to get AWS credentials?
options: Call STS AssumeRole at startup with the role ARN, then refresh it every hour
Read the access key and secret from a Kubernetes Secret mounted into the pod
Pass the service account token to every client constructor
Nothing: clients created without credentials use the SDK's default chain
explain: Per the EKS docs, EKS sets environment variables in the pod's containers that point the AWS SDKs to the Pod Identity Agent, which issues temporary, rotated credentials. The default credential chain picks them up, so new S3Client({}) is enough. A static key in a Secret is exactly what Pod Identity removes.

q: With Helm 4, the deploy step runs helm upgrade --install orders-api ./chart with no wait or rollback option. The new pods crash-loop. What does the CI job report?
options: Success: without a wait option, Helm 4 waits only for hooks
Failure: Helm 4 always waits until every pod of the Deployment is ready
Failure, and Helm rolls back to the previous release automatically
The job hangs until the 5-minute default timeout, then fails
explain: Helm 4's upgrade docs give hookOnly as the wait strategy when --wait is omitted, so the command returns once the manifests are applied. Add --wait, or --rollback-on-failure, which also sets the wait to watcher and returns to the last successful release on failure.

q: Why does the export Lambda create its pg pool and its S3 client at the top level of the module, and give the pool max: 1?
options: Top-level code runs again before each invocation, which keeps the connection fresh
Init runs once per environment and is reused; an environment runs one invocation at a time
Lambda forbids opening network connections inside the handler function itself
max: 1 is required by RDS Proxy, which rejects any client pool holding more than one connection
explain: The Lambda docs recommend initialising SDK clients and database connections outside the handler, because the init phase runs once per environment and later invocations reuse them. Each environment serves one request at a time, so a second connection would sit idle and count against the database's limit. Top-level code does not run again for each invocation.

q: Two engineers start terraform apply on the same state at the same moment. The S3 backend has use_lockfile = true. What happens?
options: Both applies run, and the one that finishes last overwrites the state
Terraform merges both plans into one and applies them in order
S3 versioning rejects the second write of the state file
The second run fails to acquire the lock and stops
explain: Locking exists so that one run at a time can write a state. With use_lockfile, generally available since Terraform 1.11, the lock is a file stored next to the state in S3, and the second run fails to acquire it. Versioning only keeps old copies of the state; it does not prevent concurrent writes.

q: An interviewer asks: "Lambda or containers for the Orders API itself?" It serves a steady 400 requests per second all day, each about 80 ms and mostly waiting on PostgreSQL, with Black Friday peaks five times higher, and the company runs EKS. What is the best answer?
options: Lambda, because it scales to zero and is therefore the cheapest option at any traffic level
Lambda behind API Gateway, since cold starts no longer exist on the Node 24 runtime
Containers on the existing EKS cluster, with Lambda kept for side jobs like the export
One large EC2 instance, so that the whole API shares a single connection pool
explain: Steady traffic keeps containers busy, while Lambda would bill every environment for its full duration, database waits included, with one request per environment and one set of connections each. The company already runs EKS, so the marginal cost is low. Scaling to zero helps only workloads with idle time, and cold starts still exist.

q: In review you find this Dockerfile, and the repository has no .dockerignore. What do you ask to fix first?
code:
FROM node:24-trixie-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm install
RUN npm run build
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
options: Multi-stage, manifests before source, npm ci, and a .dockerignore
Switch CMD to the shell form so that environment variables are expanded at start
Move to node:24-alpine first, because the image size is the main risk here
Add EXPOSE 3000, otherwise Kubernetes cannot send traffic to the container
explain: COPY . . before the install rebuilds the dependencies on every commit and, without a .dockerignore, copies the host's node_modules and .env into an image the company can pull. A single stage also ships the compiler and dev dependencies, and npm install does not install the lockfile exactly. The shell form would break signal delivery; EXPOSE is documentation.

q: The image ends with USER node. The pod sets securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true and no runAsUser. What happens when the pod starts?
options: It starts normally, because the node user of the image is not root
It starts as root, because Kubernetes ignores the USER line of the image
Kubernetes replaces the user with uid 65534 (nobody) and starts it
It fails to start: the kubelet cannot verify a non-numeric user
explain: With runAsNonRoot and no runAsUser, the kubelet checks the image's user, and its source returns the error "image has non-numeric user (node), cannot verify user is non-root". Write USER 1000 in the Dockerfile or set runAsUser: 1000. Kubernetes uses the image's user when no runAsUser is set; it does not ignore it.

q: The build installs a private npm package, so a colleague adds ARG NPM_TOKEN and passes it with --build-arg. What do you suggest?
options: It is fine if the next RUN deletes the .npmrc that holds the token
Use a secret mount: build arguments persist in the image
Move the token to an ENV line, because ENV values are not stored in the image
Keep the build argument, but push the image only to a private registry
explain: Docker's documentation says build arguments and ENV values persist in the final image, and M12 treats such a token as leaked to everyone who can pull. A secret mount exposes the token as a file during one RUN without writing it to a layer. Deleting a file in a later layer leaves it in the earlier one, and a private registry does not make the token secret.

q: Two pull requests are merged one minute apart. The second merge cancels the first workflow run while its helm upgrade is halfway through. Which setting causes this, and what is the fix?
options: The group name: use github.sha instead, so that two runs never share a group
Nothing in this block: Helm cancels itself whenever a newer release starts
cancel-in-progress also cancels runs on main: limit it to pull requests
The workflow lacks permissions: actions: write, so GitHub cancels it
explain: GitHub documents that cancel-in-progress: true cancels the running job or workflow in the same group, and every push to main shares the refs/heads/main group. An expression such as github.event_name == 'pull_request' limits cancellation to pull requests, and a deploy-production group with cancel-in-progress: false serialises deploys. A per-SHA group would allow two deploys at once.

q: Production manifests use orders-api:latest, pushed by every merge to main. During an incident, what is the main problem?
options: Nobody knows which commit runs, and there is nothing precise to roll back to
ECR does not scan images whose only tag is latest, so CVEs go unnoticed
Kubernetes refuses to pull an image tagged latest in a production namespace
The latest tag makes every pull download the full image, which slows deploys
explain: A movable tag says nothing about content: a pod rescheduled after a new push can pull a newer image than its neighbours, and "roll back to latest" means nothing. Commit-SHA tags in an immutable repository, deployed by digest, fix all three. ECR scans by image, not by tag name, and Kubernetes pulls latest without complaint.

q: This condition is in the trust policy of orders-api-deploy. What is the risk?
options: None: the audience check already limits the role to the Orders API workflows
Only forks of shop/orders-api in other organisations can now assume the role
The credentials now last 12 hours instead of the default of one hour
Any repository, branch or pull request of the shop organisation can deploy
explain: The wildcard matches every subject that starts with repo:shop/, so every repository, branch and pull request of the organisation qualifies. The audience only proves the token was minted for STS, by any GitHub workflow. Pin the subject with StringEquals to repo:shop/orders-api:environment:production. Session duration is set by the role and the action, not by this condition.

q: Pod Identity is configured for the Orders API, yet CloudTrail shows its S3 calls signed by the IAM user vm-legacy. What is the most likely cause?
options: Pod Identity falls back to IAM users whenever the node agent is overloaded
An old AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID in the pod wins: the SDK checks env vars first
CloudTrail logs Pod Identity calls under the last IAM user that edited the role
The bucket policy forces every request to be signed by that IAM user
explain: The SDK for JavaScript v3 tries fromEnv() before the container credential provider, so leftover static keys silently win. Remove the variables from the pod, then deactivate the key in IAM. CloudTrail records the identity that really signed the request, which is why it reveals the problem.

q: The nightly drift job runs terraform plan -detailed-exitcode on production and exits with code 2. What does it mean, and what do you do?
options: Terraform crashed during the refresh; rerunning the job usually clears it
The state is locked by another run; delete the lock file and rerun
Changes are present: inspect them, then codify or revert
No changes: exit code 2 only means that two providers were checked
explain: Per the plan docs, exit code 0 is an empty diff, 1 an error, and 2 a successful plan with changes. A refresh-only plan shows what changed outside Terraform; the team then writes the change into the code or applies to undo it, after reading the plan. Never auto-apply a drift fix: the console change may have been an incident fix.

q: Version 42 renamed orders.total to orders.total_cents in the same migration and is broken. The team rolls back to the digest of version 41. What happens?
options: Version 41 fails on queries that read orders.total
The rollback also reverts the migration, so version 41 works again
Helm detects the schema change and refuses to roll the release back
Kubernetes keeps the version 42 pods running until the migration is undone
explain: Redeploying a digest changes the code, never the database. A rename in one step breaks the previous version, which is why migrations follow expand and contract (M10): add the new column, write both, switch reads, and drop the old one only when no running version needs it. Neither Helm nor Kubernetes knows anything about the schema.

q: The repository is private, the company is on GitHub Team, and the production environment lists two required reviewers. Deploys still run without any approval. Why?
options: Required reviewers only apply to jobs that read secrets from the environment
The deploy job also needs permissions: deployments: write to request approval
Approvals given on earlier runs carry over to the following runs
On Free, Pro and Team, required reviewers work only in public repositories
explain: GitHub's environments documentation states that on the Free, Pro and Team plans, required reviewers and wait timers are only available for public repositories. A private repository needs a higher plan for this gate, or another one, such as a protected branch that only release managers can push to. Approvals are per run; they do not carry over.

q: The export Lambda used to e-mail a presigned link created with expiresIn of seven days. Customers report that links fail after a few hours. Why, and what is the fix?
options: S3 caps presigned URLs at one hour, so the e-mail must be resent every hour
It expired with the role's temporary credentials; sign at click time
A bucket lifecycle rule deleted the files; lifecycle rules must be disabled
Seven days exceeds the SDK maximum, so it silently signs for one hour
explain: Per the S3 docs, a URL signed with temporary credentials expires when those credentials do, even if it asked for longer; seven days is only possible with long-term IAM user credentials, which the team just removed. Signing at click time in GET /exports/orders.csv keeps links short-lived and needs no long-term key. The CLI and SDKs accept up to seven days.

q: EventBridge Scheduler retried the nightly export after a timeout, and finance found two files for the same night: orders-2026-10-29-a81f.csv and orders-2026-10-29-c3d0.csv. Which change makes retries safe?
options: Turn off retries on the schedule, so each night runs exactly once
Add a random delay before the export so two attempts never overlap
Derive the key from the scheduled time, so a retry overwrites
Raise the Lambda timeout to 15 minutes so the export never times out
explain: Scheduler delivers at least once, so the handler must be idempotent; the scheduled time is the same for every attempt of a run, so a key derived from it turns a retry into an overwrite. Turning retries off trades duplicates for missing exports, and a longer timeout reduces retries without removing them.

q: The team considers moving the payment webhook to Lambda. On Black Friday it receives 2,000 calls per second, each taking 0.5 s. What happens with default settings?
options: 1,000 environments: the whole default regional quota, and 1,000 connections
4,000 environments, and Lambda queues the extra calls until one is free
A single environment, because Node handles all those concurrent calls asynchronously
2,000 environments, one for each call arriving in the same second
explain: Concurrency = 2,000 requests per second × 0.5 s = 1,000, which equals the default per-region concurrency quota, so the other functions of the account get throttled too. Each environment handles one request at a time and opens its own connections, ten times PostgreSQL's default limit of 100, so this design also needs RDS Proxy and reserved concurrency.

q: After moving aws_db_instance.orders into modules/postgres, the plan shows the old address "will be destroyed" and module.orders_db.aws_db_instance.this "will be created". What is the right fix?
options: Apply, then restore the database from the final snapshot
Run terraform apply -refresh-only so Terraform notices the move
Add create_before_destroy so the new database exists before the old one goes
Add a moved block from the old address to the new one
explain: Terraform tracks objects by address, so a new address looks like a new resource and the missing one like a deletion. A moved block renames the address in the state without touching the object. create_before_destroy would create a second, empty database; restoring from a snapshot loses every order written since.

q: A "cleanup" pull request deletes the whole module "orders_db" call. Inside the module, the RDS resource has lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }. What actually stops the database from being deleted?
options: prevent_destroy, which stays recorded in the state after the block is removed
deletion_protection, which AWS enforces whatever the tool
Nothing: once merged, the apply deletes the database whatever is set
The S3 backend, which refuses plans that remove whole modules
explain: The lifecycle docs say prevent_destroy does not prevent destruction once the resource's configuration is removed, because the setting disappears with the block. deletion_protection is an attribute of the AWS instance, so RDS refuses the delete call. A plan guard on protected types and a final snapshot add two more layers.

q: The guard script of section 11 runs on this plan.json. What does it print, and with which exit code?
options: "No protected resource is deleted." with exit code 0, because the database is recreated first
Both addresses, because both plans contain a delete
It flags module.orders_db.aws_db_instance.this (create, delete) and exits with code 1
It throws, because ["create", "delete"] is not a valid action list
explain: A replacement is written as two actions, and includes('delete') catches both orders, as Terraform's JSON format docs intend; create-before-destroy still destroys the old database. The SQS queue is not a protected type, so only the database is listed. Measured on Node 24.11 with this exact plan: one line, exit code 1.

q: Each module connects with its own PostgreSQL role, and ordering_module was only granted rights on schema ordering. What happens when Ordering code runs SELECT * FROM payments.payments?
options: It fails with 42501 permission denied for schema payments
It works, because both schemas live in the same database and the same cluster
It returns an empty result set
It works for SELECT and fails only for INSERT
explain: Without USAGE on the schema, the role cannot even reach the objects inside it: measured on PostgreSQL 18.6 (PGlite), both the select and a join failed with 42501. Being in the same database grants nothing by itself; privileges are per schema and per table, which turns the module boundary into a runtime rule.

q: What distinguishes the integration event shop.ordering.order-placed.v1 from the domain event OrderPlaced?
options: Nothing: they are two names for the same object, used in different folders
It is raised before the commit, while the domain event is raised after it
It is a versioned public contract in plain data, delivered after the commit
It may only be consumed by handlers that run inside the same Node.js process
explain: Domain events are internal to a module and change with its model; integration events are a published contract, plain JSON with a version, and per Microsoft's guide should occur only if the change was persisted. The second option reverses the timing, and in-process consumption describes domain events.

q: Several consumers read order-placed.v1. Which change can ship without a new event type?
options: Renaming totalCents to amountMinor
Adding an optional couponCode field
Sending totalCents in euros instead of cents
Removing the lines field that Invoicing reads
explain: Adding an optional field is additive: tolerant readers ignore it (measured with Zod 4.6.7, an extra field was simply dropped). Renaming, removing a field someone reads, or changing a unit are breaking; the unit change is the most dangerous, because the type stays a number and nothing fails loudly.

q: What does CQRS mean in the back-office example?
options: Writes go through aggregates; the search reads a separate model built from events
Every request goes through a CommandBus or a QueryBus, as in @nestjs/cqrs
Commands use POST and PUT while queries use GET, on separate controllers per screen
Reads go to a PostgreSQL replica of the same tables, writes to the primary
explain: CQRS uses a different model to update information than to read it (Fowler): here a denormalised order_summaries table fed by events. Buses are a dispatch mechanism and give no separate model on their own, and a read replica serves the same model from another server.

q: With event sourcing, what does the payment ledger store?
options: The current amounts of each payment, plus an updated_at column per row
The current amounts, plus a full copy of the row in an audit table after each change
Every event of each payment, in order; the state is computed by replaying them
Only the most recent event of each payment
explain: Event sourcing captures all changes as a sequence of events, and the state is a fold of the stream (evolve in section 10). Copies of the row after each change are an audit table: they show what the row became, not what happened, such as a refund versus a correction.

q: ADR-006 said "keep Payments in the monolith". A year later the team decides to extract it. What happens to ADR-006?
options: It is deleted, so that nobody follows an outdated decision by mistake
It is edited in place so that it describes the new decision
It stays unchanged, and the new decision is written in the wiki
It is kept as it is, marked superseded by a new, numbered ADR that links to it
explain: Nygard's format numbers ADRs sequentially and keeps reversed decisions, marked superseded, so the history of why stays readable. Editing or deleting the old record loses the context in which it was the right call, which is the main reason to keep ADRs at all.

q: With this dependency-cruiser rule, which import fails the CI job?
options: src/modules/ordering/application/place-order.ts imports src/modules/ordering/domain/order.ts
src/modules/ordering/index.ts imports src/modules/payments/domain/payment.ts
src/modules/ordering/http/orders.ts imports src/modules/payments/index.ts
src/main.ts imports src/modules/payments/infrastructure/pg-payments.ts
explain: Even the module's own index.ts matches the from path, so $1 is ordering; the target is in another module and is neither under src/modules/ordering/ nor an index.ts, so the rule fires (checked by evaluating the rule's regular expressions on these four paths). Imports inside the module and into another module's index.ts are excluded by pathNot, and src/main.ts, the composition root, does not match the from path at all.

q: Payments publishes payment-captured; Ordering sends "issue the invoice for ord_42" to Invoicing. How do you classify them?
options: An event, then a command; both of them travel as messages through channels
Both are events, because both are published through the same broker topic
Both are commands, because both cause another context to do some work
A command, then an event, because the invoice is the fact being recorded
explain: An event states something that happened and expects no reply; a command asks one receiver to act (Fowler, and the command and event messages of Enterprise Integration Patterns). Message is the envelope, not a third kind of intent, and travelling through the same broker says nothing about intent.

q: After payment-captured, Invoicing issues an invoice and Loyalty adds points, independently. At checkout, a failed payment must release the reserved stock and cancel the order. Which coordination fits each?
options: Orchestration for both, so that one component sees and controls every step of each flow
Choreography for both, with compensating events published by each service on failure
Orchestration for invoicing and loyalty, choreography with compensations for checkout
Choreography for the independent reactions, a saga with orchestration for checkout
explain: Independent reactions to a fact suit choreography: each consumer subscribes and the producer does not know them. A multi-step flow with money and compensations is easier to follow, time out and support with an orchestrator, as the saga of M13 shows. Choreographing checkout spreads the flow over several services, so nobody sees it whole.

q: On each order-placed event, Invoicing calls Ordering's API to fetch the lines. During the sale, Ordering slows down and invoicing falls hours behind. Which change addresses the cause?
options: Give Invoicing more replicas so that it can process the backlog of events in parallel
Carry the lines in the event itself, so that Invoicing stops calling Ordering back
Cache Ordering's API responses inside Invoicing for 24 hours to absorb the peak
Have Ordering call Invoicing synchronously instead, so invoices never lag behind
explain: A notification followed by a call back ties the consumer to the producer's load and uptime; carrying the needed data removes the call, so consumers do not need to contact the source (Fowler). The cost is data copies and a larger contract to version. More Invoicing replicas would only add load to the struggling Ordering module.

q: With readOrderPlaced from section 8, what does this print?
options: A ZodError, because couponCode is not in the v1 schema
{"orderId":"ord_981","totalCents":1999,"currency":"EUR","couponCode":"BF26"}
{"orderId":"ord_981","total":{"amountMinor":1999,"currency":"EUR"}}
An UnknownEventTypeError, because v1 is no longer the current version
explain: z.object drops unknown keys, so the extra field is ignored (a tolerant reader), and the v1 branch upcasts the event to the v2 shape. Measured with Zod 4.6.7: exactly that output. z.strictObject would have rejected the extra key, which is the wrong choice for an event consumer.

q: Your Kafka topic uses Confluent Schema Registry with its default compatibility, BACKWARD. You add an optional field to the schema. In which order do you deploy?
options: Consumers first, then producers
Producers first, then consumers
Both at the same time, in one release
The order does not matter with BACKWARD
explain: Confluent documents that with BACKWARD, consumers using the new schema can read data produced with the last schema, so you upgrade all consumers before you start producing new events. Producers first is the FORWARD order, and "either order" is FULL compatibility.

q: "How do you test event-driven services?" Which answer would you give?
options: Only end-to-end tests with every service and a real broker, since unit tests cannot see the messages
Mock the broker client in each test and assert that publish was called with the right topic
Mostly manual tests in staging, because message timing is unpredictable in automated tests
Handlers tested with fixture events, contracts with Pact, a few end-to-end tests
explain: Separating the payload handler from the transport makes most tests fast and precise, and Pact checks that the consumer can handle a message and that the provider produces it. A thin layer of end-to-end tests with Testcontainers covers the wiring. Mocking the broker client proves a method was called, not that the message is right.

q: The payment event arrives before the order event, and the order event is delivered twice. With the projector of section 9, what is in order_summaries afterwards?
options: Two rows for ord_42, one per producer
One complete row: customer cus_7, total 49,998, payment pay_7
An error on the first call, because the order row does not exist yet
One row with the customer and the total, but no payment id, because the payment came too early
explain: Each event upserts only its own columns, so the early payment created a partial row and the order event completed it, while the duplicate was skipped by processed_events. Measured on PGlite: one row with all three values and two recorded event ids. An UPDATE-only projector would have lost the early payment.

q: A colleague says: "We use @nestjs/cqrs, so we do CQRS." What do you check?
options: That every handler class is decorated with @CommandHandler or @QueryHandler
That the QueryBus is faster than calling the service directly, since that is the point of CQRS
Whether a separate read model exists; buses alone only route calls in memory
That the package version matches the NestJS major version used by the rest of the app
explain: CQRS is about separate models for writing and reading; CommandBus and QueryBus only dispatch in-process. The Nest docs also warn that event handlers run in memory and that exception filters cannot catch their errors, so anything that must survive a crash goes through an outbox. @nestjs/cqrs is at 12.1.2 as of October 2026, alongside Nest 12.

q: Two support agents refund 300 EUR on the same captured 499.98 EUR payment at the same moment. With the code of section 10, what happens?
options: One is appended; the other fails with WrongExpectedVersionError and must retry
Both are appended, refunding 600 EUR on a 499.98 EUR payment
Both fail, because each transaction sees the other one's uncommitted row
The second overwrites the first one at version 3, so only the late refund remains
explain: Both read version 2, so both try to write version 3, and the primary key (stream_id, version) accepts only one (measured on PGlite). Reloaded at version 3, decideRefund sees 19,998 cents refundable and throws. Without the expected version, both decisions would have passed on the same stale state.

q: An architect proposes event-sourcing the whole Orders API "so we have the full history everywhere". Which reply shows the trade-off best?
options: Yes: event sourcing makes every query simpler, because every single fact is stored as an event
Yes: it removes the need for schema migrations, because events are never updated
No: event sourcing needs a dedicated event store and cannot run on PostgreSQL at all
Only where history is the requirement, such as the payment ledger: the costs are permanent
explain: Event sourcing pays off where the history itself is needed, and its costs are permanent: every event version must stay readable, queries need projections, long streams need snapshots, and replays must not resend side effects. It makes queries harder, not simpler, and an append-only PostgreSQL table works, as section 10 shows.

q: The team extracts Payments into a service. Which plan avoids a distributed monolith?
options: Deploy the new service and let it keep reading and writing the payments tables in the shared database, to avoid a data migration
A facade routes it step by step; its schema moves to its own database via CDC; others use its API and events
Rewrite Payments from scratch with the new team, then switch all traffic to it in one night
Extract all five contexts at once, so that the boundaries and contracts stay consistent
explain: The strangler fig moves one piece at a time behind a facade, and data ownership keeps the new service's data reachable only through its API. Sharing the old tables keeps the coupling and adds the network: neither side can change the schema or deploy alone. A big-bang rewrite gives up the step-by-step rollback that makes an extraction safe.

q: "When would you not use microservices?" Which answer is the most senior?
options: When latency matters, because a network call is always slower than an in-process function call
When the team lacks Kubernetes experience; otherwise they are the default for any new product
A small team, boundaries still moving, and nothing that must scale, deploy or be owned on its own
When the domain is simple; for a complex domain, start with microservices so each team owns a service
explain: Microservices buy independent deployment, scaling and ownership at the price of running a suite of services, a premium Fowler warns slows teams down, and boundaries are hardest to get right early. Starting with services for a complex domain is the reverse of his observation that successful stories began as monoliths; latency and Kubernetes skills are factors, not the reason.

q: Which situation is the strongest argument for keeping the catalogue in MongoDB rather than PostgreSQL with a jsonb column?
options: The team wants to avoid writing migrations for the orders table
The data needs foreign keys between products, stock and orders
Each product is read as one unit, its fields vary by category, and queries filter on those fields
The product page must join products with customers on every view
explain: MongoDB fits records read as one unit whose shape varies, with normal indexes on fields inside the documents. Foreign keys and joins on every view are arguments for PostgreSQL, and the orders table is relational data that stays in PostgreSQL.

q: Product documents embed every review in an array. A popular product has 60,000 reviews of about 300 bytes each. What happens?
options: The document passes the 16 MiB limit, so the update adding a review is rejected
MongoDB moves the oldest reviews to an overflow collection automatically
The document grows without limit, but reads stay fast because only the needed fields are loaded
The server splits the document into two documents with the same _id
explain: 60,000 × 300 bytes is 18 MB, above the 16 MiB (16,777,216 bytes) BSON document limit, so the write fails. Nothing moves data automatically: the outlier or subset pattern does it by design, in your code. And every read of the product loads the whole array before that point.

q: Which of these writes is atomic in MongoDB without a transaction?
options: Inserting a review and updating its product in two calls
An updateMany that marks 500 reviews as published
Two updateOne calls sent with Promise.all
One updateOne that pushes a preview and increments two counters in the same document
explain: Per the docs, a write is atomic at the level of a single document, even when it modifies several fields. updateMany is atomic per document, not as a whole, and separate calls are independent writes whatever the client-side grouping.

q: The reviews collection is sharded on { createdAt: 1 }. Under launch traffic, one shard is at 100% CPU while the others are idle. Why?
options: createdAt always increases, so every insert goes to the chunk holding the highest values, on one shard
The balancer is disabled during the day
mongos sends every write to the primary shard of the database
Range sharding never spreads data; only hashed sharding does
explain: The shard key docs explain that with a monotonically increasing key, all new inserts are routed to the chunk with maxKey as its upper bound, making its shard the write bottleneck. Range sharding does spread existing data, but not new inserts on a monotonic key.

q: You shard reviews on { _id: 'hashed' }. Writes are now even. What happens to the reviews tab query by productId?
options: It is targeted to one shard, because productId is indexed
It is broadcast to every shard, because it does not contain the shard key
It fails until you add productId to the shard key
It is targeted, because hashed keys support any equality query
explain: mongos targets queries that contain the shard key or a prefix of it; a query on productId contains neither, so it is a scatter-gather to all shards. Having an index on productId on each shard does not tell mongos where the documents live.

q: Why does a resolver that loads "the customer of this order" send 21 queries for a page of 20 orders?
options: graphql-js turns each selected field into its own SQL join, one per order
Each call sees only its own parent order, so it loads one customer
The back office sent one GraphQL operation per order on the page
graphql-js retries every resolver once before returning its value
explain: graphql-js calls the customer resolver once per order, with that order as the parent, so the naive code sends one query per order plus one for the list: 21 measured with graphql-js 16.14.2. GraphQL does not generate joins; batching with DataLoader is the fix.

q: Why are DataLoaders created per request, in the context factory, rather than once at startup?
options: A DataLoader instance can run only one batch, then must be thrown away
Loaders created per request collect more keys in each of their batches
Its cache is per instance: shared, it would leak data across users and go stale
graphql-js refuses a context object that was already used by another request
explain: DataLoader memoises results per instance; its README recommends a new instance per request and warns that its cache does not replace Redis or Memcache. A process-wide loader would leak data between viewers and serve stale rows. Batching works the same either way.

q: The GraphQL server answers 200 for partial results. Which metric tells on-call that the order screen is failing?
options: The rate of 5xx responses returned by /graphql, per minute
The average response size of /graphql, compared with last week
The number of HTTP 4xx responses, grouped by client application
Errors per operation and per extensions.code, read from bodies
explain: Field errors arrive in the errors array next to partial data, usually with a 2xx status, so 5xx and 4xx rates stay flat while the screen breaks. Counting errors per operation and per code from the body is what shows it. Status codes only separate request errors (400, 422 in the draft spec) from executed ones.

q: Order status updates flow only from the server to the customer's browser. Which transport is the sensible default?
options: Server-sent events over HTTP/2
WebSockets with ws
Short polling every second
A GraphQL mutation called every few seconds
explain: SSE is built for one-way push over plain HTTP: cookies, load balancers and logs work unchanged, and EventSource reconnects with Last-Event-ID. WebSockets add a protocol, heartbeats and reconnection you do not need for one-way traffic, and polling every second would cost a request per client per second.

q: What is wrong with this code, which does batch correctly?
options: Nothing: a loader shared across requests batches more keys, so it is faster
The loader must be created inside the resolver function, on every call
load must be awaited inside the resolver, or batching breaks
Its cache lives as long as the process: stale rows, shared across viewers
explain: DataLoader caches per instance, so a module-scope loader is a process-wide cache with no expiry and no per-user scope; the README recommends one instance per request. Creating it inside the resolver would break batching, since each call would get its own loader. Returning the promise without await is fine.

q: This batch function returns the rows as PostgreSQL gives them. Two of the requested ids were deleted. What goes wrong?
options: Values pair with keys by position, so a short array in any order breaks the contract
PostgreSQL rejects = ANY($1) when the parameter is a text array
DataLoader retries the two missing ids one by one, in a second batch
Nothing: DataLoader pairs each row with its key by reading the id field
explain: The DataLoader README requires an array of values of the same length as the keys, where each index corresponds to the same index in the keys. Rows come back in no guaranteed order and missing ids shorten the array. DataLoader never inspects an id field: map rows by id and return ids.map(...) with null for missing ones.

q: A page of 20 orders belongs to 5 distinct customers. With DataLoader's default options, how many keys does the batch function receive?
options: 20, one per order
5, one per distinct customer
1, because DataLoader loads one key per tick
25, the orders plus the customers
explain: With the cache enabled (the default), a key already requested in this loader is not sent again; its promise resolves from the same batch, per the README. Duplicates reach the batch function only with cache: false. Batching sends all distinct keys of the tick at once, not one.

q: The prototype executes queries with graphql-js directly. A resolver throws the error below. What does the client receive?
options: A masked message, "Unexpected error.", with the real one in the logs
An HTTP 500 with an empty body, and the order screen shows nothing
order: null, and the raw message, IP included, in errors
Nothing visible: the field is silently null and errors stays empty
explain: graphql-js puts the thrown message in the error as is (measured), so database addresses leak. Masking to "Unexpected error." is what Yoga does by default; with Apollo Server you mask in formatError. Only a deliberately thrown GraphQLError should reach clients.

q: An agent tries to cancel an order that has already shipped. How should cancelOrder report it?
options: A union result with an OrderAlreadyShipped type and its shippedAt
A thrown GraphQLError, with the HTTP status set to 409 Conflict
null, and the screen tells the agent that something went wrong
CancelOrderSuccess, with a warning added under extensions
explain: An expected business outcome is data the client must act on, so it belongs in the schema as a typed result; generated client types then force the screen to handle it. A thrown error lands in an untyped errors array, and the HTTP status of a GraphQL response does not carry per-field outcomes.

q: The catalogue team wants product queries over GraphQL to be cached by the CDN. What works?
options: Add Cache-Control: public to the POST responses of /graphql
Configure the CDN to use the request body as part of its cache key
Expose the products through subscriptions instead of queries
Persisted query hashes over GET, with Cache-Control on the response
explain: HTTP caches key on method and URL, and every POST to /graphql looks the same. The spec allows GET for queries, and Apollo's docs pair hashed queries over GET with CDN caching, since full queries rarely fit in a cacheable URL. Subscriptions push events and are not cached.

q: Socket.io runs on 6 pods behind a Kubernetes Service without session affinity. Clients keep failing to connect and fall back again and again. What is the likely cause?
options: Socket.io cannot run on more than one pod without its cluster adapter
The Redis adapter is missing, and Socket.io refuses connections without it
Kubernetes Services do not forward the WebSocket upgrade between pods
Long-polling requests of one session land on different pods: no stickiness
explain: Socket.io's docs say long-polling needs sticky sessions because a session spans several HTTP requests that must reach the server holding it; with only the WebSocket transport, one connection stays on one pod. The Redis adapter is about broadcasting across pods, not about connecting.

q: The back office uses SSE over HTTP/1.1. An agent opens order streams in seven tabs, and the seventh never loads. Why?
options: Over HTTP/1.1 a browser opens about 6 connections per domain; use HTTP/2
EventSource supports a single open stream per page and per tab
Node closes the oldest open response once six streams are open
The load balancer pins each agent to one pod, which refuses a seventh stream
explain: MDN documents the limit of 6 connections per browser and domain for SSE over HTTP/1.x; over HTTP/2 the number of streams is negotiated, 100 by default. Nothing in Node or EventSource limits streams per page.

q: Replica 5 holds a customer's SSE stream. While replica 5 spends 2 seconds reconnecting to Redis, replica 2 publishes SHIPPED on the pub/sub channel. What happens?
options: Redis keeps the message until replica 5 subscribes to the channel again
Redis retries the delivery three times, then drops it with a warning
The browser notices, reconnects with Last-Event-ID and gets it
It is lost (at-most-once): resync from the database or use Redis Streams
explain: The Redis docs state that a pub/sub message a subscriber cannot handle, for example during a disconnect, is lost forever. The browser's stream to replica 5 never broke, so EventSource does not reconnect and nothing replays: the replica must resync itself, or read from a stream that keeps entries.

q: In the support chat, the customer's app resends a message after a timeout, but the first attempt had been stored. How do you make sure it is shown once?
options: Socket.io delivers exactly once, so the app should never resend at all
Deduplicate on the agent's screen by comparing the texts of messages
A client clientMessageId, a unique constraint and ON CONFLICT
Lock the conversation row until the client acknowledges the ack it got
explain: Resending until acked gives at-least-once delivery, and a client-generated id with a unique constraint turns it into once-only storage: the idempotency key of M05 applied to chat. Socket.io's default is at-most-once, per its docs, and two identical texts can be two real messages.

q: In the code review round, in what order should you read and comment on the pull request?
options: Security and data integrity, then failure handling, then concurrency, then style
Naming and style first, since they are the quickest wins and set the tone of the review
Top to bottom, commenting each line in the order the author wrote it
Tests first, and the code itself only if the tests look incomplete or wrong
explain: Reading by risk makes sure the bugs that break production (an injection, a missing deadline, a race) are raised first, whatever time remains. Line-by-line reading spends the round on whatever comes first in the file, often style, and a passing happy-path test says little about those bugs.

q: In Conventional Comments, what does the decoration (blocking) on a comment mean?
options: The reviewer will block the author on the chat tool until it is fixed
The comment is a nitpick about formatting
The change should not be accepted until the comment is resolved
The comment can be ignored unless the change is minor
explain: The Conventional Comments page defines blocking as a comment that should prevent the change from being accepted until it is resolved. Skipping unless the change is minor is the meaning of (if-minor), and a nitpick is a label, not a decoration.

q: In a bug bash, a checkout test fails in a repo you have never seen. What is the first step of the method?
options: Read the whole codebase so that you understand it before touching anything
Rewrite the function the test calls, since it is probably wrong
Ask the interviewer where the bug is
Reproduce it by running only that test, then read the whole error
explain: Reproducing alone (with --test-name-pattern or vitest -t) gives a fast loop, and the full error (message, actual and expected values, first stack frame in the repo) usually points to the hypothesis. Reading the whole codebase wastes the round, and rewriting before understanding is the guessing the round grades against.

q: During git bisect run ./check.sh, the script exits with code 125 on one commit. What does git do?
options: It marks the commit as bad, like any non-zero exit code
It skips that commit as untestable and continues
It aborts the bisect, because 125 is outside the range for bad commits
It marks the commit as good and moves to the next midpoint
explain: The git documentation reserves 125 for "cannot be tested": the commit is skipped. Codes 1 to 127 other than 125 mean bad, 0 means good, and any other code (128 and above) aborts the bisect.

q: In a STAR answer, where should most of the time go?
options: The Situation, so that the interviewer understands the context fully
The Result, with as many numbers as possible
The Action: what you did yourself, said with "I"
The Task, to show how important your responsibility was
explain: The interviewer evaluates your behaviour, which lives in the actions you took, so they should be the core of a two-minute story, in the first person. A long situation is the common mistake: two sentences of context are enough.

q: The orders table holds three orders. What does this query return when orderId is x' OR '1'='1?
options: No row, because no order has that id
An error, because the quotes are unbalanced
All three orders, because the condition becomes always true
Only the first order, because a WHERE on id returns at most one row
explain: The SQL becomes WHERE id = 'x' OR '1'='1', which is true for every row: run on PostgreSQL 18.6, it returned all 3 orders, while the same value passed as $1 returned none. The quotes balance because the injected value closes and reopens them, which is exactly how injection works.

q: In the PR, the restock query has no await. One day that query fails with a deadlock error. With Node 24's default flags and no rejection handler, what happens?
options: It has already returned success; the rejection is unhandled and the process exits with code 1
The function waits for the query anyway, because every promise inside an async function is awaited
The error is silently ignored and the stock stays wrong
The caller's try/catch receives the deadlock error
explain: Without await, the function returns before the query settles, so the caller sees success and its try/catch never sees the error. Measured on Node 24: the handler returned, then the unhandled rejection crashed the process with exit code 1, taking the other in-flight requests with it. It is not ignored either: since Node 15 an unhandled rejection is raised as an uncaught exception.

q: Two cancel requests for order 1042 arrive at the same moment, on two replicas. The code reads the status, refunds if it is paid, then sets cancelled. Which fix would you ask for?
options: An in-memory Map of the order ids being cancelled, checked by the handler before the refund
A 500 ms delay before the refund, so the first request has time to finish its update
A unique index on orders.status, so two rows cannot change state together
A conditional UPDATE … WHERE status = 'paid' RETURNING, and a refund only if a row comes back
explain: The conditional UPDATE makes the database decide which request wins: in a scratch run, two concurrent check-then-act calls refunded twice, and the conditional UPDATE refunded once. An in-memory Map only protects one process, and here the requests are on two replicas; a delay only narrows the window.

q: Which review comment on the injection bug is best?
options: "This is wrong, please fix it before I look at the rest of the pull request."
"issue (blocking): orderId is concatenated into the SQL, so callers can inject SQL. Pass it as $1."
"nitpick (non-blocking): maybe use a parameter here instead of building the SQL string by hand?"
"Why would anyone write SQL like this in 2026? We have had parameters for years."
explain: It states the problem, its severity, the evidence and the fix, in the Conventional Comments format. Labelling a security bug as a nitpick tells the author it is optional, which is the opposite of the truth, and the other two comments give no reason and no way forward.

q: You ask for AbortSignal.timeout(3_000) on the refund call and a retry when it times out. What else must the retry have?
options: A longer timeout on each new attempt, so that the last attempt always has time to succeed
Nothing: a call that timed out never reached the provider
The same idempotency key on every attempt, so the provider refunds only once
A new payment id for each attempt, so the provider does not reject duplicates
explain: A timeout only tells you that you stopped waiting: the provider may have processed the first refund. Sending the same idempotency key on every attempt lets it recognise the retry and answer with the first result (M02). A new id per attempt is precisely how a customer gets refunded twice.

q: This integration test against PostgreSQL fails with '4500499' !== 4999. What is the cause?
options: sum() is a bigint, which node-postgres returns as a string, so + concatenates
The cart has a second line priced 499 cents that the test fixture forgot to remove
TypeScript compiled + as string concatenation because of the generic type on query
PostgreSQL returned the sum in euros, not in cents
explain: On PostgreSQL 18.6, pg_typeof of the sum is bigint, and the pg-types README states that node-postgres returns int8 results as strings. '4500' + 499 is '4500499'. TypeScript emits no code for +: the generic on query is an unchecked assertion, so the type said number while the value was a string.

q: A test of the export "orders sorted by total" fails. What does this line print?
explain: Without a comparator, sort converts the values to strings and compares them in UTF-16 order, so "999" comes after "4500" (verified on Node 24). Pass a comparator: toSorted((a, b) => a - b) printed [ 999, 1200, 4500 ] and leaves the original array untouched.

q: paymentStatus() takes about 300 ms and deliveryEta() about 600 ms; neither needs the other's result. How long does this handler take, and what is the fix?
options: About 600 ms already, because Node starts the awaits in parallel by default
About 900 ms; with Promise.all over the two calls it drops to about 600 ms
About 900 ms, and nothing can be done without worker threads
About 300 ms, because the second await starts while the first one is still pending
explain: Each await waits before the next call starts, so the times add up: measured on Node 24 with timers, 911 ms sequentially and 604 ms with Promise.all, which starts both calls and waits for the slower. Waiting on I/O needs no worker thread.

q: In the bug bash, only GET /orders/:id is slow. The trace shows 850 ms in one SQL span; other routes and the event loop metrics are normal. What do you do next?
options: Add replicas of the API
Take a CPU profile of the Node process
Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on that query and read its plan
Add a cache in front of the route before investigating further
explain: The measurement already points at one query, so the next step is its plan, which shows a sequential scan or a bad join (M08). A CPU profile is the tool when every route is slow and the event loop is busy (M01), which is not the case; a cache or replicas hide the cause without finding it.

q: The CEO asks you in one sentence: "Make checkout faster." What do you do before writing any code?
options: Start optimising the slowest SQL query you already know of in the checkout
Add a cache in front of the checkout so that the CEO sees quick results
Ask what "faster" means, measure the baseline, and agree on a target
Plan a rewrite of the checkout in a faster framework such as Fastify
explain: "Faster" can mean server latency, page load, fewer steps or higher conversion, and each leads to different work. Clarifying the goal, measuring the baseline and agreeing on success is what the question is designed to hear. Starting with the query you already know solves a problem nobody has confirmed.

q: In an ES module, what does this function print when called?
options: 5000, then EUR, because both declarations are hoisted with their values
undefined, then a ReferenceError
A ReferenceError on the first line, before anything prints
undefined, then undefined, since both are hoisted
explain: The var is hoisted and initialized to undefined, so the first log prints undefined. The const is hoisted but uninitialized: reading it in its temporal dead zone throws "Cannot access 'currency' before initialization" (measured on Node 24). Two undefined values would be the behaviour if both were var.

q: A function created inside another function reads one of its variables. What does the inner function keep?
options: A copy of the variable's value at the moment the function was created
Nothing: the variable is freed when the outer function returns
Access to the variable itself, so it sees later changes
A copy that is refreshed only when the outer function is called again
explain: A closure keeps the variable binding, not a snapshot, and keeps it alive as long as the inner function is reachable. That is why listeners created in a var loop all read the final index. The "copy at creation" idea is the misconception the loop question tests.

q: In an ES module, [1250, 399].map(priceFormatter.format) throws "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'locale')", while priceFormatter.format(1250) works. Why?
options: map calls it as a plain function, so this is undefined in strict code
map calls it with this set to the array, which has no locale property
Intl.NumberFormat cannot be created inside an array callback
Methods written with the shorthand syntax lose their body when passed as values
explain: Passing priceFormatter.format hands over the function without its object, and map calls it as a plain function; ES modules are strict, so this is undefined (measured). map only uses its optional second argument as this, and none was given, so the array is not this.

q: Which statement about arrow functions and this is true?
options: call and bind set its this, exactly as they do for regular functions
Its this is always the global object, even inside a method
Its this is the object it is stored on, like a method shorthand
It takes this from the surrounding code; call and bind cannot change it
explain: Arrows have no this of their own: they read the this of the scope where they are written. Measured: calling an arrow class field with .call({ count: 99 }) still used the instance's count. Storing an arrow on an object does not make the object its this.

q: For const cart = new Cart(), where does the addLine method defined in the class body live?
options: On cart itself, copied there by the constructor on every new
On Cart.prototype, shared by every instance through the prototype chain
On the Cart function itself, as a static property shared by instances
In a hidden per-instance method table created by the engine
explain: Class methods are installed once on Cart.prototype; each instance links to it. Measured: Object.hasOwn(cart, 'addLine') is false and Object.hasOwn(Cart.prototype, 'addLine') is true. Only fields, such as #lines or an arrow function field, are created on each instance.

q: A TypeScript class declares private lines; another declares #lines. What differs at run time?
