Tab reached it, but neither Enter nor Space triggered its click handler
It exposed it as a link, because the pointer cursor changes on hover
explain: A click handler adds no role and no focusability: Tab went straight to the next control and the tree listed "text: Pay now". "Tab reached it but keys did nothing" describes a div with role="button" and tabindex="0", which still lacks the keyboard behaviour of a real button.

q: What is the accessible name of <button aria-label="Close">Remove item</button>?
options: "Remove item", because the visible text always wins over attributes
"Remove item Close", because both sources are joined together
"Close", because aria-label comes before the content
No name at all, because the two sources conflict with each other
explain: In the accessible name computation, aria-label comes before naming from content, so Chromium named the button "Close". That is exactly why it is a bug: the visible label is no longer in the name (WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name), so a voice control user saying "click Remove item" fails.

q: In the back office SPA, the agent presses Enter on the "Order 42" link. The router removes the old page, link included, and renders the new one. Where is keyboard focus, measured in Chromium?
options: On body, because the focused element was removed
On the new page's h1, moved by the browser
On the first focusable element of the new page
Still on the removed link, which keeps focus while detached
explain: When the focused element leaves the DOM, document.activeElement falls back to body and a screen reader announces nothing. The browser never moves focus to the new heading on its own: that is the job of code such as the PageHeading component, which focuses an h1 with tabindex="-1".

q: A button is styled with button:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid }. Which interaction showed the outline in Chromium?
options: A mouse click on the button
Any focus, whatever the input device
Only a programmatic button.focus() after a mouse click
Reaching the button with Tab or Shift+Tab
explain: Measured: keyboard focus matched :focus-visible, while a mouse click on the same button focused it without matching. Browsers use heuristics so that keyboard users always see focus and mouse users clicking a button do not, which is why styling :focus-visible beats deleting the outline.

q: In the OrderTabs component, the "History" tab is selected. What are the tabIndex values of Details, Payments and History?
options: 0, 0, 0, so that the Tab key visits every tab in turn
-1, -1, 0: only the selected tab is in the Tab sequence
-1, -1, -1, and the tablist container itself has tabindex 0
1, 2, 3, so that the Tab key follows the visual order of tabs
explain: This is the roving tabindex: one tab has tabindex 0 and the others -1, so the whole list is one Tab stop and the arrow keys move between tabs. Measured after pressing End: Details -1, Payments -1, History 0. Positive tabindex values must never be used.

q: What does role="status" give the cart announcer?
options: An assertive live region that interrupts whatever the screen reader says
Focus moves to the message element each time its text changes
A landmark that users can jump to from the screen reader landmarks menu
A polite live region: changes are announced when the user is idle
explain: role="status" is a live region with polite announcements by default; role="alert" is the assertive one. A live region announces changes without moving focus, which is exactly what a cart update needs.

q: After an RGAA audit, 60% of the applicable criteria are validated. Which mention goes into the accessibility declaration?
options: "Partiellement conforme", since it is at least 50%
"Non conforme", because anything under 100% is non-conformant
"Totalement conforme", because a majority of criteria is met
No mention at all: only public bodies publish a declaration
explain: The RGAA defines "totalement conforme" when every criterion is met, "partiellement conforme" from 50%, and "non conforme" below 50% or without a valid audit. "Non conforme under 100%" is the common confusion; the declaration also lists non-accessible content and a contact.

q: Which problem can an axe scan of the checkout detect on its own?
options: An alt text that describes the wrong product
An input that has no accessible name
A focus order that jumps from the postcode to the footer
A refund dialog that does not return focus on close
explain: A missing name is a fact a rule can check in the DOM. Whether an alt text is right, whether the order of focus makes sense, and what happens after an interaction need a human or a behaviour test, which is why the module adds a focus test and manual passes.

q: With @layer base, components;, base contains #checkout button { color: red } and components contains .pay-button { color: green }. What colour is the Pay button?
options: Red, because an id selector is more specific than a class selector
Red, because base is declared first and keeps priority
It depends on which of the two rules comes last in the file
Green: a later layer wins whatever the specificity
explain: Layers are compared before specificity: the later layer, components, wins. Measured in Chromium, the button was green. Specificity only decides between declarations of the same layer, which is what makes layers useful against legacy id selectors.

q: Code review on the storefront. Which change do you ask for?
options: Add role="button" and tabIndex={0} to the div so keyboards reach it
Add aria-label="Pay" so that screen readers can announce a name
Replace the div with <button type="button">
Add an onKeyDown handler that calls onPay when Enter is pressed
explain: A native button brings the role, focusability, Enter and Space activation, the disabled state and form behaviour. Role and tabindex alone left Enter and Space doing nothing in Chromium, and an Enter handler still misses Space; aria-label would only name a control that keyboard users cannot reach.

q: What name does Chromium compute for the button?
code: Delivery address
options: "Delivery address"
"Edit address"
"Edit"
"Edit address Delivery address"
explain: aria-labelledby comes first in the accessible name computation and overrides both aria-label and the content: measured, button "Delivery address". The tempting "Edit address" would be right only without aria-labelledby.

q: A voice control user says "click Remove item" on a cart line and nothing happens, while a mouse click works. The markup is <button aria-label="Close">Remove item</button>. What is the cause?
options: Voice control only activates links, so the button must become a link
The name is "Close", so the spoken label matches nothing
The button needs tabindex="0" before voice control can reach it
Voice control reads the title attribute, and this button has none
explain: aria-label replaced the visible text in the name, and voice control matches what the user can see. WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name requires the visible text to be part of the name. A button is already focusable, so tabindex changes nothing here.

q: The back office is a React SPA. Which fix would you ship so that screen reader users notice a page change?
options: Put aria-live="assertive" on main so the new page is read out
Call document.body.focus() after each navigation to reset focus
Give the h1 of every page tabindex="0" so Tab reaches it
Update the title and focus the new h1 (tabindex="-1")
explain: Focusing the heading makes the screen reader read it and makes the next Tab start there (measured). tabindex="-1" allows focus() without adding the heading to the Tab order, whereas tabindex="0" would add a useless Tab stop on every page. An assertive live region around main turns every content update into an interruption, which MDN advises against.

q: For the search autocomplete, why does the APG use aria-activedescendant rather than a roving tabindex?
options: Because options inside a listbox are not allowed to receive focus
Because DOM focus must stay in the input while the user types
Because a roving tabindex cannot be implemented with React state
Because aria-activedescendant scrolls the active option into view for free
explain: The combobox pattern keeps DOM focus on the text input while aria-activedescendant tells assistive technology which option is active. The scrolling claim is backwards: the APG says that with aria-activedescendant you must scroll the active option into view yourself, while roving tabindex gets it from focus().

q: In the OrderTabs component, focus is on the selected "Payments" tab and the user presses Tab. Where does focus go?
options: To the "History" tab, the next one in the list
Back to the first tab, "Details"
To the next focusable element after the whole tabs block
To the Payments tab panel, which has tabIndex={0}
explain: The tab list is a single Tab stop, so Tab leaves it; the next stop is the visible panel, focusable because the APG asks for tabindex 0 when the panel starts with non-focusable content (measured). Arrow keys, not Tab, move between tabs.

q: Screen reader users report that "Added to cart" is never announced. What is the most likely bug?
options: The region appears with its text, before it could be registered
role="status" is not a live region by itself; it needs aria-live too
Live regions only announce text that is set through innerHTML
The paragraph must receive focus before a screen reader reads it
explain: MDN advises establishing the live region first, empty, and changing its content later; the most reliable way is to have it in the initial markup. This component mounts the region and its message in the same render. role="status" is a polite live region by default, so the second option is wrong.

q: Which statement about the shop's legal position in France is correct?
options: Only companies with over 250 million euros of turnover in France are obliged
Since 28 June 2025 e-commerce must be accessible, micro-enterprises aside
The obligation only starts with RGAA 5, planned for the end of 2026
The obligation only covers shops whose customers include public bodies
explain: The European Accessibility Act, transposed in France, has covered e-commerce since 28 June 2025; per the DGCCRF, providers with fewer than 10 employees and under 2 million euros are exempt. The 250 million threshold is the older Article 47 rule, which still applies but is not the only one.

q: An interviewer asks what WCAG 2.2 changed compared with 2.1. Which answer is accurate?
options: It replaced the A, AA and AAA levels with a single score out of 100
It raised the AA contrast minimum for body text from 4.5:1 to 7:1
It made every AAA criterion mandatory for public sector websites
It added nine criteria, such as Target Size, and dropped 4.1.1 Parsing
explain: WCAG 2.2 (October 2023) kept the 2.1 criteria, removed 4.1.1 Parsing as obsolete, and added nine criteria, six of them at A or AA. 7:1 is the AAA contrast level (1.4.6), unchanged, and the A, AA and AAA levels remain.

q: Your Playwright test runs axe with the WCAG 2.2 AA tags on /checkout and passes. What can you honestly claim?
options: The checkout now conforms to WCAG 2.2 level AA
The checkout would pass an RGAA audit by an external firm
No violation those rules detect, in the states scanned
Screen reader users can complete a purchase from start to end
explain: A scan checks only what its rules can decide, in the states present at scan time: a closed dialog or an error state is not scanned. Deque itself claims about 57% of issues on average, and Playwright's docs say automated tests cannot detect all WCAG violations, so conformity needs manual testing too.

q: You have time for three screen reader passes before the audit. Which set covers the RGAA test environment and most real users?
options: NVDA + Firefox, VoiceOver + Safari on iOS, TalkBack + Chrome
JAWS + Internet Explorer, VoiceOver + Chrome on macOS, Narrator + Edge
Three runs of axe, in Chrome, in Firefox and in Safari
NVDA with Chrome three times, at 100%, 200% and 400% zoom
explain: The RGAA test environment names NVDA with Firefox on desktop, VoiceOver with Safari and TalkBack with Chrome on mobile, and WebAIM's 2026 survey shows VoiceOver on 72.2% of mobile setups. Rule engines are not screen readers, and a single pairing misses mobile entirely.

q: What colour is the Pay button, measured in Chromium?
options: rgb(0, 0, 255), because unlayered styles always beat layered ones
rgb(1, 1, 1): important reverses the layer order
rgb(2, 2, 2), because components is the later of the two layers
rgb(0, 0, 255), because it is the last declaration in the file
explain: For !important declarations the order is reversed: earlier layers beat later ones, and layered important beats unlayered important. Measured: rgb(1, 1, 1). "Unlayered beats layers" is true only for normal declarations, which is the trap here.

q: Which rule colours the Pay button?
options: Green, because four classes add up to more than one id
Green, because it comes later in the file
Both apply and the browser blends them
Red, because one id outweighs any number of classes
explain: Specificity is compared column by column: (1,1,0) against (0,4,0), and the id column decides before classes are counted. Measured in Chromium: red. Source order only matters when specificity is equal.

q: The Filters menu has z-index: 9999 but opens under the sticky header (z-index: 10). Its toolbar has transform: translateZ(0). Which fix works?
options: Raise the menu to z-index: 99999 so it beats the header
Add position: relative to the menu so z-index applies
Make the menu a popover (top layer)
Add isolation: isolate to the toolbar to reset stacking
explain: The transform makes the toolbar a stacking context, so the menu's z-index only competes inside it. A popover is drawn in the top layer, above the header (measured). Any child z-index fails, and isolation: isolate creates the same kind of context, so the menu stayed under the header in that test too.

q: A developer adds container-type: inline-size to an inline-block wrapper around a product card, and the card disappears. Why?
options: Container queries only work on elements inside a grid layout
It cannot size from its content, so it shrinks to 0
Inline-size containment hides any content that overflows it
The @container rule needs a container name to match anything
explain: Inline-size containment means the container is sized as if it had no content; a shrink-to-fit element such as an inline-block then measured 0 px wide in Chromium. Give the container a width from outside, for example a block or a grid track. Unnamed @container rules match the nearest container, so the name is not the problem.

q: The agent clicks Refresh in OrderHeader, which updates its state. Its child StatusBadge receives the same status prop as before and is not wrapped in memo. What does React do with StatusBadge?
options: It skips calling it, because React compares its props first and they did not change
It calls it again, compares the result, and leaves its DOM untouched
It calls it again and replaces its span in the DOM
It calls it only after the commit of OrderHeader
explain: A state change renders the component and, by default, all its children, whatever their props. Rendering is not committing: measured on React 19.3.1, the child was called once more and a MutationObserver saw zero DOM mutations. Skipping a child with unchanged props is what memo or the React Compiler adds; it is not the default.

q: Which of these is allowed in the body of a component, during render?
options: Pushing each rendered line into an array declared at module level
Sorting the lines array received in props with lines.sort()
Creating a local array and pushing into it before returning the JSX
Writing the id of the displayed order to localStorage
explain: Mutating a value created during this render is local mutation, and react.dev says it is fine: each render starts from scratch. lines.sort() is tempting because it looks like local work, but it mutates the array the parent (or the query cache) owns; use toSorted(). The module-level array and the localStorage write change things that exist outside the render.

q: From selectedCount === 0, a click handler runs setSelectedCount(selectedCount + 1) three times. What does the counter show, and after how many renders?
options: 3, after three renders
1, after one render
3, after one render
1, after three renders
explain: During the handler, selectedCount is the snapshot value 0, so each call asks for 0 + 1, and React batches the three into one render: measured, 1 after one render. "3 after one render" is what updater functions give: setSelectedCount((count) => count + 1).

q: An async click handler awaits a call to the BFF, then calls two different setters one after the other. How many renders does React 19 perform for those two updates?
options: One: React batches updates in promises and timeouts too, since React 18
Two: updates after an await are no longer inside the event, so each renders
None until the next user event
One per setter, unless the handler is wrapped in startTransition
explain: Automatic batching, introduced in React 18, groups updates made in promises, timeouts and native events, not only in React event handlers. Measured on React 19.3.1: one render for two setters after an await. "Two renders" was the behaviour before React 18, which is why the misconception survives.

q: A component stores selectedLineIds in state and copies its size into a second state, selectedCount, with useEffect. What happens when the selection goes from 1 line to 3?
options: One render, because React batches the effect's update with the click
One render, because the effect runs before the commit, so the stale count is never visible
Nothing until the next click, because effects only run on mount
Two renders: the first commits the stale count 1, then the effect's update renders 3
explain: Effects run after the commit, so the copy is updated one render too late: measured, the component rendered with 1, then with 3. The update set in the effect is a new render, not part of the click's batch. Computing selectedLineIds.size during render gives one render and no drift.

q: RefundForm holds useState(order.refundableCents). The parent renders it for order A (1000), then, at the same place and without a key, for order B (2500). What does the amount field show?
options: 1000: the argument of useState is only read on the first render
2500: a new prop triggers a re-render, which re-reads the initial value
2500 after a short flash of 1000
0: React resets state when a prop changes
explain: The argument of useState is the initial value, used once when the component mounts; later renders ignore it. Measured: the field kept 1000. The re-render does happen, which makes the 2500 options tempting, but rendering never re-initialises existing state.

q: What does <RefundForm key={order.id} order={order} /> do when the agent moves from order 1042 to order 1043?
options: It only speeds up the comparison of the form with its previous version
It keeps the form state and only passes the new order prop to it
React unmounts the old form with its state and DOM, and mounts a fresh one
It triggers a warning, because key is reserved for elements rendered in a list
explain: A key is the identity of an element at its position: a new key means a different component, so React destroys the old subtree and mounts a new one with initial state. Keeping state and updating props is what happens without the key, which is the bug. Keys are not limited to lists.

q: The agent can add a manual adjustment line to the refund before it is saved, so it has no database id yet. What key should its row use?
options: Its index in the list, since new lines are always appended at the end
Math.random() in the JSX, which gives each row a unique key
An id from crypto.randomUUID(), created with the line and stored on it
The label the agent typed, since two adjustment lines rarely share a label
explain: react.dev says locally created data should get an id when the item is created, from a counter, crypto.randomUUID() or a package. A random value generated in the JSX changes on every render and remounts every row. The index breaks on deletion, and a typed label is neither unique nor stable while the agent edits it.

q: The refund reason input is <input value={reason} onChange={…} />, and reason starts as undefined. The agent types a letter. What does React 19 report?
options: A warning that a component is changing an uncontrolled input to be controlled
Nothing: React treats undefined as an empty string for a controlled input
An error that stops the render
A warning that the input is read-only
explain: value={undefined} means uncontrolled; a string means controlled, and an input cannot switch. Measured on React 19.3.1, the warning reads "A component is changing an uncontrolled input to be controlled". The read-only warning is for value without onChange. Start from ''.

q: The status is 'paid'. The agent clicks the refund button. What does the log print one second later?
options: refunded, because the re-render finished long before the timeout fired
undefined, because the closure was reset by the render
paid: the callback closed over the snapshot of the clicked render
It depends on whether React has committed the update yet
explain: The handler and its timeout callback belong to the render where status was 'paid'; a later render creates new variables but cannot change that one. Measured: the screen showed refunded while the log printed paid. The tempting answer assumes the variable is updated in place, which never happens.

q: From selectedCount === 0, what does the counter show after this handler runs?
explain: React processes the queue in order: a plain value replaces the result so far, an updater computes from it. 0 + 5 = 5, then 6, then 42, then 84; measured on React 19.3.1. 42 is tempting if you think the last plain value wins, but the updater queued after it still runs.

q: The refund panel must show the total of the selected lines. A colleague proposes const [total, setTotal] = useState(0) and an effect that recomputes it when the selection changes. Which version would you ship?
options: The colleague's version, but with useLayoutEffect so the stale total is never painted on screen
Store the total in the BFF and refetch it after each click
The colleague's version, because effects keep render pure
Compute it during render from the lines and selected ids; add useMemo only if profiling says so
explain: A derived value computed during render is always in sync and costs one render; the effect version adds a render with a stale value (measured: two renders). A layout effect hides the flicker but keeps two sources of truth and the extra render. Refetching from the server for a local sum adds latency for nothing.

q: When a dispute is open, the order page wraps its content in a <section className="disputed"> instead of a <div>. Agents notice the refund form empties when a dispute opens. Why?
options: The className change forces a remount of every child
A different element type at that position destroys the subtree, form state included
The parent re-renders with new props, and React resets the state of children on re-render
The form is uncontrolled, so a new class clears its inputs
explain: Reconciliation tears down a subtree when the type at a position changes, and div to section is a type change. Measured: a counter inside went back to 0. A className change alone only updates the attribute on the same DOM node, and re-rendering never resets state by itself.

q: Each RefundLineRow keeps the typed quantity in local state. The agent types mug 1, T-shirt 2, cap 3, then removes the mug. What do the remaining rows show?
options: T-shirt 2, cap 3
T-shirt 1, cap 2
T-shirt 1, cap 3
T-shirt empty, cap empty
explain: After the removal, the T-shirt has key 0 and the cap key 1, so they inherit the state of the old rows 0 and 1: measured, T-shirt 1, cap 2. "T-shirt 2, cap 3" is what key={line.id} gives, which is the fix.

q: To silence the missing key warning, a pull request adds key={crypto.randomUUID()} to each row of the refund lines. What is the bug?
options: None, as long as every generated id is unique among the sibling rows
Long UUID strings make React compare keys slowly in large lists of refund lines
crypto.randomUUID is not available in the browsers agents use
Keys change on every render, so every row remounts and loses its state each time
explain: Keys must be stable between renders. A key generated during render never matches the previous one, so React destroys and recreates every row: measured, a typed quantity vanished after one parent re-render, and the input was a new DOM node. Uniqueness is necessary but not enough; generate the id once, when the item is created.

q: The order page renders the order lines in two places: the lines table and the refund panel, both with key={line.id}. A reviewer says keys must be unique on the page. Is that right?
options: Yes: React keeps a global key registry and warns on duplicates
Yes: otherwise both lists share the same state
No: keys only have to be unique among the children of one parent
No: React ignores keys outside of a map
explain: react.dev states that keys are not globally unique: they only identify an element among its siblings. Two lists under different parents can use the same ids safely. Duplicates warn only among siblings of the same parent, and keys also work outside map, for example to reset a form.

q: The shared RefundAmountInput is used by the refund form, which must validate the amount, and by a quick filter that only needs a callback. Which API do you design?
options: Always controlled: every caller must pass value and onChange and own the state
Always uncontrolled, with a ref the parent reads on submit
value + onValueChange, or defaultValue; the mode follows from value being defined
A controlled boolean prop that callers can flip at any time
explain: Mirroring the native input lets each caller pick the cheapest mode, and the mode follows from value being undefined or not. Measured both ways in section 8. Always-controlled works but forces state on callers that do not need it; a flippable mode reproduces the controlled-to-uncontrolled problem React warns about.

q: The refund form renders <input value={amount} /> with no onChange. The agent types a digit. What happens?
options: The field keeps showing amount, and React warns about a read-only field
The digit appears, and React updates amount for you through the value prop
The digit appears, because the DOM owns the value until the next render
React throws, because a controlled input requires a handler
explain: With value, React forces the displayed value; with nothing updating amount, each keystroke is reverted. Measured: typing left the field unchanged and the console warned "You provided a value prop to a form field without an onChange handler". Use defaultValue, add onChange, or set readOnly.

q: The BFF returns refundReason: null for orders without a reason, and the form renders <input value={order.refundReason} onChange={…} />. What is the fix you ship?
options: Remove value and rely on defaultValue={order.refundReason} plus the state
Turn off the warning in development
Pass value={order.refundReason || undefined}
Pass value={order.refundReason ?? ''}, controlled from the first render
explain: A controlled input must always receive a string; ?? '' turns null into an empty string and keeps the mode fixed. Measured, a null value warns that "value prop on input should not be null". Mapping it to undefined makes the input uncontrolled at first, which leads to the switching warning as soon as a value arrives.

q: An interviewer asks: "What are Fiber and reconciliation?" Which answer is accurate at the level expected?
options: Fiber is a virtual DOM library React uses to render HTML on the server, and reconciliation merges that HTML into the page
A tree of fibers holds state; React compares each render with it by type, position and key, then commits the differences
Reconciliation is the browser comparing the old and new DOM trees before painting, and Fiber is its scheduler
Fiber is the hook system, and reconciliation is React checking that hooks are called in the same order on every render
explain: Fiber has been React's core engine since React 16, and each node of its tree is a fiber that holds state; reconciliation is React's comparison, using element type and key, before the commit. The browser does not diff anything: React computes the minimal DOM operations itself. Hook order matters, but it is not what reconciliation means.

q: The orders table shows the orders of the selected status. Where should the filtered list be computed?
options: In a useEffect that stores it in state when orders or status change.
During render, as a constant computed from the props and the state.
In a useLayoutEffect, so that the list is ready before the browser paints.
In a ref, updated by the handler that changes the status filter.
explain: Derived data is computed during render: it is always in sync and costs one render. The effect version is the tempting one, but it renders once with the stale list, then again after storing the new one, and react-hooks/set-state-in-effect flags it.

q: The refund form keeps the amount typed for the previous order when the agent opens another one. Which fix is the idiomatic one?
options: An effect that calls setAmount('') whenever orderId changes.
Keeping the amount in a ref so that it is not preserved between renders.
Wrapping RefundForm in memo so it re-renders only when the order changes.
Rendering it as <RefundForm key={order.id} order={order} />.
explain: A new key makes React treat the form as a new component with fresh state; measured, the typed amount was emptied on the change of key. The effect works too, but it renders the old amount first and adds an effect with no external system.

q: In development, inside <StrictMode>, LiveStatusFeed mounts with status="paid". Its effect logs "connect" in setup and "disconnect" in cleanup. What is logged?
options: connect paid, disconnect paid, connect paid
connect paid, connect paid
connect paid
connect paid, disconnect paid
explain: StrictMode runs one extra setup and cleanup right after the first mount, in development only; measured with React 19.3.1. "connect paid" alone is what the production build logs.

q: The badge calls setNewCount(newCount + 1) from a stream listener created in an effect with [status]. After three events it shows 1. Why?
options: React batches the three updates into a single one, so only the last of them is applied.
The listener captured newCount from the first render, so each call computes 0 + 1.
The stream delivers events faster than React can re-render the badge.
Updates from outside a React event handler wait for the next user interaction.
explain: The listener is a closure over the first render's newCount, which is 0 forever: a stale closure. Batching is real but not the cause: each event is applied, it just computes the same value; the updater form fixes it.

q: The listener must read soundEnabled, but toggling the sound must not reconnect the stream. What do you use?
options: Add soundEnabled to the dependency array of the stream effect.
Wrap the listener in useCallback with [soundEnabled] as its dependency list.
Disable the exhaustive-deps rule on the dependency array line.
Move the chime logic into a function created with useEffectEvent.
explain: An effect event always sees the latest props and is not a dependency, so the stream stays open; measured, no reconnection. useCallback with [soundEnabled] changes identity when the sound toggles, so the effect that uses it reconnects anyway.

q: The panel fetches in an effect without cleanup. The agent clicks order A, then order B; B's response arrives first. What does the panel show at the end?
options: Order A, because its response arrived last and its setOrder ran last.
Order B, because React discards updates from an effect whose dependencies changed.
Order B, because the second fetch cancels the first one automatically.
Nothing: React throws because two effects updated the same state.
explain: Without a cleanup, both responses call setOrder and the last one wins; measured, the naive panel ended on A. React does not discard those updates by itself: that is the job of the ignore flag or the AbortController in the cleanup.

q: The page writes the stream's last event id to lastEventIdRef.current on every event. What happens on screen when it changes?
options: The page re-renders, as it would after a setState.
The page re-renders only if the ref is listed in an effect's dependencies.
Nothing: writing to a ref never triggers a render.
React logs a warning, because refs are read-only after the mount.
explain: A ref is a mutable box that React does not watch; measured, mutations left the render count unchanged. Listing a ref in dependencies does not help either: the ref object itself never changes identity.

q: The actions menu measures itself and flips above when it overflows. Why use useLayoutEffect instead of useEffect?
options: It runs before the DOM is updated, so the measure uses the previous layout.
Its code, and the state update it schedules, are processed before the browser repaints.
It also runs during server rendering, so the first HTML already has the right position.
It runs on a separate thread, so measuring the menu does not block the main thread.
explain: React guarantees that a layout effect and its updates are processed before the repaint; measured in Chromium, the browser never saw the unflipped menu. It runs after the DOM update, not before, otherwise there would be nothing to measure.

q: Two components each call useDebouncedValue(query, 300). What do they share?
options: The debounced value: the second call reads the state of the first one.
The timer: a keystroke in one component cancels the other's update.
Nothing at all until both are wrapped in the same context provider.
Only the code: each call has its own state and its own timer.
explain: A custom hook shares logic, never state; measured, two components using the same hook kept separate values. Sharing state needs a store, a context or lifted state, not a hook.

q: The detail panel throws during render and no error boundary wraps it. What does the agent see with React 19?
options: Only the panel disappears; the table and the toolbar stay on screen.
The last successful render stays frozen on screen until a reload.
The whole root is unmounted: an empty page until a reload.
React retries the render three times, then shows a default fallback.
explain: Without a boundary, React unmounts the whole root; measured, the container was empty and onUncaughtError was called. Keeping the rest of the screen alive is exactly what a boundary around the panel does.

q: What does this log when Parent mounts (no StrictMode)?
options: child layout, parent layout, child effect, parent effect
parent layout, child layout, parent effect, child effect
parent effect, parent layout, child effect, child layout
child layout, child effect, parent layout, parent effect
explain: All layout effects of the commit run before any passive effect, and within each phase children run before their parent; measured on React 19.3.1. Rendering goes parent first, which makes the second option tempting, but effects run bottom-up so a parent can rely on its children being set up.

q: The "time since order" ticker was written like this. What does it show after ten seconds?
options: 10 s, because the interval fired ten times and each tick added one.
0 s, because state set from an interval is ignored.
1 s, because every tick computes 0 + 1 from the first render.
A growing number, twice as fast under StrictMode.
explain: The interval callback closes over seconds = 0 forever, so each tick sets 1; measured, it stayed at 1. exhaustive-deps flags the missing seconds and suggests the updater setSeconds((s) => s + 1), which counts correctly.

q: What does the screen show after this component mounts?
options: 0, because updates made inside an effect are discarded
Nothing: it loops, because the effect sets state
explain: Both calls read the same count of 0 and set 1; measured, the renders saw 0, then 1. Two updater calls, setCount((c) => c + 1), would give 2; the empty dependency array prevents any loop.

q: A colleague sees "connect paid" twice in development and adds a hasConnectedRef so that the second setup returns early. Which change do you ship instead?
options: The ref flag as written, since the production build runs the effect only once anyway.
Removing <StrictMode>, since the double run is only a development artefact.
Opening the stream in the component body, guarded by a module-level variable.
A cleanup that closes the stream, so setup, cleanup, setup leaves one stream open.
explain: The double run reveals a missing cleanup, and react.dev lists the ref flag as a pitfall: production would still leak on every filter change and unmount. Removing StrictMode hides the symptom and keeps the leak.

q: This panel aborts the previous request. The agent clicks order A, then order B. What do they see?
options: Order B, because the aborted request for A never settles.
An abort error message instead of order B.
Order A, because aborting does not stop the first response.
Order B briefly, then order A when its response arrives.
explain: An aborted fetch rejects with an AbortError, and this catch stores it as an error; measured, the panel showed "AbortError: This operation was aborted" although B loaded. The fix checks controller.signal.aborted before setError; an aborted fetch does settle, by rejecting.

q: The panel now works with an AbortController. In review, what is the strongest reason to replace the effect with useQuery?
options: Effects have no way to cancel a request, and useQuery can cancel it.
useQuery fetches during render, so there is no extra render.
React 19 deprecated fetching from inside useEffect.
It adds the cache, retries and deduplication the effect lacks.
explain: The effect already cancels correctly; what it lacks is everything around the request (cache, retries, deduplication, refetching), which TanStack Query provides. Effects can cancel with an AbortController, as the code under review does, so the first option is false.

q: Which use of useEffectEvent is a bug?
options: Passing onStatusEvent as a prop to a child that calls it on click.
Calling onStatusEvent from the stream listener set up in an effect.
Reading soundEnabled inside onStatusEvent without listing it.
Leaving onStatusEvent out of the effect's dependency array.
explain: react.dev says effect events must only be called from effects or other effect events, never passed to other components or hooks; use a regular function or useCallback for a child's handler. Leaving it out of the dependencies is the intended use: effect events are not dependencies.

q: After five stream events, what is on screen?
options: 5 received
0 received
1 received
An error: refs cannot be read during render
explain: The ref is incremented, but nothing re-renders, so the screen keeps the first render's 0; measured. React does not throw, but the react-hooks/refs lint rule reports reading current during render as an error: a count shown on screen belongs in state.

q: In a React 19 codebase, the parent of SearchInput needs its input element. What do you write?
options: Wrap SearchInput in forwardRef, the only way a function component receives a ref.
Accept a prop named inputRef, because ref never reaches a function component.
Accept ref as a regular prop and pass it to the <input>.
Return the input node from useImperativeHandle inside SearchInput.
explain: Since React 19, ref is a normal prop for function components, and react.dev says forwardRef is no longer necessary and will be deprecated. forwardRef still works, but it is no longer the only way, nor the recommended one.

q: The Next.js storefront, rendered on the server, reuses the actions menu and its useLayoutEffect. What should you expect?
options: The effect runs on the server with a default viewport of 1280 by 720 pixels.
Next.js turns it into a useEffect during the build.
The server render fails and the page answers with a 500.
It does not run on the server; the menu is measured in the browser.
explain: Effects only run on the client; measured with react-dom/server, the layout effect neither ran nor raised an error. There is no layout on the server, so there is no viewport to measure with.

q: The table and the stats bar both call useLiveOrders('paid'), and the BFF now sees two streams per agent. Which fix keeps the hook correct?
options: Add a module-level flag so that the second call to the hook skips its own effect.
Merge the table and the stats bar into one larger component that calls the hook.
Call it once in the page and pass the data down, or count subscribers in the store.
Wrap the hook's effect in useMemo so it runs once per status.
explain: One caller per screen, or a store that opens the stream for its first subscriber and closes it after its last, gives one stream with correct cleanup. A module-level flag breaks as soon as the first caller unmounts: the second one is left without a stream.

q: The displayed order goes from paid to refunded. What happens?
options: Nothing goes wrong: early returns placed before a hook are allowed since React 19.
The draft is kept and comes back when the order returns to paid.
Only a lint warning appears; at runtime React skips the missing hook.
React throws, because this render called fewer hooks than the previous one.
explain: Measured: "Rendered fewer hooks than expected. This may be caused by an accidental early return statement." The lint rule reports it as an error too (rules-of-hooks), so the fix is to call every hook before the early return.

q: The refund button's click handler throws when the API answers 409. The panel is inside PanelErrorBoundary. What happens, and what do you ship?
options: The boundary catches it and shows its fallback, so there is nothing to change.
The boundary does not catch it; catch it in the handler and show it from state.
The whole root unmounts, so you add a second boundary around the refund button.
React swallows it silently; add onUncaughtError to see it.
explain: Boundaries do not catch event handler errors; measured, the boundary stayed untouched and the error reached the window's error event. A 409 is an expected outcome, so the handler catches it and sets an error state the panel renders.

q: The Profiler shows that OrderRow rendered 5,000 times during one keystroke. How do you make React DevTools tell you why each row rendered?
options: Wrap each row in <StrictMode>, which logs the cause of every render
Tick "Record why each component rendered while profiling", then record again
Log the props in the row and compare them by hand
Switch to a production build, where the Profiler names the cause of each commit
explain: The Profiler setting "Record why each component rendered while profiling" adds a "Why did this render?" section to the selected component, with reasons such as "The parent component rendered." or "Props changed:". StrictMode only double-calls render functions to expose impure code; it explains nothing about causes.

q: Which of these does not, on its own, make a component render?
options: Its parent component rendered, with identical props
A context that the component reads received a new value
A prop object was mutated in place
A custom hook it calls updated a state variable it holds
explain: React renders a component when its state (including a hook's state) changes, when its parent renders, or when a context it reads changes. Mutating an object does not notify React at all, which is why mutation leads to stale UI. "Parent rendered" is the tempting wrong answer, but it is precisely the default cause: React renders all children of a rendering component.

q: The page keeps isColumnMenuOpen in OrdersPage, which also renders the 5,000-row table. What is the cheapest change that stops the table from rendering when the menu opens?
options: Move the open state into a ColumnMenu component
Wrap setColumnMenuOpen in useCallback so the table gets a stable setter
Store the open state in a ref instead
Wrap OrdersPage in memo so its children skip the render
explain: With the state inside ColumnMenu, toggling it renders the menu only, and OrdersPage has no state left to re-render the table: no memoization needed. Wrapping OrdersPage in memo is the tempting answer, but memo only skips renders caused by the parent, never by the component's own state; and a ref would not update the UI at all.

q: How does memo decide to skip a render?
options: It deep-compares the old and new props, recursively
It compares the rendered output of the last render with the new one
It skips when the parent rendered for a reason unrelated to this child
It compares each prop with Object.is and skips when all are equal
explain: By default memo compares each prop with Object.is, a shallow comparison: equal primitives match, but two different objects with the same content do not. React never deep-compares props by default, and comparing rendered output would require rendering, which is what memo avoids.

q: OrderSummary is cheap; MemoPanel is wrapped in memo. Each keystroke renders OrdersPage. Does MemoPanel render?
options: No: none of its props depends on query
No: memo leaves children out of its comparison, since they are only elements
Yes: children is a new element object on every render
Only in development, because of StrictMode
explain: JSX creates a new element object on every render, and children is an ordinary prop, so Object.is sees a change each time: measured on React 19.3.1, the memoized wrapper and its child rendered after one keystroke. React has no special case that ignores children; memoize the element or let the compiler do it.

q: Rows are memoized and keyed by array index. A new order arrives and is inserted at the top of the 5,000 orders. How many existing rows render?
options: All of them: every index now holds a different order
None: a memoized row renders only when its own order object changes
Only the last row
One: React detects the insertion and shifts the existing rows
explain: With key={index}, the row at position 0 now receives the new order, the row at position 1 the former first order, and so on: every row's order prop changed. Measured on React 19.3.1: 5,001 renders with index keys, 1 with key={order.id}. React cannot detect an insertion without stable keys.

q: Each memoized row calls useContext(BackOfficeContext) to read selectedOrderId. The provider value also holds query. What happens to the rows on a keystroke?
options: None: memo stops renders while the row's own props are unchanged
Only the rows matching the new query
Each row renders, but React skips its commit, so it costs nothing
Every row renders: every reader of a changed context does
explain: When the provider's value changes, React re-renders every component that reads that context, and react.dev states that memo does not prevent it. Measured: 5,000 row renders per keystroke until the query moved to its own context. Renders are not free just because the DOM does not change.

q: What does the React Compiler do?
options: At runtime, it skips components whose props did not change
At build time, it adds memoization to components and hooks
It turns slow renders into transitions
At runtime, it deep-compares props in place of memo, so memo becomes useless
explain: The compiler is a build-time Babel plugin that rewrites components and hooks to cache values, callbacks and JSX, equivalent to memo, useMemo and useCallback, even conditionally. It does not change update priorities, and nothing in it deep-compares props at runtime.

q: The page passes useDeferredValue(query) to FilteredOrdersTable, which is not wrapped in memo. How many times does the table render for one keystroke?
options: Once, with the new query, after the input has painted
Once, with the old query only
Twice: with the old query, then with the new one
Zero times until the user stops typing, as with a debounce
explain: The urgent render renders the parent, and without memo the table renders too, with the old deferred value; then the background render runs with the new value. Measured on React 19.3.1: 2 renders without memo, 1 with it. That is why react.dev says the optimisation requires memo.

q: Which is a real cost of virtualising the orders table?
options: Find-in-page cannot find orders whose rows are not rendered
Every row must be wrapped in memo, or virtualisation has no effect
The list must be sorted on the server
Only fixed row heights are supported, so long rows get truncated
explain: A virtualised list renders only the visible rows, so the rest is not in the DOM, and find-in-page, printing and "select all" only see what is rendered. TanStack Virtual handles variable heights with measureElement, and works without memo because it renders only a few dozen rows.

q: The Refunds tab is wrapped in <Activity mode="hidden"> while the agent looks at History. What is true for the hidden tab?
options: It is unmounted: its state is lost and its effects are cleaned up
Its DOM is hidden, its effects destroyed, its state kept
It keeps its effects running but stops re-rendering
Its DOM is removed and its state is saved to sessionStorage until shown
explain: A hidden Activity keeps the children's state and DOM, hides the DOM with display: none, and destroys their effects; showing it again restores the state and re-creates the effects (measured on React 19.3.1). Unmounting is what conditional rendering does, and is the cause of the lost refund note.

q: An interviewer shows this code: "OrderRow is memoized, yet the Profiler shows all rows rendering on each keystroke, with 'Props changed: (onOpen)'. Which fix would you ship?"
options: Give memo a custom comparison that ignores onOpen, since it always navigates
Remove memo: it cannot work with callback props
Deep-compare every prop in a custom comparison
Create onOpen once with useCallback, or enable the compiler
explain: The inline arrow is a new function on every render, so Object.is sees a changed prop. A stable function from useCallback fixes it, and the compiler would cache it automatically. Ignoring onOpen in a custom comparison is the tempting shortcut, but react.dev warns that the row would then keep calling a stale handler from an older render.

q: Rows are memoized and the handler stable. An order changes from paid to shipped through this live update. What does the agent see?
options: The row updates to shipped, because the array is a new reference
Every row renders again
The row still shows paid: memo sees the same order object
React throws in development, because state was mutated in place
explain: The table renders because the array is new, but each row receives the same order object as before, mutated in place, so memo skips all of them: measured, 0 row renders and a stale badge. React does not detect mutation and throws nothing. The fix is to replace the changed order with { ...order, status }.

q: After every route change, all components that read AuthContext render, although the user did not change. What is the most likely cause?
options: The value is a new object on every render of App
setCurrentUser gets a new identity on every render, which changes the value
Calling trackPage during render resets the context
Readers of a context always re-render on navigation
explain: App renders on each route change, creating a new { currentUser, setCurrentUser } object; Object.is sees a different value and every reader renders. Wrapping it in useMemo with [currentUser] fixes it, as react.dev shows. State setters are stable, so they are not the cause.

q: In a Redux back office, the orders toolbar re-renders after every dispatched action, even actions about notifications. Its code is below. What is the bug?
options: React-Redux does not support destructuring a selector result
The selector returns a new object each time, compared with ===
useSelector re-renders on every action by design, whatever the selector returns
The toolbar should read the store with useContext
explain: useSelector runs the selector after every dispatched action and re-renders when the result is not === to the previous one; a new object literal is always different. Select each field separately, use a memoized selector (Reselect) or pass shallowEqual. It does not re-render on every action when the result is stable.

q: What happens when this hook is used in a row, on React 19?
options: It works, and the row renders only when isSelected flips from one value to the other
It works, but every row renders on every store change
It fails to type-check: getSnapshot must return a primitive
React warns that the snapshot should be cached, then throws
explain: getSnapshot must return the same value while the store has not changed; a new object on each call looks like a change every time. Measured on React 19.3.1: the error "The result of getSnapshot should be cached to avoid an infinite loop", then "Maximum update depth exceeded". Objects are allowed if cached; returning the boolean itself is the simple fix.

q: Your team enables the React Compiler in an existing app full of useMemo and useCallback. A colleague opens a PR that removes all of them "since the compiler does it now". What do you answer?
options: Approve: the compiler ignores manual memoization, so the hooks are dead code
Reject: the compiler needs manual memoization to work
Keep them, or remove them with tests: removal can change the output
Approve, with 'use no memo' in every touched file
explain: react.dev recommends leaving existing memoization in place, because removing it can change compilation output, or removing it carefully with tests; effects that depend on a memoized value are the usual risk. The compiler does not ignore manual hooks, and does not need them either; in new code, it is the default and the hooks are escape hatches.

q: You introduce the React Compiler into the back office, a large Vite app with patchy tests. Which plan would you defend?
options: Turn it on everywhere with ^1.0.0, ship, and fix what agents report
Lint first, then compile part of the app, with an exact version pin
Remove every useMemo first, then enable it everywhere at once
Wait: the compiler is still experimental
explain: This is the rollout react.dev describes: the recommended config of eslint-plugin-react-hooks surfaces Rules of React violations, incremental adoption limits the blast radius, and an exact version avoids silent behaviour changes without good test coverage. The compiler has been stable since 1.0 (7 October 2025), so waiting is not justified.

q: The lint reports on the virtualised table: "Compilation Skipped: Use of incompatible library" on useVirtualizer. What does it mean?
options: The build fails until the call is removed
TanStack Virtual does not work with React 19, so the table breaks at runtime
The compiler memoizes the component anyway and warns in the browser at runtime
The compiler leaves this component unmemoized, to avoid stale UI
explain: The message is a warning: the compiler skips memoizing that component to avoid stale UI, because useVirtualizer() returns functions that cannot be memoized safely (measured with eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7.1.1). The component still works as plain React; only automatic memoization is lost there. TanStack Table and React Hook Form's watch are on the same list.

q: The compiler is enabled and the ✨ badge shows on OrdersTable, yet each keystroke still takes over 100 ms. The table filters 5,000 orders by query. Why?
options: A new query is a new input: the filter must run again
The compiler only optimises development builds, not production
The compiler never memoizes the result of Array.prototype.filter
The compiler disables concurrent rendering
explain: Memoization caches results for unchanged inputs; a new query is a new input, so the expensive part runs anyway. That is the "one render is too slow" problem, solved by deferring (useDeferredValue), rendering less (virtualisation) or computing less. The compiler targets production builds, and react.dev shows it memoizing calculations made during render, such as this filter.

q: To fix the lagging filter, a colleague writes this. What is wrong?
options: isPending is never read, so React ignores the transition
Nothing: react.dev recommends this pattern for search inputs
The input's own value must not be in a transition
startTransition must be imported from react-dom, not taken from the hook
explain: An input must update synchronously with its change event, and transitions are non-blocking, so react.dev states they cannot control text inputs. Keep query urgent and either set a second tableQuery state inside the transition or pass useDeferredValue(query) to a memoized table. Reading isPending is optional.

q: The back office has two searches: filtering the 5,000 orders already in memory, and a customer search that calls GET /customers?q=. What would you use for each?
options: useDeferredValue for both: deferring the value also limits network calls
A deferred value for the filter, a debounce for the API
A 300 ms debounce for both, to keep one pattern
A transition for the API call, nothing for the filter
explain: Deferred rendering has no fixed delay and is interruptible, which suits rendering work; it does not reduce the number of requests. react.dev notes that debouncing still helps for non-rendering work such as network calls. A debounce on the in-memory filter only postpones the moment the render blocks the keystroke.

q: Product asks for "all 50,000 orders of the year in one table, fast". What would you propose first?
options: Server-side pagination first; virtualise only if a long scroll is needed
Render all 50,000 rows with the React Compiler, which skips unchanged rows
Render all rows in one transition
Load all rows and hide off-screen ones with CSS
explain: Rendering cost grows with the number of rows in the DOM: measured, 5,000 rows took 0.6 to 3.6 s to mount against under 30 ms for a 40-row window. Pagination also cuts the data sent; virtualisation is the answer when one long scrollable list is a real need. The compiler and transitions do not reduce the work of rendering rows that change.

q: An accessibility review of the virtualised orders table says a screen reader announces "table with 30 rows". What is missing?
options: aria-busy on the table while the agent scrolls
aria-rowcount on the table and aria-rowindex on rows
A tabindex on every rendered row so it can be counted
Nothing: screen readers cannot announce the size of a virtualised list
explain: MDN says aria-rowcount is needed when not all rows are in the DOM, to give the real size of the table, and each rendered row then carries its position with aria-rowindex. Without them, assistive technology counts only the rendered rows. aria-busy signals updates in progress, not the size.

q: Where would you put Suspense boundaries on the order detail page (header, lines, refunds tab, history tab)?
options: Around every component that loads something, so each piece appears as soon as it can
One boundary around the whole app
Where the design shows loading states: the panel, the lazy tab
None: Suspense only works with Server Components
explain: Everything inside one boundary appears together, so boundaries encode the loading sequence; react.dev advises against a boundary around every component and suggests following the designers' loading states. One boundary for everything makes the slowest part hold back the page. Suspense works on the client with lazy and use too.

q: Clicking the Refunds tab, whose code is not loaded yet, replaces the whole panel with a skeleton. With startTransition(() => setTab('refunds')) instead of a plain setTab, what happens?
options: Details stays on screen, with isPending true until Refunds is ready
The skeleton still shows, but for a shorter time because the code loads in parallel
The Refunds tab renders empty, then fills in
React throws: lazy cannot load inside a transition
explain: A transition tells React not to hide already revealed content with a fallback: it keeps the Details tab and reports isPending. Measured on React 19.3.1: the plain switch showed the fallback, the transition kept Details with isPending true, then showed the form when the code arrived. Transitions do not speed up loading.

q: The History tab subscribes to live order events in an effect, and is wrapped in <Activity>. What happens to the subscription while the tab is hidden?
options: It keeps running, and the hidden tab updates in real time
It keeps running, but React buffers the events until the tab is visible again
It is cancelled, and the tab's state is reset when shown
Cleanup runs on hide, the effect re-runs on show, state is kept
explain: Hiding an Activity destroys its children's effects, which runs their cleanups, and showing it re-creates them; the state is kept throughout (measured on React 19.3.1). So the subscription stops while hidden, and the effect must refetch or resubscribe on show. State is not reset: that is the difference with conditional rendering.

q: In the back office, which piece of state is server state?
options: Whether the refund dialog is open
The status of order ord_42
The status filter of the orders table
The amount an agent is typing in the refund form
explain: The order status is owned by the server and can change while the page is open (another agent refunds the order), so the client only holds a cache of it. The status filter is tempting because it is about statuses, but it is chosen by the agent: it is URL state.

q: Two components mount at the same time and both call useQuery with the key ['orders', 'list', { status: 'paid' }]. How many requests reach the server?
options: One: same key, one cache entry, one shared request
Two: each useQuery call owns its fetch and its copy of the data
Two, unless staleTime is above 0, which turns on deduplication
None until one of the components calls refetch() explicitly
explain: Measured with MSW: one request. Components with the same query key share one cache entry, and a request already in flight is reused. staleTime controls whether a later mount refetches, not whether simultaneous requests are deduplicated.

q: What is the difference between staleTime and gcTime?
options: staleTime is the request timeout; gcTime is the delay between two retries
They are the same setting, renamed between TanStack Query v4 and v5
staleTime: how long data is fresh; gcTime: how long unused data is kept
staleTime applies to queries shown on screen; gcTime applies to mutations
explain: Fresh data is served with no request; after staleTime it is refetched on triggers such as mount or focus. gcTime (5 minutes by default) is how long an entry no component uses is kept before removal. gcTime was called cacheTime in v4, but staleTime is a different setting.

q: After a refund, the hook calls invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['orders'] }). A refunded list is in the cache but not on screen. What happens to it?
options: It is removed from the cache, and the next visit starts from a spinner
It is marked stale and refetches when a component uses it again
It refetches immediately, in parallel with the queries on screen
Nothing: the key ['orders'] only invalidates an exact match
explain: Measured: the list and detail on screen refetched at once, while the inactive refunded list was only marked invalidated. Prefix matching is the default, so ['orders'] does match it; it just has no observer to refetch for.

q: What is a request waterfall?
options: Requests started one after another although they did not depend on each other
A failed request retried several times with exponential backoff until it finally succeeds
Several components sending the same request at the same moment
A long list loaded page by page, each page waiting for its cursor
explain: In the order detail, the refunds request waited for the order request only because RefundList rendered after the order loaded: about 300 ms instead of 130 ms with 100 ms per request (measured). Duplicate simultaneous requests are a different problem, solved by deduplication.

q: In the optimistic priority toggle, why does onMutate return { previous }?
options: TanStack Query requires onMutate to return the variables it received
To send the previous value to the server so it can detect conflicts
To let the mutation retry automatically with the previous value
So onError can restore the snapshot if the server refuses
explain: What onMutate returns reaches onError and onSettled; the snapshot is how the rollback restores the cache. Measured with a 409: the toggle showed true, then false again. The server never sees that object.

q: A cart Context has the value { items, addItem }. Product cards read it only to get addItem. What happens to the cards when an item is added?
options: Nothing: they do not read items, so React skips them
Only the card that was clicked re-renders, because it called addItem
All of them, because the Context value is a new object
They re-render only if they are not wrapped in memo
explain: Every component that reads a Context re-renders when its value changes by Object.is, whatever field it uses. Measured: one addition re-rendered all 20 cards. memo does not help, because a Context change bypasses it; splitting actions into their own stable Context does (zero card renders).

q: Which sequence is the Redux data flow?
options: Dispatch, reducers compute new state, subscribers notified, selectors re-run
Components write to the store directly, then the reducers validate and log the change
Selectors fetch the data, then dispatch it to the reducers to be stored
Reducers call the API, then dispatch an action with the response
explain: Actions describe what happened, reducers compute the next state without side effects, and useSelector re-runs after every dispatched action, re-rendering on a new reference. Reducers never call APIs: async work happens before the dispatch (a thunk or RTK Query).

q: With useActionState(placeOrder, initialState) on a form, what does placeOrder receive?
options: The submit event, on which it must call preventDefault
The previous state first, then the form's FormData
The FormData only
The new state and a setState function
explain: The docs: the action receives the previous (or initial) state first, then the payload, which for a form is FormData. A function passed directly to a form's action prop receives FormData alone; useActionState adds the state in front, so a function moved from one to the other must change its parameters.

q: An agent adds a note with useOptimistic and the save fails. The code catches the error and does not update notes. What does the list show after the Action ends?
options: The note, marked "sending", until the page reloads
The note, because optimistic state is kept until replaced
An empty list
The notes as they were before, without the failed one
explain: Optimistic state only renders while an Action runs; afterwards React shows the real value, which never changed. Measured: the note disappeared and the error message showed. Nothing to roll back by hand, unlike the cache writes of section 6.

q: The orders table uses the default options. An agent opens it, goes to an order for two minutes, then comes back. What do they see?
options: The cached rows at once, while a background refetch updates them
A spinner: the data was removed when the table unmounted
The cached rows, and no request, because the data is still in memory
An error until they reload
explain: Two minutes is within the 5-minute gcTime, so the entry is still cached and paints at once; with staleTime 0 it is stale, so the remount refetches in the background. Measured: cached text on first paint and a second request. "No request" would need a staleTime longer than two minutes.

q: A row prefetches on hover; the detail page then mounts. Both use the same key. How many detail requests are sent?
options: One: the prefetch filled the cache, so the page reads it without a request
One, and the page shows a spinner until the prefetch resolves a second time
Two: the page's staleTime is 0, so the cached data is stale on mount
Zero for the page: useQuery never fetches when the cache has data
explain: Measured: two requests with staleTime 0 on the page, one when both used 60 s. Freshness is judged by the observer's own staleTime. The cache was filled, so the page paints at once, but it refetches. Share one queryOptions factory so both sides agree.

q: Which change removes the waterfall in this order detail?
options: Wrap RefundList in memo so it renders before the order arrives
Also call the refunds query in OrderDetailPage, before the early return
Set staleTime: Infinity on the order query so it never blocks the page
Fetch the refunds in a useEffect inside RefundList to start them earlier
explain: The refunds request waits only because RefundList is rendered after the order arrives. Calling useQuery for refunds in the parent (result ignored, notifyOnChangeProps: []) starts it at once; RefundList reads the same cache entry. Measured: about 130 ms instead of 300 ms with 100 ms per request.

q: After a refund, the button re-enables while the table still shows paid for a moment. Which change makes the mutation stay pending until fresh data is in?
options: Call refetchQueries instead of invalidateQueries, which only marks data stale
Move the invalidation to onSettled, which runs after the cache is updated
Add retry: 3 to the mutation so it waits for the server to be consistent
Return the promise from invalidateQueries in onSuccess
explain: The braces discard the promise, so the mutation succeeds as soon as the POST does. The docs say returning the promise from onSuccess keeps the mutation pending until it settles, here until the refetch finishes. refetchQueries has the same issue if its promise is also dropped.

q: An agent toggles priority on, then off, 60 ms apart. Each onSettled invalidates the order. The toggle shows on, off, on, off. What causes the third value?
options: The first edit's refetch landed while the second PATCH was still in flight
onError rolled back the second edit to the snapshot taken by the first one
React batched the two optimistic cache writes and applied them in reverse order
The server applied the two PATCH requests out of order and saved the wrong value
explain: Measured: the first mutation settled, invalidated, and its refetch landed while the second PATCH was still in flight, so the server still said true. The fix: invalidate only when isMutating for that key equals 1 (the current one), and cancel queries in onMutate. Nothing failed, so no rollback ran.

q: Why does the optimistic hook call cancelQueries on the order before writing the cache?
options: To stop the mutation itself from being sent twice by a double click
Because setQueryData throws an error while the same query is fetching
So a refetch already in flight cannot overwrite the optimistic value
To free the memory used by the old data before writing the new value
explain: A refetch started before the click carries the old server state; if it resolves after setQueryData, the toggle jumps back. Cancelling it removes that window. setQueryData does not throw during a fetch, which is exactly why the race exists.

q: A teammate says: "We do not need TanStack Query, we load the orders once in a Context provider." Which argument is the strongest?
options: Context can only hold primitive values and stable functions, not arrays of objects
Context does not cache, dedupe, expire or invalidate: we would rebuild that
Context is deprecated in React 19 in favour of the use hook and stores
Context values cannot be read from custom hooks, only from components
explain: Context only hands a value down the tree; every concern of server state (freshness, sharing requests, invalidation after writes, cancellation) would be hand-written. It is fine for rarely-changing client values. React 19 did not deprecate Context; it added the <Context value> provider syntax.

q: This back office component re-renders on every keystroke in an unrelated search box (the search text is in Redux). Why?
options: The search reducer mutates the selection slice by accident on each keystroke
useSelector re-renders the component after every action, whatever it returns
Destructuring the result subscribes the component to the whole store
The selector builds a new object on each call, and the check is ===
explain: useSelector re-runs after every dispatched action but re-renders only when the result is a new reference, and an object literal always is. Select each value separately, pass shallowEqual, or memoise. The second option is the tempting half-truth: the selector re-runs every time, the render does not have to.

q: A Zustand cart store is read by a badge with useCartStore((state) => state.lines.length). An "add to wishlist" action in the same store changes only state.wishlist. Does the badge re-render?
options: No: the selected length is unchanged, and Zustand compares it with ===
Yes: every set call re-renders every component subscribed to the store
Yes, unless the store is created inside a provider at the root of the app
No, because Zustand only re-renders components on route navigation
explain: Zustand's README says it detects changes with strict equality on the selected value. A primitive like a length stays equal, so no re-render. A selector building a new object would re-render each time; useShallow is the fix there. Zustand needs no provider.

q: Why does the button never show "Placing your order…"?
options: useFormStatus only works with Server Functions, not with client actions
It only reads a form rendered by a parent: move the button into a child
The action must first be wrapped in startTransition to report its status
The button needs a formAction prop instead of type="submit" to be tracked
explain: Measured: pending stayed false in the component that renders the form and became true in a child. The docs state the hook only reports on a parent form. It works with any function action, not only Server Functions.

q: A checkout form uses useActionState and does not disable its button. The customer double-clicks. What happens?
options: React ignores the second submit while the first one is still pending
The second submit aborts the first request and only the second order is sent
Both run, one after the other: React queues them, so two orders are posted
Both run in parallel, and the server keeps whichever request finishes first
explain: Measured: two clicks, two action calls, the second starting when the first finished (the docs: calls are queued and run sequentially). Nothing is aborted or ignored. Disable the button with useFormStatus and send the same idempotency key so the server answers a duplicate with the first order.

q: The checkout action catches a 503 and returns { error }. The customer sees the error, and the email field is now empty. Why?
options: React resets uncontrolled fields after the action, even with an error state
The 503 response told the browser to clear its autofill data for the whole form
useActionState remounts the form with fresh fields on every new state
The email input lost its name attribute when the error was rendered
explain: The docs say uncontrolled fields are reset after the action succeeds, and an action that returns normally has succeeded. Measured: the field was empty after a returned error, and kept the email with defaultValue={state.email}. The form is not remounted; the fields are reset to their default values.

q: After a successful save, the notes list briefly shows the new note twice: once saved, once "sending". What is the fix?
options: Call addOptimisticNote after the await, once the server has answered
Wrap the setNotes that follows the await in startTransition
Give the optimistic note the same key as the saved note so React merges them
Replace useOptimistic with useState and remove the note manually on success
explain: Updates after an await are not yet part of the Action (react.dev documents this caveat), so setNotes rendered while the optimistic note was still applied. Measured: a duplicate frame without startTransition, none with it. Moving the optimistic call after the await would remove the instant feedback.

q: The cart lives in useState in the product page component, which renders the header, the filter panel and 20 cards directly. One item is added. What re-renders?
options: Only the header, because it is the only component that shows the count
The header and the card that was clicked, because they took part in the event
Nothing until the cart is saved to the server and the response arrives
The page and everything it renders, cards and filter panel included
explain: A state change re-renders its component and, by default, every child it renders. Measured: 20 cards and the filter panel re-rendered. Moving the cart into a provider that receives the page as children, with actions split out, reduced it to the badge.

q: "My orders" uses useInfiniteQuery and the customer has loaded 5 pages. After cancelling an order, the code invalidates the query. What happens?
options: Only the first page is refetched, and the other four pages are dropped
All 5 pages are refetched in sequence, each cursor from the previous page
All 5 pages are refetched in parallel, one request per stored cursor
Nothing happens: infinite queries are never matched by invalidateQueries calls
explain: Measured with two loaded pages: the refetch requested page 1, then page 2, in sequence, since the second cursor comes from the first response. With many pages that is a slow chain; maxPages limits how many pages are kept.

q: What is the main difference between a Server Component and a Client Component rendered with SSR?
options: A Server Component produces HTML on the server, while SSR produces a JSON payload that the browser turns into HTML
Its code never reaches the browser; an SSR-rendered Client Component still ships its code to hydrate
SSR runs only once at build time, while Server Components run on every request and cannot be cached
Server Components cannot fetch data themselves, so SSR is still needed for every page that shows data
explain: SSR is about when HTML is produced; a Client Component rendered that way still sends its JavaScript so it can hydrate. A Server Component runs only on the server, at build or request time, and sends none. The first option inverts things: the RSC Payload is the serialised output of Server Components, and HTML comes from prerendering.

q: add-to-cart-button.tsx starts with 'use client' and imports formatPrice from lib/money.ts, which has no directive. Where does formatPrice end up?
options: Only on the server, because a module without a directive defaults to the server
It depends on whether formatPrice is async: async helpers always stay on the server
Nowhere: the build fails until lib/money.ts gets its own 'use client'
In the client bundle, because the directive covers everything the module imports
explain: React documents that 'use client' marks the module and its transitive dependencies as client code, so you do not repeat the directive in every helper. Having no directive does not keep a module on the server; only import 'server-only' would turn that import into a build error.

q: Which prop can the product page (a Server Component) pass to a Client Component?
options: A promise of the reviews, which the Client Component unwraps with use() inside a Suspense boundary
