An onAddToCart arrow function defined in the page, which the button calls on click
A Product class instance, so the button can call product.formatPrice() itself
A Symbol('cart') created in the page, used as a stable identity for the cart
explain: Promises are in React's list of serialisable props, and Next.js documents passing an unawaited promise and reading it with use() under Suspense. Plain functions (other than Server Functions), class instances and symbols not registered with Symbol.for cannot cross the boundary.

q: The header and the price box both call getCurrentCustomer, wrapped with React.cache in a shared module. What does that guarantee?
options: The customer is cached across requests for as long as the session cookie is valid
The result is shared between all visitors until the next deploy invalidates it
Within one server request, components calling the same wrapped function share one call
The result is memoized in the browser too, so hydration does not fetch the customer again
explain: React clears the cache for each server request and shares it only among components that call the same memoized function during rendering. It is not a cross-request cache (that is 'use cache'), so the first two options are wrong, and it is for Server Components, not the browser.

q: A page renders a heading and a price inside <Suspense fallback="Loading price...">; the price resolves after 300 ms. What does renderToReadableStream send?
options: Nothing until the price resolves, then the whole page in a single chunk
The heading and the fallback first, then the price with a small swap script
The price first, because suspended content is sent with a higher priority than the shell
The complete page twice: once with the fallback and once more with the price
explain: Measured on React 19.3.1: the first chunk left at 58 ms with the heading and "Loading price...", the second at 305 ms with the price in a hidden element and the inline swap script. Waiting for everything is what non-streaming rendering would need; renderToString does not even wait and sends the fallback.

q: The server rendered "Delivered by Tuesday" and the first client render produces "Delivered by Wednesday". What did React 19.3.1 do (measured)?
options: It reported a recoverable error and rebuilt the tree on the client: Wednesday
It kept Tuesday silently: hydration ignores text differences
It threw an uncaught error, and the customer saw a blank page instead of the product
It patched only the text node to Wednesday, without reporting anything to monitoring
explain: Measured with hydrateRoot in jsdom: onRecoverableError received "Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client. As a result this tree will be regenerated on the client", and the DOM ended with the client text. Keeping the server text happens only with suppressHydrationWarning.

q: With Cache Components enabled, a component reads cookies() and is not inside any Suspense boundary. What happens?
options: cookies() returns an empty cookie store during prerendering, without any warning
The whole application silently switches to request-time rendering, page by page
Next.js caches it per visitor, keyed on the cookie
Next.js flags the route as blocking and asks you to add a Suspense boundary
explain: Cache Components requires runtime data to sit behind a Suspense boundary so every route keeps a static shell; the dev overlay shows the blocking-route insight and the build guides you to fix it. Returning empty values is what dynamic = 'force-static' does in the previous model, not this one.

q: In a Server Action, a customer updates their saved delivery address, and the page must show the new address in the same response. Which call?
options: revalidateTag('address-' + customer.id, 'max')
revalidatePath('/') from a Client Component
updateTag('address-' + customer.id)
cacheLife('seconds') on the address reader
explain: updateTag expires the tag immediately, for read-your-own-writes, and is reserved for Server Actions. revalidateTag with a profile is stale-while-revalidate: the action's own re-render does not wait for fresh data, so the customer could still see the old address.

q: Which statement about a Server Action exported from app/checkout/actions.ts is true?
options: Anyone able to send the POST can call it, so it must check the session, ownership and input itself
It is private, because Next.js encrypts action ids and removes the actions you do not use
The sign-in check in app/checkout/page.tsx protects it too, since the page renders the form
Only the form that imports it can call it, because Next.js compares Origin and Host
explain: Next.js documents that actions are reachable by direct POST requests and that a page-level check does not extend to the actions it renders. Encrypted ids and dead-code removal reduce exposure but are explicitly not a substitute for checks inside each action; the Origin check stops cross-site forms, not a direct request.

q: An interviewer asks: "Is 'use server' the opposite of 'use client'?" Which answer is accurate?
options: No: Server Components have no directive; 'use server' marks Server Functions
Yes: 'use server' marks a component as a Server Component, the default being client
Yes, but only in Next.js
No: 'use server' marks code that runs once at build time and never per request
explain: react.dev says it directly: a common misunderstanding is that Server Components are denoted by 'use server', but there is no directive for them; the directive is for Server Functions. That is also why a file marked 'use server' exposes callable endpoints.

q: Each call takes about 200 ms and none depends on another. Which change would you ship?
options: Wrap the three functions with React.cache so their results are reused within the request
Mark the page 'use client' so the browser fetches the three in parallel after hydration
Promise.all for product and stock; reviews in a child under Suspense
Add a loading.tsx and keep the code
explain: The three sequential awaits are a server waterfall of about 600 ms; parallel requests cut it to the slowest one, and streaming the optional reviews keeps the LCP content from waiting. React.cache only deduplicates repeated calls, and loading.tsx shows a fallback but leaves the waterfall in place.

q: How many times does fetchCurrentCustomer run in one request?
options: Once: cache recognises that both wrappers point to the same underlying function
Twice: each call to cache creates a new memoized function with its own, separate cache
Zero: cache defers the call until a Client Component actually reads the customer
Once per customer, because the memoized value is shared across their requests
explain: React documents that calling cache with the same function several times returns different memoized functions that do not share a cache, so components must import one memoized function defined at module level. And the cache never spans requests, which rules out the last option.

q: A returning customer has 3 items in a cart stored in localStorage. What happens on page load?
options: A mismatch: the server renders 0 and the client 3; read storage after mount
It works: the typeof window check is the recommended way to avoid hydration errors
The server throws a ReferenceError on localStorage and the whole page fails to render
React patches 0 into 3 silently
explain: The check runs differently on the server and in the browser, so the first client render differs from the HTML: measured in jsdom, the server sent 0, hydration reported a text mismatch and the badge ended at 3 after a client re-render. The guard avoids the ReferenceError, which is why the code looks safe, but it creates the mismatch.

q: A CMS description renders as <p><p>In stock</p></p> in a Client Component. React renders the same elements on server and client. Why does hydration still fail?
options: React's reconciler refuses nested paragraphs on the client, but accepts them on the server
Next.js minification drops the inner paragraph
The browser's parser closes the first <p> at the second, so the DOM differs
The server escapes the inner paragraph as text, so the client sees different content
explain: Measured in Chromium 156: the markup became <p></p><p>In stock</p><p></p>, so React found a different DOM and reported a hydration error, after warning that a <p> cannot be a descendant of a <p>. The fix is valid markup, such as a <div> wrapper.

q: What is wrong with this cached function?
options: Nothing: Next.js adds the cookie value to the cache key automatically for cached functions
The lifetime is too long for a price
getCurrentCustomer must also be wrapped with React.cache for the key to work
Cached functions cannot read cookies, even via a helper: pass the id in
explain: Next.js documents that 'use cache' scopes cannot access cookies() or headers(), and the restriction follows the call stack, failing with next-request-in-use-cache. Passing the customer id as an argument makes it part of the key; nothing is added to the key automatically.

q: The back office calls the storefront's POST /api/revalidate Route Handler after an agent edits a description. A few seconds of stale content are fine, and the handler must not block. Which call?
options: updateTag('product-' + slug) from the handler
revalidatePath('/', 'layout') to clear everything
revalidateTag('product-' + slug, 'max')
cacheLife('seconds') on getProduct instead
explain: revalidateTag with a profile gives stale-while-revalidate and is allowed in Route Handlers; tags invalidate just that product. updateTag is restricted to Server Actions, invalidating the root layout path is far wider than needed, and a seconds lifetime takes the product out of the static shell for every visitor.

q: A candidate says: "fetch in a Server Component is cached by default." Which answer is accurate as of October 2026?
options: True in Next.js 14; not by default since Next.js 15; with Cache Components you cache explicitly with 'use cache'
True in every version: Next.js always caches GET requests made with fetch until a revalidation
False in every version: Next.js has never cached fetch results, only whole rendered pages
True only when Cache Components is enabled, because it caches every fetch made during render
explain: Next.js 15 changed the default: fetch requests and GET Route Handlers are no longer cached by default, and Cache Components (Next.js 16) makes caching opt-in with directives. Cache Components does the opposite of the last option. Stating the version first is the point of the question.

q: What is the vulnerability in this Server Action?
options: It lacks a CSRF token, and Next.js does not check the origin of Server Action requests
No ownership check: any signed-in customer can cancel any order by its id
It should be a GET Route Handler, because cancelling an order twice is idempotent anyway
Throwing on a missing session leaks the stack trace and the message to the customer
explain: Authentication is checked, authorisation of the object is not: the order id comes from the client, so this is an IDOR. Next.js already compares Origin and Host for actions, and production errors from the server reach the browser as a generic message with a digest, so the other options are not the issue.

q: A double click created two orders. A teammate says: "Next.js dispatches Server Actions one at a time per client, so this cannot happen any more." Your answer?
options: Correct: sequential dispatch makes every Server Action idempotent on the server side
Disabling the button while the action is pending is enough; no server change is needed
Call it through Promise.all to merge clicks
Dispatch is client-side; the server does not queue: use an idempotency key
explain: The Next.js docs state that sequential dispatch belongs to the client dispatcher and that the server runs each action as it arrives: a second tab, a retry or a replayed POST still creates a second request. Only a key stored by the Orders API (M05) makes the retry return the first order.

q: An attacker adds totalCents=1 to the form data of the "Place order" form. What does parsed.data contain (measured with Zod 4.6.7)?
code:
const PlaceOrderInput = z.object({ cartId: z.uuid(), idempotencyKey: z.uuid() });
const parsed = PlaceOrderInput.safeParse(Object.fromEntries(formData));
options: Only cartId and idempotencyKey: keys the schema does not declare are dropped
cartId, idempotencyKey and totalCents: '1', kept as a string
Nothing: safeParse fails because the object contains an unknown key
totalCents: 1, converted to a number, next to the two ids
explain: A Zod object strips keys it does not declare: the measured result held only the two UUIDs. Failing on unknown keys would need a strict object. And the action never reads a price from the client anyway: the Orders API computes the total.

q: The order is created, yet the customer sees "Could not place the order." Why?
options: redirect is forbidden in Server Actions
createOrder throws after the order is saved, because the API answers 201 Created
redirect throws, and the catch swallows it: call it after the try/catch
redirect needs an explicit 303 status argument when it is called in a Server Action
explain: The redirect docs say it throws a control-flow error and must be called outside the try block; here the catch turns a successful redirect into an error message. Redirects are allowed in Server Actions, and Next.js picks 303 itself for form submissions without JavaScript.

q: Which test would have caught the Pay button that stayed disabled after a declined card?
options: A snapshot of the checkout's first render, updated whenever the markup changes on purpose
A test asserting that the submitted state becomes true on click and false after a success
A component test that answers POST /orders with 402, clicks Pay, then expects Pay enabled
A unit test checking that placeOrder throws a typed error on a 402 response
explain: Only that test reaches the declined-card path and checks what the customer can do next. The snapshot records the first render, the state test checks an implementation detail (it would pass with the bug), and the unit test proves placeOrder throws but says nothing about the button.

q: Which checkout behaviour cannot be checked reliably in a jsdom component test?
options: The alert shown after a 402 response, with the text the customer reads
The order summary staying visible while the customer scrolls
The Pay button being disabled while the order request is in flight
The accessible name the address field gets from its label element
explain: jsdom has no layout engine: measured, getBoundingClientRect() returned zeros and IntersectionObserver was undefined, so scrolling and sticky positioning need a real browser. The other three are DOM state and accessibility information, which jsdom and Testing Library handle well.

q: Which query should a test use first to find the Pay button?
options: screen.getByTestId('checkout-pay-button')
container.querySelector('button.btn-primary')
screen.getByText('Pay', { selector: 'button' })
screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' })
explain: Testing Library ranks getByRole first: it finds the element the way assistive technology does, by role and accessible name. getByText with a selector finds it too, but ties the test to the tag and skips the accessible-name check; test ids are the last resort, and a CSS class is an implementation detail that broke the old suite.

q: Before the customer clicks Pay, no error message must be shown. Which assertion is right?
options: expect(screen.getByRole('alert')).not.toBeInTheDocument()
expect(screen.getAllByRole('alert')).toHaveLength(0)
expect(screen.queryByRole('alert')).not.toBeInTheDocument()
await expect(screen.findByRole('alert')).rejects.toThrow()
explain: queryBy returns null when nothing matches, so the negative assertion can run. getBy and getAllBy throw on zero matches before expect is even reached, so those tests fail. The findBy version works but waits a full second for nothing.

q: How should MSW be organised for the storefront's component tests?
options: A new setupServer inside each test, listening and closing in that test, with only the handlers it needs
One server, happy-path handlers, server.use per error case, resetHandlers after each test
No handlers by default, with unhandled requests passed through to a staging Orders API
One handler set per file and no reset, since each test file already runs in its own worker
explain: Default happy-path handlers keep most tests short, server.use overrides one endpoint for one test, and resetHandlers removes that override so it cannot leak into the next test of the same file. Files are isolated from each other, but tests inside one file share the server.

q: A test calls vi.useFakeTimers(), then userEvent.setup() with no options, then await user.type(input, '10 rue'). What happens?
options: The text is typed instantly, because fake timers skip every delay
The text is typed, but the debounce timer fires after the first key
Typing stalls: user-event waits with setTimeout between keys
Vitest throws an error saying fake timers are not supported by user-event
explain: user-event waits between keystrokes with setTimeout, and fake timers only move when the test moves them: measured, not one character was typed after 2 s. The user-event docs say advanceTimers is necessary with fake timers: userEvent.setup({ advanceTimers: vi.advanceTimersByTime }).

q: When should a custom hook get its own renderHook tests?
options: Always: every hook is a unit, and testing it through a component hides its failures
When several components share it and its contract has many cases
Never: renderHook was deprecated with React 19 and its test utilities
Only when the hook holds no state, since state needs a real component to render
explain: A shared hook with its own contract deserves direct tests at its boundaries. A hook written for one component is better tested through that component, as the Testing Library docs advise preferring render. renderHook is part of @testing-library/react 16, not deprecated.

q: Why did the Pay button snapshot stay green through the incident, then fail last week?
options: Snapshots ignore boolean attributes such as disabled, but they do compare whitespace
The snapshot file was never committed, so each CI run wrote a new one and passed
It held the first render only, and it compares markup, classes included
Snapshot serialisers only understand class components, not hooks
explain: A snapshot records the states the test reaches, and this one never clicked Pay. It compares serialised HTML, classes included: measured, renaming btn-primary produced a diff although nothing was broken. That pairing (misses the bug, fails on the refactor) is the usual case.

q: What does the last line do?
options: It returns the second input, because its placeholder becomes its accessible name
It returns the first input, the only textbox that has a label at all
It throws "Found multiple elements with the role "textbox"", as two inputs match
It throws "Unable to find an accessible element…": no textbox is named "Postcode"
explain: Testing Library computes an empty accessible name for an input with only a placeholder (measured: Name ""), so no textbox is named "Postcode" and getByRole throws. That is also a real accessibility bug: give the field a label. "Multiple elements" only happens without a name filter.

q: With MSW 2 and onUnhandledRequest: 'error', a new component calls GET /cart, which has no handler. What happens in the test?
options: The request goes to the real network, and the test continues with whatever comes back
MSW answers with an empty 200 response, so the component renders an empty cart
MSW logs a warning, and the previous test's handler answers the request
MSW prints an error naming the request, and the fetch rejects
explain: Measured on MSW 2.15: "[MSW] Error: intercepted a request without a matching request handler" listed the method and URL, and fetch rejected. The forgotten mock fails visibly instead of hitting the network. In MSW 3 the option is onUnhandledFrame, and the old name is no longer read.

q: You need to assert that the button shows "Paying…" and is disabled while POST /orders is pending. Which approach is deterministic?
options: Hold the handler on a promise the test resolves after asserting
Add a 200 ms delay to the handler and assert within the first 200 ms of the click
Mock useMutation to return isPending: true for the whole test
Click Pay, sleep 50 ms so the request starts, then assert on the button
explain: A held response stays pending until the test releases it, so the in-flight state is checked with no timing at all (measured, then the paid status appeared after resolve). A delay or a sleep races the clock, and mocking useMutation no longer tests the component's real wiring.

q: Under Vitest, this test hits the 5 s test timeout. Why?
options: Testing Library waits for a setTimeout(0) it only advances under Jest
advanceTimers must be vi.runAllTimers, or the remaining keystrokes never fire
MSW cannot answer requests while fake timers are installed, so the query hangs
act cannot wrap an async function, so the debounce update is never applied
explain: Testing Library's asyncWrapper waits for a setTimeout(0) and only calls jest.advanceTimersByTime when it detects a jest global; under Vitest fake timers that timer never fires (measured: the test timed out). vi.useFakeTimers({ shouldAdvanceTime: true }) fixed it. MSW kept answering in the passing version.

q: What is result.current after the last line, and what else happens?
options: "10 rue de Rivoli", since the 300 ms have passed, with no warning
"10 r", plus an act(...) warning from React
undefined, because the cleanup cleared the timer and the state
It throws, because renderHook does not support fake timers
explain: The timer fired setDebounced outside act, so React had not rendered the update when the test read it: measured, result.current was still "10 r" and the act warning was printed. Wrapping the advance in act() gave "10 rue de Rivoli".

q: The storefront has a DOM snapshot for every component, and people update them with vitest -u without reading the diff. Which plan would you ship?
options: Run vitest -u automatically in CI, so that snapshots stop blocking merges for markup changes
Role-based assertions for behaviour, aria snapshots or screenshots for a few pages
Keep them all and add a review rule: every snapshot diff needs two approvals before merge
Convert every snapshot to toMatchInlineSnapshot, so reviewers see the HTML in the test file
explain: DOM snapshots miss behaviour they never reach and fail on harmless markup, so the fix is different assertions, not more process. Behaviour goes to role-based tests, structure to aria snapshots that ignore classes, and visuals to a few screenshots. Inlining large HTML only moves the noise into the test file.

q: A developer adds await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('checkout.png') and runs it on a Windows laptop, then pushes. CI runs on Linux. What happens?
options: Local run writes checkout-win32.png; CI has no Linux baseline
The first run passes and writes one baseline that every platform then shares
Playwright converts the Windows baseline to each platform when CI first runs it
The test is skipped on CI with a warning, because the platform differs from the baseline
explain: Measured on Playwright 1.64: the first run failed with "A snapshot doesn't exist … writing actual" and wrote checkout-win32.png. The platform in the name means a Linux run looks for a different file, and fonts render differently anyway, so generate baselines in the same environment as CI, such as its container.

q: In <Tabs.Root><Tabs.List><Tabs.Tab /></Tabs.List><Tabs.Panel /></Tabs.Root>, how does a Tab know which value is selected?
options: It reads the selected value from a context that Root provides
Root clones each child element and injects the selected value as a prop
Each Tab keeps its own state and syncs it with an effect
The caller passes selected to every Tab by hand
explain: Root renders a context provider, and every part reads it with use (or useContext), however deep it sits. Cloning children only reaches direct children, so it breaks as soon as a Tab is wrapped in a List or a tooltip. Syncing local states with effects duplicates the state.

q: What does a headless component library such as Radix, React Aria or Base UI give you?
options: Fully styled components in its own visual language, ready to theme
Behaviour and accessibility (ARIA, focus, keyboard) without styles
Design tokens and a Figma kit, but no components
Components that render only on the server
explain: Headless means unstyled: Base UI describes itself as "unstyled UI components for building accessible user interfaces", and Radix components "ship without styles". Styled libraries such as MUI are the ones that bring a visual language.

q: In a two-tier token system, which tokens should the Button's CSS use?
options: Raw hex values, so the button never depends on a theme
Primitive tokens such as --indigo-600
Semantic tokens such as --color-action
Whichever tier the designer used in the mock-up
explain: Components use semantic tokens, which name a role, and themes remap those roles to primitives. A button using --indigo-600 directly stays indigo 600 in dark mode, because the theme changes the semantic layer.

q: Why does the react.dev page on useInsertionEffect not recommend runtime <style> injection?
options: It makes the browser recalculate styles more often, and can be very slow
Injected styles are dropped by the browser as soon as hydration has finished
React 19 removed support for style elements rendered by components
Injected styles cannot read CSS custom properties defined in tokens
explain: The page gives those two reasons and recommends static CSS files for static styles plus inline styles for dynamic values. Injected styles do apply, and React 19 still renders style elements; the problem is cost, not correctness.

q: The next @shop/ui release renames the Tabs prop onChange to onValueChange. Which version bump is correct?
options: Patch, because no new feature was added
Minor, because the new name is an addition
Major, because existing callers break
None, because TypeScript users will see the error anyway
explain: Semver reserves the major version for incompatible API changes, and a renamed prop breaks every caller using the old name. Shipping it as a patch is exactly the incident of section 8. A compile error is how users find out, not a reason to hide it in a patch.

q: In the feature-based back office, the refunds screen needs the order's total. What does the structure rule say?
options: Import OrdersTable from features/orders and read the total from its props
Compose both in the page under app, or fetch it through the API layer
Move the refunds feature inside features/orders
Copy the order types into features/refunds
explain: Features do not import each other; the app layer composes them, and shared data comes from the API layer. A cross-feature import is exactly what the lint rule forbids, and nesting or copying features only moves the coupling.

q: In the monorepo, apps/back-office depends on "@shop/ui": "workspace:*", and @shop/ui is at 2.3.0. What happens to that range when a package that depends on @shop/ui is published?
options: pnpm replaces it with the exact version, 2.3.0
pnpm publishes it as is, and consumers need pnpm to install it
pnpm replaces it with latest
pnpm refuses to publish a package with a workspace dependency
explain: The pnpm docs say workspace:* becomes the exact version of the local package when packing or publishing (and workspace:^ becomes ^2.3.0). So consumers outside the monorepo see an ordinary semver range.

q: For a 10% rollout of the new orders table, why should the flag be evaluated with the agent id as the targeting key?
options: Flag services refuse to evaluate a flag without a user id attached
It makes the flag service answer faster thanks to its cache
It lets each agent switch tables from their settings page
The same agent gets the same table every visit, so groups compare
explain: The targeting key identifies the subject the flag is evaluated for, so a stable key keeps each agent in one group: the experience is consistent and the metrics of the two groups mean something. A random or per-page-load decision would flip agents between tables. The key is about consistency, not speed or permission.

q: A teammate creates the Tabs context with a default object, createContext({ selected: '', select: () => {} }), to "avoid null checks". What changes when someone renders <Tabs.Tab> outside <Tabs.Root>?
options: Nothing changes, because React throws in both versions anyway
It renders, clicks do nothing, and the bug ships silently
The tab silently creates its own Root and works on its own
TypeScript rejects the JSX at compile time with a context error
explain: With a default value, use returns the default outside a provider: measured, the tab rendered with aria-selected="false" and clicking changed nothing. With null and a guard, the same mistake throws "<Tabs.Tab> must be rendered inside <Tabs.Root>" during development. TypeScript cannot see where a component is rendered.

q: The first Tabs used hard-coded ids: id={'tab-' + value} and aria-controls={'panel-' + value}. The order detail page now shows Tabs in the main area and in a customer side panel, both with a details tab. What breaks, and what is the fix?
options: Nothing breaks: ids only need to be unique inside one component tree
React detects duplicate ids and renames the second set automatically
Duplicate ids point ARIA to the wrong panel; prefix them with useId
The second Tabs fails to render until it gets its own separate Root
explain: Ids must be unique in the whole document, and assistive technology follows aria-controls and aria-labelledby to the first match. useId gives each instance its own prefix: measured, two instances got _r_1_-tab-details and _r_2_-tab-details. React does not rewrite ids.

q: The refund confirmation is built on Base UI's Dialog with default options. The agent presses Escape. What happens to focus?
options: Focus stays on the last focused element inside the closed dialog
Focus moves to the top of the document
The dialog closes and focus returns to the Refund button
Escape is ignored until the agent clicks Cancel
explain: The Base UI docs say a modal dialog traps Tab inside, closes on Escape, and returns focus to the trigger or the previously focused element by default. Focus restoration is exactly the kind of behaviour that hand-made dialogs forget, which is the main argument for a headless primitive.

q: A team writes <Dialog.Trigger render={<BrandButton />}>Refund</Dialog.Trigger>, with function BrandButton({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) { return <button className="brand">{children}</button>; }. What is wrong?
options: BrandButton drops the props and ref Base UI passes to it
Nothing: Base UI attaches its handlers to the DOM node after render
The render prop only accepts native elements such as button
The label must be passed to BrandButton, not to Dialog.Trigger
explain: The Base UI docs state that the custom component must forward the ref and spread all received props on its DOM node; BrandButton ignores them, so the click handler, ARIA attributes and ref never reach the button. The section 1 Button, which spreads rest including ref, meets the requirement.

q: To darken one panel, a developer writes .panel { --gray-900: #f9fafb; }. What colour is the text of a <p> inside the panel?
options: #f9fafb, because the closest --gray-900 declaration always wins
#111827: --color-text was resolved on :root and inherited
The initial colour, because the variable reference is circular
It depends on which rule comes later in the file
explain: A custom property's var() is substituted on the element where it is declared, and descendants inherit the result. Measured in Chromium: the text stayed rgb(17, 24, 39). Redefine --color-text in the panel or theme scope instead of the primitive.

q: With the tokens file of section 5, an agent's OS is in dark mode and the back office sets <html data-theme="light"> from the agent's saved choice. What does the page use?
options: Dark tokens, because the media query is more specific than the attribute
Dark tokens, until the agent reloads the page
A mix of both: dark surface and light text
Light: the dark block no longer matches, so the :root values apply
explain: The dark media block applies only when data-theme is not "light", so the explicit choice wins. Measured in Chromium with emulated dark mode: text stayed rgb(17, 24, 39). Without the :not() guard, the media query would override the saved choice.

q: The storefront team wants @shop/ui styled with styled-components and its ThemeProvider, as their old code was. In Next.js App Router Server Components, which statement is true?
options: styled-components cannot render in Server Components, in any version
ThemeProvider works exactly the same in Server and Client Components
It renders there, but ThemeProvider is a pass-through: no context
Next.js converts ThemeProvider themes to CSS variables automatically
explain: The styled-components docs state native React Server Components support since 6.3, with ThemeProvider as a pass-through ("no context in RSC") and themes moved to CSS custom properties. Next.js documents React context as unsupported in Server Components. So themes must be CSS variables anyway, and static CSS is the simpler choice for a shared package.

q: The partner portal broke after a patch release renamed onChange to onValueChange. Which plan would you ship to fix the process?
options: Ask the agency to pin exact versions and stop upgrading the package
Restore onChange as deprecated, remove it in the next major
Keep the rename and publish a blog post that explains the change
Move the partner portal into the monorepo so it gets changes at once
explain: Fix the semver contract: bring the old prop back marked @deprecated with a development warning, then remove it in a major whose changeset explains the migration. Pinning forever stops all fixes, and the agency's repository is not yours to move.

q: CI fails on import { OrdersTable } from '../orders/orders-table' inside src/features/refunds. The refunds page needs to show the order lines. Which fix would you ship?
options: Add ./orders to the except list of the refunds zone in the config
Disable the rule for that line with an eslint-disable comment
Copy orders-table.tsx into features/refunds and adapt it
Compose both features in the page, or use the shared DataTable
explain: The rule exists so features stay independent; the page layer is where features meet, and a generic table belongs in the design system. Widening except or disabling the rule reintroduces the coupling that broke the customers page, and a copy drifts.

q: The agency proposes Module Federation so its partner screens load inside the back office at runtime. One back-office team ships weekly, and partners use their own portal. What do you answer?
options: Yes: Module Federation is the standard way to share a design system
Yes, and mark React as non-shared so each part gets its own copy
No: keep the portal a separate app using the published packages
No, because Module Federation only works with Next.js apps
explain: Micro-frontends pay off when several teams must deploy parts of the same page independently; here the portal is its own app, so a package is enough. Two copies of React cause the invalid hook call error (react.dev), which is why federated React must be a shared singleton. Module Federation works with Webpack and Rspack and lists Vite and Next.js integrations.

q: Which flag design would you ship for the new orders table?
options: A flag checked in each column and cell component, so each part can be rolled out alone
One page-level flag, default false, keyed by agent id, with an end date
A flag read once at build time from an environment variable
One flag per agent, created by hand in the flag service
explain: One page-level flag keeps two tested states, the safe default protects agents if the flag service fails, the agent id keeps groups stable, and an end date gets the flag and the old table deleted. Per-cell flags multiply untested combinations, and a build-time variable cannot be rolled back without a redeploy.

q: In the APG combobox pattern, where is DOM focus while the customer moves through the suggestions with the arrow keys?
options: On the input, while aria-activedescendant points to the active option.
On the active option, moved there with focus() on each arrow key press.
On the listbox, which needs tabindex="0" so that it can receive the arrow keys.
On the document body, until the customer presses Enter to pick an option.
explain: The APG says DOM focus stays on the combobox; assistive technology follows aria-activedescendant. Moving real focus to the option would stop the customer from typing, which is why the second option is wrong despite being a common implementation.

q: In Chromium, the list is open in this <input type="search"> and the customer presses Escape once. What happens?
options: The list closes and the browser also clears the text.
The list closes and the text stays, which is what the APG expects from a combobox.
Nothing happens, because Escape is not delivered to keydown handlers in a search input.
The list closes and the surrounding form is submitted with the current text.
explain: Measured with Playwright 1.64: Escape in a search input cleared the field. Calling event.preventDefault() while the list is open makes the first Escape only close it, and leaves the second to clear the field.

q: A mouse click on a suggestion picks nothing: the list just closes. The input closes the list in onBlur, and options only have onClick. What is the bug?
options: Options need tabindex="0", otherwise the browser does not deliver clicks to list items.
React does not fire onClick on elements that carry role="option", only on buttons and links.
mousedown blurs the input, and onBlur removes the list before click fires.
aria-selected must be true before an option can be clicked, so the first click only selects.
explain: Measured in Chromium: without the mousedown guard nothing was picked; with it, mouse clicks and touch taps picked the option. Adding tabindex would make it worse, since the option would take focus away from the input.
